unverified.quoted_phrase: Galileo observed Venus through its full cycle
unverified.description: Date compression. Galileo's Venus observations ran from the autumn of 1610 to February 1611; the gibbous and near-full phases that make the argument were observed from December 1610 into 1611, so a *full cycle* was not observed within 1610. The Royal Belgian Institute for Space Aeronomy page cited in our own sources gives 'During the autumn of 1610' through 'February 1611'. Dating the discovery to 1610 is standard usage; saying the full cycle was observed in 1610 is not.

unverified.quoted_phrase: The sea stands 21.4 km higher at the equator.
unverified.description: We use 'higher' in exactly the sense the page has just spent two sections denying. By the definition the refutation adopts — orthometric height, referred to the geoid — the equatorial sea is not higher than the polar sea at all: both lie on the same equipotential, and that is the whole point of the paragraph the heading introduces. The TLDR gets it right ('further from the centre at the equator than at the poles'), which shows the distinction was understood; the heading then hands a defender the line 'you equivocate on height in your own headline while accusing me of equivocating on level'.
unverified.recommendation: (i) The sea surface stands 21.4 km further from the Earth's centre at the equator than at the poles — and it is not, on that account, “higher”.

Either the 1849 sentence is not from the Old Bedford trials, or Rowbotham's own accounts differ between 1849 and 1865 — which is itself worth saying, since Schadewald notes 'his later accounts are contradictory'. Asserting the identification as settled, in the same document that prints the contrary evidence, is a cheap catch for a defender.

Note that the 1849 sentence quoted above names the New Bedford river, while the celebrated trials and the 1865 and 1881 books use the Old Bedford — one of several points on which, as Schadewald observes, Rowbotham's own accounts of what he did in the Fens do not agree with each other.

unverified.quoted_phrase: The 8-inches-per-mile-squared figure is the flat model's own arithmetic
unverified.description: Wrong as stated, and refuted by our own next sentence. Eight inches per mile squared is the drop predicted by a sphere of radius 6,371 km; the flat model predicts no drop at all. We then say, correctly, that Rowbotham took the figure from the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling — i.e. from the spherical model — which makes 'the flat model's own arithmetic' a claim about origin that our following sentence contradicts. (Verified: the 1865 Gutenberg text of Earth Not a Globe reprints the Britannica passage, including 'the curve of the Earth being the true level, and the tangent to it the apparent level' and 'it is raised eight inches very nearly above the Earth's surface at one mile's distance; four times as much, or 32 inches, at the distance of two miles'.)
unverified.recommendation: The 8-inches-per-mile-squared figure is the spherical model's arithmetic, adopted wholesale by the flat-earth argument as its own yardstick, and it is a prediction with a threshold.

unverified.quoted_phrase: A level surface is one of constant gravitational potential
unverified.description: Wrong in the one place it most matters. The geoid is a surface of constant GEOPOTENTIAL — gravitational potential plus the centrifugal potential of rotation. A surface of constant purely gravitational potential on a rotating Earth is not the sea surface and is not oblate, so as written the TLDR removes the very term that produces the bulge the next clause credits to rotation. The refutation gets it right ('an equipotential surface of the gravity field'), which is standard geodetic usage; the TLDR does not, and readers may never expand past it.
unverified.recommendation: A level surface is one of constant gravity potential — gravitation plus the centrifugal effect of the Earth's rotation — perpendicular to gravity everywhere, and on a rotating Earth that surface is curved:

unverified.quoted_phrase: Two further hardening moves if this argument recurs.
unverified.description: The preemptive answers the advocate's weakest demand and leaves its strongest one standing. The defence's sharpest line is not 'show me a photograph' but 'every direct measurement anyone has ever made of a water surface with an instrument in their hands returns a plane' — and the preemptive answers it with the Lapland and Peru arcs, which measured latitude with zenith sectors on land and are not measurements of a water surface at all. We own two direct instrumental measurements of standing water that return curvature and neither is named: Wallace's three-point 1870 repeat on the Bedford Level (already ours, at ARG-B03) and the levelling networks run between tide gauges, which is the same measurement at continental scale and is the evidentiary basis of every published orthometric height.
unverified.recommendation: Three further hardening moves if this argument recurs. First, meet the "it's all models with the radius baked in" charge with pre-satellite, pre-model measurements: the Lapland and Peru arcs (1735-40) measured a degree of latitude with theodolites and zenith sectors and found the degree longer near the pole, which is oblateness measured directly, a century and a half before anyone had a datum to assume. Second, answer the "instrument in hand on water" demand on its own ground, because it is the strongest form of the objection and the arcs do not touch it: Wallace's three-point 1870 repeat on the Bedford Level was a direct instrumental measurement of a standing-water surface and it returned the curvature (ARG-B03), and every national levelling network run between tide gauges is that same measurement at continental scale, which is why published orthometric heights exist at all. Third, decline the photograph demand explicitly rather than by omission - a photograph of a lake is an optical measurement and belongs to ARG-B04, where refraction is the controlling term; B01 rests on gravimetry, levelling and tide-gauge data precisely because those do not depend on light paths at all. Do not answer a hydrostatic argument with a picture.

The point actually being made is that none of the four depends on a long horizontal sightline through the atmosphere, where refraction is the controlling term; say that instead.

unverified.quoted_phrase: Radio-path engineering uses the same construction with
unverified.description: Symbol collision inside a single sentence, and it lands on the one attack surface our own advocate section identifies. The sentence defines the effective radius as R' = R/(1 - k) with the geodetic k of 0.13-0.14, then says radio engineering uses "the same construction with k = 4/3". Under the formula just given, k = 4/3 yields a negative radius. The radio k-factor is conventionally defined as the effective-radius multiplier itself, so radio's k = 4/3 corresponds to a refraction coefficient of about 0.25 in the geodetic convention. Our own cited source (Bislin, "Deriving Equations for Atmospheric Refraction") keeps the two apart, using k for the coefficient and a for the multiplier. The advocate block predicts precisely this line of attack — "a coefficient you are free to tune ... that is not a prediction, it is a spare parameter" — so leaving an undeclared change of definition in the paragraph that introduces the coefficient is a gift.
unverified.recommendation: Radio-path engineering uses the same device with a larger allowance, and with a different convention worth naming: the radio k-factor is defined as the multiplier itself rather than as the refraction coefficient, so its median value of 4/3 corresponds to a coefficient of about 0.25 in the geodetic notation used above. That is why ITU-R P.530 has designers draw straight lines over a 4/3-radius Earth.

unverified.quoted_phrase: the same 7/6 effective-radius rule surveyors and radio engineers use today

In the TLDR this is a flat misstatement of who uses what, and it is the sentence carrying the whole "the source printed the correction himself" finding, so it is the sentence most likely to be quoted back at us.
unverified.recommendation: the same effective-Earth-radius device surveyors and radio engineers still use — 7/6 for surveying, 4/3 for radio paths

unverified.quoted_phrase: The square of 24, multiplied by 8 inches, shows a declination of 384 feet.
unverified.description: Our quotation begins one sentence too late, and the omission hides the source's own care — the exact failure the hedge rule exists to prevent, committed by us in our own quoting. The preceding sentence at sacred-texts za14.htm reads: "Deducting 6 miles from 30, the distance from the horizon to Holyhead, on the one hand, and to Dublin Bay on the other, would be 24 miles." Without it a reader cannot tell where 24 came from, and Rowbotham appears to be naively squaring a distance — which directly contradicts the gloss two inches below, where we credit him with subtracting the observer's horizon first and call it "the correct geometric procedure". The one sentence that evidences our own central concession to him is the one we cut.

12. What would refute us. Four observations this model forbids and a flat plane permits, each cheap enough to attempt in an afternoon. (i) A ship's hull recovered by magnification alone at a fixed eye height — Carpenter's proof 63 asserts exactly this; the controlled form is to photograph, zoom by two and photograph again, then enlarge the first frame by two and compare the gap between waterline and horizon. unverified.quoted_phrase: which concedes that he does not know what the theory he is refuting predicts

The harness's charitable-interpretation rule asks us to distinguish what a person said from what we infer they believed, and the substantive point survives without the psychology: the prediction is determinate, and a ship's rail is not a level. Keeping the inference costs us the moral high ground on a page whose complaint about the other side is that it attributes to sources what the sources do not say.

unverified.quoted_phrase: projections built to make geodesics look straight

So the sentence explains an appearance by a mechanism that does not produce it. Any reader with a navigation background lands on this immediately, and it sits in the paragraph where we are otherwise at our strongest.

unverified.quoted_phrase: found three octopole planes orthogonal to the ecliptic
unverified.description: Misreads the abstract we are quoting from in the same sentence. Schwarz et al. (PRL 93:221301, 2004), verified verbatim: "The quadrupole plane and the three octopole planes are remarkably aligned. Three of these planes are orthogonal to the ecliptic at a level inconsistent with gaussian random statistically isotropic skies at 99.8% C.L. … The remaining octopole plane is orthogonal to the supergalactic plane at >99.9% C.L." "These planes" is the set of four — one quadrupole plane plus three octopole planes — so the three orthogonal to the ecliptic include the quadrupole plane, and the fourth plane, which is an octopole plane, goes with the supergalactic plane instead. We have converted "three of four planes, one of them the quadrupole's" into "three octopole planes". The quoted C.L. is correct and the substance of our argument is untouched, but this is a defender's free win in a paragraph we introduce as "the point that matters most", and it is the same error class already logged twice in corrections.json: attributing to a source a claim adjacent to but not identical with what it says.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "Schwarz et al. (2004) found the quadrupole plane and the three octopole planes remarkably aligned, with three of the four orthogonal to the ecliptic"

unverified.quoted_phrase: aligned with the Galactic pole at 0.8–1.6%
unverified.description: States the geometry backwards relative to the paper and to the rest of our own entry. Schwarz, Copi, Huterer & Starkman (CQG 33:184001, 2016), §2.2, verified from the arXiv PDF: the quadrupole-octopole plane is jointly perpendicular to the ecliptic plane at p = 2-4%, perpendicular to the Galactic pole at p = 0.8-1.6%, and aligned with the dipole direction at p = 0.09-0.37% (tightening to 0.06-0.23% after proper kinematic correction — which confirms our separate claim that correct removal of the kinematic quadrupole makes the alignments worse). Perpendicular to the Galactic POLE means lying in the Galactic PLANE, which is the opposite of "aligned with the Galactic pole". Our own surrounding text has it right twice — the TLDR says "the Galactic plane", and the sentence three lines above says "the plane of our galaxy" — so the entry contradicts itself in a list of quantitative results.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "perpendicular to the Galactic pole at 0.8–1.6%"

unverified.quoted_phrase: Its producer: the film “is not about geocentrism per se
unverified.description: A direct quotation from a living person, used to characterise his position as inconsistent, with no citation anywhere in the entry and with a presentation that implies the wrong provenance. The quote is real — I verified it as part of DeLano's statement of 9 April 2014 — but our source_wording field runs it on immediately after the press-release material ("framed by the same release as a question… Its producer: the film…"), which reads as though it came from the press release. It did not: I fetched the release and it contains no attributed statement from DeLano at all. E01's twelve sources contain no link to the statement. The note then draws a conclusion about him — "so the scoping is not consistent" — which is a characterisation of a living person's rhetorical consistency resting on an uncited quote, and a further paraphrase, "he has elsewhere called geocentrism a profoundly important part of the story", which is not his wording; what he actually wrote in the same statement is that "any film about the Copernican Principle that does not involve an examination of geocentrism is a fatally flawed film". The characterisation survives on his own words, but only once those words are quoted accurately and cited. Under the harness this escalates rather than auto-patches.

The two sentences scope the film narrowly and widely in turn; the list items keep only the wide reading." unverified.quoted_phrase: it is our own velocity written across the sky
unverified.description: The TLDR states as settled the one thing the entry elsewhere refuses to state as settled. The body concedes that the boosting measurement's 'error bars are wide enough that an intrinsic contribution of order 100 km/s is not excluded by this test alone', the straw_man field warns in our own voice against writing 'as though the whole subject were closed', and the file docstring makes E01's restraint rule binding here. The RMP 2025 Colloquium I verified puts the matter dipole excess above 5 sigma and says it demonstrates 'either the rest frames in which matter and radiation appear isotropic are not the same, or that there is an unexpected intrinsic anisotropy in at least one of them' - the second disjunct is a live possibility that the CMB dipole is not wholly kinematic. unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "it is, to the precision anyone has measured it, our own velocity written across the sky"

unverified.quoted_phrase: recomputed here, and equal to the measured amplitude to four figures
unverified.description: This is a definition dressed as a confirmation, and it is the first quantitative move in the refutation. Planck derives v = 369.82 km/s from the measured amplitude 3362.08 uK by dividing by T_0 - so recomputing beta*T_0 from that velocity and finding 3362.1 uK cannot test anything; it recovers the input. I ran it: 1.23357e-3 x 2.7255 K = 3362.095 uK, which is arithmetic on Planck's own quoted beta, not a check of it. The framing 'worth doing rather than trusting' invites the reader to treat it as verification, and the closing paragraph then lists it first among four pillars of the verdict: 'a signal whose amplitude matches our velocity to four significant figures'. A defender who spots this gets to say the page does not understand which of its own numbers are independent - unnecessarily, since the orbital modulation and the Doppler-boosting measurement are genuinely independent and do the work.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "recomputed here, and identical to the measured amplitude, because the two are the same statement: Planck's quoted velocity is that amplitude divided by T0. Nothing is confirmed by the arithmetic; what it fixes is the exchange rate, so that the independent tests below can be read as velocities." And in the closing paragraph, replace "a signal whose amplitude matches our velocity to four significant figures, whose annual variation" with "a signal whose annual variation".

unverified.description: We trim a scoping clause out of a quotation without an ellipsis, in the paragraph we call the clincher. Planck 2018 results I reads 'In the 2015 data release, photometric calibration from 30 to 353 GHz was based on the "orbital dipole"...' - I retrieved the sentence from the A&A full text. Our version silently promotes a statement about the 2015 release into an unscoped present-tense claim, which we then reinforce with 'Planck does not merely detect it. It calibrates on it.' The substance survives (the 2018 release also calibrates on the orbital dipole), so this is not a false claim - but it is precisely the compression manoeuvre this project exists to document, performed by us, on the load-bearing quotation of the entry.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "“In the 2015 data release, photometric calibration from 30 to 353 GHz was based on the ‘orbital dipole’, i.e., the modulation of the Solar dipole induced by the orbital motion of the satellite around the Solar System barycentre” — and the 2018 release calibrates the same way."

(2023) report - I checked the abstract - less than a 0.03% chance at 150 h^-1 Mpc and less than 0.003% at 200 h^-1 Mpc, which the paper deliberately states as probabilities rather than sigmas. Since the refutation's reply to bulk flows does not depend on the size of the tension - a bulk flow is a peculiar velocity field either way - there is nothing to gain by rounding it down and a straightforward accusation of shaving to invite.

The Local Group velocity is obtained by removing the Sun's orbit about the Galactic centre and the Galaxy's motion within the Local Group from the solar-dipole velocity, not by adding them back: v_LG = v_Sun(CMB) - v_Sun(LG). The point being made - that the two figures are one measurement plus known local corrections, not two independent results - is correct and worth keeping.

unverified.quoted_phrase: it is implicit in the word
unverified.short_summary: Straw-man block contradicts the compression block
unverified.description: The straw_man block locates a misrepresentation of cosmology inside the wording of a two-word item label, while the compression block argues in bold that 'these items are not assertions at all - they are topic labels, and a label cannot drop a hedge by itself. The assertion is supplied by the frame the labels sit in.' Both cannot hold: either a label can carry an assertion, and the compression analysis is wrong, or it cannot, and the straw man is not in the word 'alternatives'. The substance of the block - that the inhomogeneous alternative was proposed, developed and killed by cosmologists - is correct and verified, and only its location needs moving.

Standard cosmology is presented as though model-dependence were something cosmologists conceal and an outsider had noticed. The record is the reverse: the inhomogeneous alternative to dark energy was proposed by a cosmologist in Astronomy & Astrophysics, developed for a decade in Physical Review D and JCAP, and killed by cosmologists using BAO, the kSZ effect, the CMB spectrum and the local structure amplitude.

unverified.quoted_phrase: Its rough uniformity around the sky is a fact about the atmosphere being a shell we sit at the bottom of.
unverified.description: Factually wrong, and it concedes a premise we did not have to concede. Scintillation is strongly anisotropic in zenith angle: the amplitude rises steeply toward the horizon with the length of the air column (weak-turbulence theory gives roughly a sec(z) to the 11/6 scaling), which is why stars near the horizon visibly boil while a star at zenith is nearly steady, and it varies further with the high-altitude wind. What is approximately symmetric is the azimuthal distribution about the observer's vertical, not the distribution 'around the sky'. As written we grant the item's premise for scintillation while denying the identical premise for item 9 two paragraphs later - inconsistent inside one entry, and a defender will find it.
unverified.recommendation: Replace with: "It is not in fact uniform around the sky: the amplitude climbs steeply toward the horizon, where the light traverses a far longer column of air, which is why low stars visibly boil while a star overhead is nearly steady. What is roughly symmetric is the distribution in azimuth about the observer's own vertical — a fact about standing at the bottom of a spherical shell of air, and about that observer rather than about the Earth."

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Split verdict. The DEEP refutation body genuinely answers the source: it concedes outright that Michelson-Gale alone cannot assign the rotation to one body ("Taken against Michelson–Gale alone, this is unfalsifiable, and it is worth saying so"), and the compression block correctly names the force_upgraded drift from a disjunction to a proof. That part is clean. But the two fields that carry the argument at skim depth both state the fragment's claim AS the authors' own. render.py emits the cluster `name` as the H3 headline immediately followed by "first published by Robert Sungenis", and emits `basis` (clusters.py `note`, ending "Cited backwards.") as the summary line of section 3 — both visible without expanding anything. So a reader who never opens the accordion meets exactly the proposition our own compression block says Sungenis and Bennett did not assert, with a living author's name attached to it. That is the A10 failure (corrections.json, 2026-08-05) recurring one cluster over, at the level the harness says outranks paragraph nine. Marking hedge_rule_ok false on the headline, not on the refutation prose.
reviews.summary: A02's physics is sound and its numbers check out — MGP's 2010x1113 ft rectangle at 41°46', 0.236 predicted vs 0.230 observed, the 4AΩsinφ/λc arithmetic, Ashby's 207.4 ns, Bowden p. 80 and the Knodel quote all verified against primary sources. The problems are provenance and headline. The passage locator says "Vol. I, ch. 10 … p. 191", but that chapter is Volume II of the 7th ed. (2013), starting p. 157, with "Michelson-Gale: Claims and Responses" at pp. 189–192 — the same wrong-volume error the standing facts and two prior corrections already flag, and the sources list compounds it by labelling the Vol. II scan "Vol. I". The cluster headline and basis line attribute the stationary-Earth claim to Sungenis and Bennett, which our own compression block says they did not make; the TLDR's uniqueness claim is contradicted by our own A12 and A06; and the refutation's pivotal move treats the geocentrist escape as optical-only when the same chapter has sections on the Foucault pendulum and atmospheric circulation and the next chapter is an aether model built to supply that mechanism.

holes.description: False on our own data, in the field with the highest reader impact, and the first thing a defender picks off. The list contains other named experiments that returned positive readings: cluster A12 is 'Dayton Miller detected a real aether drift that was suppressed' — a claimed non-null fringe shift, which is the obvious counterexample any geocentrist raises instantly; item 11 (A06) is the Foucault pendulum, whose signal our own refutation later relies on; item 225 (A07) is 'Ring laser gyro corrections' and item 229 (A19) 'Gyrocompass sky-locked', both positive instruments; and item 281, inside A02 itself, is 'Sagnac proves apparatus rotation'. The sentence also undercuts the refutation's own closing argument, which depends on several non-optical instruments having detected the same Ω.

holes.quoted_phrase: The escape is tailored to an optical experiment
holes.description: This is the pivot of the whole refutation ('Why it closes in combination') and it understates the source's position, which is the weakest link a well-informed defender goes for first. The TOC of the very chapter we cite shows Sungenis and Bennett address exactly the instruments we say their escape cannot reach: 'The Foucault Pendulum' at p. 172 and 'Atmospheric Circulation is Anti-Geokinetic' at p. 232, both inside Vol. II ch. 10 Part 1 'Does the Earth Rotate?'; and the next chapter, ch. 11 at p. 421, is 'ALFA: Absolute Lab Frame/Flexible Aether Model' — a mass-and-aether model constructed to supply precisely the mechanism we assert is missing. Saying 'a hypothesis about a rotating optical medium has no mechanism by which to deflect a pendulum bob or a hurricane' answers a version of the reply the source does not hold. The correct answer is already in our next sentence (broadened that far, it is the standard account with the labels exchanged) and in the advocate block's Machian preemptive — the setup just needs to stop pretending the source left the pendulum alone.
holes.recommendation: Replace the opening of that paragraph with: "The escape does not stay optical, and the source knows it: the same chapter answers the Foucault pendulum (p. 172) and atmospheric circulation (p. 232), and the next chapter offers an aether model, ALFA, intended to carry them. So take the strong form. If a rotating cosmos is to deflect a pendulum bob, a hurricane and a gyrocompass, it must drag the local inertial frame with it — and once the local inertial frame turns relative to the ground at 15.041° per hour, that is what 'the Earth rotates' means operationally. Each of those instruments independently returns Ω = 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, the value the light ring gave. The broadened hypothesis reproduces every one of them and forbids nothing, because it is the ordinary account with the labels exchanged, and the shell's angular velocity has to be set by hand to the number already measured."

reviews.hedge_rule_note: FAILS. Two ways. (1) The compression block's `source_wording` is not the source. It quotes a Sungenis & Bennett sentence about what the experiment "was called", while the cluster's recorded originator is van der Kamp, De Labore Solis (1988) — and van der Kamp asserts the physical claim outright. From the PDF we already cite: p. 40, "the Earth is at rest relative to space ... then the starry dome is revolving relative to us"; ch. title p. 19, "Geocentric? Heliocentric? The Janus-faced 'Aberration' Can't Tell"; and per Bouw's obituary of him (geocentricity.com/ba1/no084/obits.pdf, the third item in our own sources list) "Walter believed [aberration] implied a small universe 60 light days in radius." So the drift we publish — category_shifted, a historiographical claim turned physical — is derived from a downstream restatement, not from the originator, who makes the physical claim himself. (2) Worse, refutation step 3, the step our own text calls "fatal", is aimed at a model van der Kamp explicitly does not hold. We write that on a stationary Earth "there is no relative velocity between source and observer, so there is no aberration to have a magnitude at all." His model has the starry dome revolving relative to us, in a universe sized (60 light-days) precisely so the dome's tangential speed stays sub-luminal. He took the step we say the argument never takes. The compression note's sentence "The refutation above answers the source's version" is therefore false as published. Note also the genuine drift we are missing: van der Kamp concedes both escape routes — "It was, as said, feasible to explain this strange phenomenon with Fresnel's dragging coefficient" (p. 34) and Einstein "wonderfully saves the phenomena" (p. 46) — and argues from underdetermination. A conceded point re-used as a proof item is the R01 pattern, force_upgraded, and that is the honest verdict here.

holes.quoted_phrase: On a stationary Earth there is no relative velocity between source and observer, so there is no aberration to have a magnitude at all.
holes.description: scripts/deep.py:146. The refutation's third step — the one our own text calls fatal — attacks a naive stationary-Earth model in which nothing moves. Van der Kamp's model has the starry dome revolving relative to a resting Earth, so relative velocity is present and he does have an account of aberration. A defender opens De Labore Solis at p. 40 and reads 'the Earth is at rest relative to space ... then the starry dome is revolving relative to us', notes the chapter at p. 19 titled 'Geocentric? Heliocentric? The Janus-faced Aberration Can't Tell', and adds Bouw's obituary line that 'Walter believed [aberration] implied a small universe 60 light days in radius'. Our sentence is then visibly false of the source, our claim that 'this is the step the argument never takes' is visibly false, and the section reads as a debunk of a position nobody defends. He can do this using two of the six links we ourselves publish. The same error is carried at the highest-visibility point on the page, in the TLDR phrase 'aberration exists at all only because the Earth moves', and in the ARG-A03 basis line in scripts/clusters.py, 'Aberration existing at all is itself evidence Earth moves.'
holes.recommendation: Replace the third paragraph's middle with: "Stellar aberration is the annual ~20.5-arcsecond elliptical wobble Bradley discovered in 1729, and it is produced by the observer's motion, not the source's — a star's own velocity shifts where it appears only through light-travel time, which is why every star shows the same aberration constant regardless of its distance or its proper motion (de Sitter's binary-star argument, 1913). Van der Kamp saw the problem and paid for it. His geocentric account keeps aberration by having the starry dome revolve around a resting Earth, and to keep the dome's tangential speed below c he had to shrink the universe: Bouw's obituary records that 'Walter believed [aberration] implied a small universe 60 light days in radius.' That is the price of the model, and it is the refutation. In a revolving-dome cosmos the aberration angle would be the star's tangential speed over c, so it would grow with distance without limit; observed aberration is flat at 20.5 arcseconds for the nearest star and the most distant quasar alike, which is what observer motion predicts and what source motion cannot. A 60-light-day universe is also excluded by the parallaxes Gaia DR3 publishes for ~1.468 billion sources. The argument takes an experiment that measures a consequence of the Earth's orbital motion, shows the magnitude is medium-independent, and reports this as evidence the Earth does not move." Change the TLDR's closing clause to "and the aberration it measures is produced by the observer's motion, which is why the geocentric version of the argument needs a universe 60 light-days across." Make the matching change to the clusters.py basis line.

holes.quoted_phrase: The refutation above answers the source's version
holes.description: scripts/deep.py:195. The compression block sets source_wording to a Sungenis & Bennett sentence about what the experiment 'was called' and concludes category_shifted, but the cluster's own originator is van der Kamp, who makes the physical claim flatly. The published drift verdict is therefore measured against the wrong text, and the claim that our refutation answers the source's version is untrue — see the hedge_rule_note. A reader checks our own originator field (van der Kamp, De Labore Solis, 1988) against our own source_wording field (Sungenis, on what the experiment was called), finds they are different books by different authors eighteen years apart, then reads van der Kamp asserting that if no change is observed the Earth is at rest, and concludes that our flagship worked example of the hedge rule — cited as such in review/curmudgeon.md, scripts/_b7_C07.py and scripts/_b7_E13.py — was itself produced by comparing the list against a fragment of the wrong source.
holes.recommendation: Set source_wording to van der Kamp's own sentences: "'if no increase is observed ... the Earth is at rest and the starry dome is revolving relative to us' (p. 40); ch. heading p. 19, 'Geocentric? Heliocentric? The Janus-faced Aberration Can't Tell'; 'It was, as said, feasible to explain this strange phenomenon with Fresnel's dragging coefficient' (p. 34); Einstein's theory 'wonderfully saves the phenomena' (p. 46)." Set drift_type to "force_upgraded" and replace the note with: "The originator does not claim the null proves a motionless Earth on its own. He concedes in the same book that Fresnel's coefficient explains it and that relativity 'wonderfully saves the phenomena', and argues instead that aberration is Janus-faced — that it cannot decide between a moving Earth and a revolving heaven. That is an underdetermination argument, and it is a real one. On the list it becomes proof item 14, 'Airy's failure to detect starlight motion': a concession that no experiment discriminates, re-used as an experiment that discriminates. The same trade documented at ARG-R01. A second, smaller shift runs through the downstream restatement in Sungenis & Bennett, where the claim becomes historiographical — the experiment 'was called' a failure, and the name shows what its contemporaries felt — which is checkable and fails; but the physical claim on the list descends from van der Kamp directly, not from that sentence."

holes.quoted_phrase: subtitle, and ch. “The Unfailing Import of Airy's Failure”, p. 52
holes.description: scripts/deep.py:91. The passage block sets work to WRK-VDK-1988 with a locator inside De Labore Solis, so render.py prints the blockquote under 'De Labore Solis: Airy's Failure Reconsidered, 1988' with a work link and 'p. 52', while our own gloss one line later says the quote is from Sungenis & Bennett, Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I. Separately the sentence could not be located: an exact-phrase search returns nothing, and the Vol. I table of contents places 'The Experiments of George Airy and James Bradley' at ch. 5 p. 249, nowhere near p. 52 — so the locator fits neither candidate work.

If the sentence cannot be located in the volume on a page check, replace it with a quotation that can be, or drop the passage block rather than publish an unlocated quotation.

holes.quoted_phrase: Bouw's obituary credits him with the coinage by name
holes.description: scripts/deep.py:106. The cited obituary does not credit van der Kamp with coining 'Airy's failure'. geocentricity.com/ba1/no084/obits.pdf (Biblical Astronomer no. 84, Spring 1998) contains no sentence using 'coined', 'term' or 'phrase'; the only relevant sentence is 'Through Walter's pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure and the Michelson-Morley experiments, Walter may truly be called the father of modern geocentricity.' That credits an interpretation, not a coinage, and it uses the phrase as already current, which is weak evidence in the other direction. This is the same class of error as the first entry in review/corrections.json — a cited source that does not say what we attributed to it — and the overstatement is repeated in the ARG-A03 basis line in scripts/clusters.py ('Bouw credits van der Kamp with it') and in the PER-VANDERKAMP record ('Coined “Airy's failure”'; 'Bouw's obituary of him credits the coinage by name').

Walter may truly be called the father of modern geocentricity” — and the earliest use we have been able to document is his own 1988 subtitle." Make the matching edits to the cluster basis line and to PER-VANDERKAMP in scripts/people.py.

holes.quoted_phrase: fixed by the relative velocity of source and observer
holes.description: scripts/deep.py:130. Stellar aberration is a function of the observer's velocity, not of the source-observer relative velocity. Stated the second way it is wrong physics and it concedes exactly the equivalence a revolving-dome geocentrism needs. It also contradicts our own refutation three paragraphs later: a defender quotes our steelman ('fixed by the relative velocity of source and observer') against our refutation ('no relative velocity between source and observer') and observes that if relative velocity is what matters then van der Kamp's revolving dome supplies it and reproduces aberration. The physics fails on its own terms too — a source's velocity does not aberrate its apparent direction (de Sitter 1913), which is why the aberration constant is the same 20.5″ for every star irrespective of proper motion or distance.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "fixed by the observer's velocity — a source's own motion shifts its apparent place only through light-travel time, which is why every star shows the same aberration constant — so a refracting medium downstream of that transformation cannot alter it". Make the same correction to the ARG-A03 basis line in scripts/clusters.py, which currently reads "aberration depends on relative source-observer velocity, not on a medium downstream of it".

holes.quoted_phrase: Van der Kamp is also right about something more general and more serious
holes.description: scripts/deep.py:116. The steelman reaches DEEPER but not KERNEL. It omits the two things that make van der Kamp's case strongest: that he has a positive account of aberration (revolving dome, universe 60 light-days in radius, per Bouw's obituary) and that he concedes in the same book that Fresnel's coefficient makes the null 'feasible to explain' (p. 34) and that Einstein 'wonderfully saves the phenomena' (p. 46). As written we present him as making a bare underdetermination point, so our 'why it doesn't save the claim' answers a version we constructed — and the omitted material is precisely what sets up the reply our own advocate block already rates 4 out of 5.
holes.recommendation: Append to the steelman description: "He is also not merely raising a philosophical objection: he offers a rival account. In his model the Earth rests and the starry dome revolves around it, which is where aberration comes from, and he accepts the consequence — Bouw records that van der Kamp 'believed [aberration] implied a small universe 60 light days in radius.' He concedes in the same book that Fresnel's coefficient makes the null 'feasible to explain' (p. 34) and that Einstein's theory 'wonderfully saves the phenomena' (p. 46). His claim is not that those explanations fail; it is that they are not forced, and that aberration is Janus-faced — it cannot tell the two cosmologies apart. Stated that way the argument is a serious one, and it deserves a quantitative answer rather than a rhetorical one."

holes.quoted_phrase: its earliest documented use is van der Kamp's 1988 subtitle

The argument's implied opponent is a physics that was blindsided by Airy's null and has been embarrassed by it since. reviews.summary: A03 is the page's flagship hedge-rule example and it fails its own rule. The compression block compares the list item against a downstream Sungenis sentence rather than against van der Kamp, the originator we ourselves record, and van der Kamp makes the physical claim outright, so the published category_shifted verdict is measured against the wrong text. Worse, refutation step 3, which our text calls fatal, asserts that a stationary Earth has no relative velocity between source and observer; van der Kamp's model has the starry dome revolving and sizes the universe at 60 light-days to keep it sub-luminal, a fact recorded in the Bouw obituary we already link and never read past. The REFUTED verdict holds and gets stronger once fixed, because aberration tracks the observer's velocity and is flat at 20.5 arcseconds for every star, which no revolving-dome model reproduces, but the argument must be rebuilt around that and four citation problems fixed alongside it.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Targeting is correct: sections 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the refutation answer the 1881 chapter at the strength Rowbotham wrote it, and the passage block quotes him at length rather than paraphrasing the list. Two caveats, neither of which flips the flag. (a) The reverse-direction failure IS present: the compression block's headline drift and the TLDR's opening are aimed at our own cluster title ("No measurable stellar parallax", authored by us at scripts/clusters.py:46) and at Dubay's proof 19, which is not one of the 461 items - see hole 2. (b) More seriously, our reading of the source was incomplete rather than mis-aimed: we quoted p. 86 but not pp. 79-81 of the same chapter, and built the entry's central charge on the absence of something that is seven pages earlier - see hole 1. The hedge rule is about aiming at the source; we aimed there and read only part of it.

holes.quoted_phrase: No experiment follows.
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:224 (and TLDR line 51, gloss line 94, steelman line 167, verdict line 339, docstring line 36). Our load-bearing charge - that Rowbotham asserts the three-foot base line "as the result of actual experiment" and then supplies no experiment - is contradicted by the same chapter of the same edition we quote and link. Evidence: sacred-texts za21.htm, pp. 79-81, seven pages before our own quoted p. 86: "Take two carefully-bored metallic tubes, not less than six feet in length, and place them one yard asunder, on the opposite sides" of a wooden frame, axes adjusted so they "shall be perfectly parallel to each other", directed at "some notable fixed star, a few seconds previous to its meridian time", an observer at each tube - "The moment the star appears in the tube A, T, let a loud knock or other signal be given, to be repeated by the observer at the tube B, T, when he first sees the same star" - with the stated result that "a distinct period of time will elapse between the signals given", i.e. the star "is not visible at the same moment by two parallel lines of sight...when only one yard asunder". One yard IS three feet; the p. 86 sentence is a back-reference to that experiment, not a bare assertion. So "No apparatus" is simply false, and the same false claim carries into the two fields a skimming reader actually sees: the TLDR ("the right discriminating test, asserted with no experiment attached") and the verdict paragraph ("was published without an experiment"), plus the gloss ("an experiment he does not describe") and the steelman ("he offers no observation for it"). What survives is narrower and needs saying separately: he names no star, no date, no observer and no measured angle. The damaging part is that the true refutation is stronger than ours - the apparatus exists and cannot possibly measure the quantity in dispute, so what it detects is its own construction error.
holes.recommendation: Replace "No experiment follows. No apparatus, no star, no date, no observer, no number." with: "He does supply an experiment, and it is the weak point. Seven pages earlier, at pp. 79-81, he sets out the apparatus: two bored metallic tubes at least six feet long, fixed “one yard asunder” on a wooden frame with their axes made “perfectly parallel,” sighted on a bright star near meridian transit by two observers who knock when the star enters their tube. His reported result is that “a distinct period of time will elapse between the signals given.” That is the three-foot base line of p. 86. It is also the whole problem. Two genuinely parallel tubes one yard apart, sighted on a star, must show it simultaneously: the real parallax over one yard is 1.7 × 10<sup>−12</sup> arcsec, while a naked eye behind a six-foot tube resolves no better than about a minute of arc — some ten orders of magnitude coarser. A lag between the two knocks therefore measures one thing only: the residual angle between the two tubes’ axes, with the star’s diurnal drift of roughly 15 arcsec per second of time converting that misalignment into a delay he can hear. He built an instrument that reads out its own construction error and recorded the reading as a stellar parallax. He names no star, no date, no observer and no measured angle, and describes no null-alignment control. The experiment is real; what it detects is the frame." Then fix the four downstream instances: TLDR line 51 to "— the right discriminating test — and he backed it with two six-foot tubes set a yard apart, an instrument ten orders of magnitude too coarse to run it."; gloss lines 94-95 to "he answers them with an experiment whose apparatus cannot resolve the angle in dispute"; steelman line 167 to "and the only observation he offers for it is a pair of hand-aligned tubes"; verdict line 339 to "is wrong by eleven orders of magnitude, and the experiment offered for it measures the alignment of his own tubes."

holes.quoted_phrase: The dominant drift is a straight reversal.
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:408. The block publishes drift_type="reversed", which scripts/render.py:45 maps to the bolded heading "The item states the opposite of its source", printed directly beneath a blockquote of the six list items. None of the six states the opposite of Rowbotham. Items 5, 37, 103 and 264 ("Lack of stellar parallax in early measurements", "No naked-eye parallax", "Inconsistent stellar parallax") are scoped statements Rowbotham would endorse - our own note says so - and items 8 and 240 are absent from him entirely. The note's own item-by-item tally, three paragraphs down, assigns 5/37/264 to hedge_dropped-shading-into-force_upgraded, 8/240 to unsourced_addition and 103 to faithful: zero items to "reversed". The reversal is manufactured from two things that are not the list - our own cluster name at scripts/clusters.py:46, and Dubay's proof 19, a downstream artefact outside the 461-item specimen (verified verbatim at flatearth.ws/eric-dubay). On a page whose product is provenance discipline, a drift verdict our own evidence contradicts is the one thing a hostile reader can falsify without leaving the page.
holes.recommendation:
Set drift_type="hedge_dropped" and replace the note's opening paragraph with: "

The dominant drift is a qualifier doing no work. Items 5, 37 and 264 keep their scope — early measurements, naked-eye parallax — and as written are simply true; what changes is that a scoped historical observation is entered as a numbered proof of a stationary Earth, where the reader supplies the generalisation the sentence withholds. Note what the list does not do: no item here denies that parallax is measured. That denial appears downstream, in Dubay’s proof 19 — “not a single inch of parallax can be detected in the stars, proving we have not moved at all” — which is a straight reversal of Rowbotham, who prints 0″.98 and 0″.35. It also appeared in the name we first gave this cluster. We have renamed it; a summary title that overstates the items it summarises is the same fault we are documenting.

" Rename the cluster at scripts/clusters.py:46 from "No measurable stellar parallax" to "Stellar parallax reassigned to a three-foot base line", and change the TLDR opening (line 47) from "The cluster is titled “no measurable stellar parallax” and its own source prints the measurements" to "This cluster reads as a denial that parallax is measurable. Its own source prints the measurements".

holes.quoted_phrase: a single star as wide as Saturn’s orbit
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:137, repeated in the refutation at line 235 ("as wide as Saturn’s orbit, on Graney’s reconstruction"). We credit a named living scholar with a quantitative reconstruction neither cited source contains. Checked directly: the word "Saturn" does not occur anywhere in Graney & Grayson, arXiv 1003.4918. Graney's Church Life Journal article - our other citation - gives the figure as "the Copernican motion of the Earth makes any first-magnitude star well larger than the whole orbit of the Earth", and contains no Saturn comparison at all. It also confirms Ingoli's "the fixed stars to be of such size, as they may surpass or equal the size of the orbit circle of the Earth itself", which we quote in the very next clause - so our own two adjacent figures differ by a factor of 9.5 while being presented as one reconstruction. Under our own severity rubric this is a claim about what a source says that the source does not say; it stops short of critical only because it sits inside a historical steelman rather than in the verdict path.
holes.recommendation: At lines 136-137 replace "on Graney and Grayson’s reconstruction, a single star as wide as Saturn’s orbit, and" with "on Graney’s reconstruction, any first-magnitude star well larger than the whole orbit of the Earth, and". At line 235 replace "as wide as Saturn’s orbit, on Graney’s reconstruction" with "larger than the whole orbit of the Earth, on Graney’s reconstruction".

holes.quoted_phrase: 3rd ed., rev. and enl. (London: Day, 1881)
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:57. The passage locator names the wrong publisher for the 1881 third edition, in the one field whose job is edition-level bibliographic precision, against a scan we link one screen away. The title page of that scan (sacred-texts.com/earth/za/za00.htm) reads: "Third Edition, Revised and Enlarged. LONDON: SIMPKIN, MARSHALL, AND CO. [1881]". "Day" appears nowhere as publisher; the nearest thing on the page is "THE ILLUSTRATIONS BY GEORGE DAVEY, F.Z.S.", the likely source of the slip. This entry's rhetorical weight rests on our having caught an edition error the movement's own genealogy missed, so a misnamed imprint in the correcting citation is expensive out of proportion to its size. It propagates: the identical string appears at scripts/works.py:24 (WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1865 imprint) and twice in scripts/_b6_B04.py (lines 20 and 93). Everything else in the locator checks: ch. III runs pp. 62-87 (ch. IV begins p. 88), the title is exact, and the parallax material is pp. 82-87.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "3rd ed., rev. and enl. (London: Simpkin, Marshall & Co., 1881), ch. III “The Earth No Axial or Orbital Motion”, pp. 82–87. Not in the 1865 first book edition — see gloss." Apply the same substitution at scripts/works.py:24 and scripts/_b6_B04.py:20 and :93.

holes.quoted_phrase: the stars with the largest proper motions are the nearest ones
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:312-313. A bolded claim states a statistical tendency as a rule, and the two stars cited in the next two sentences break it. Proper motion is transverse velocity divided by distance, so it tracks proximity only because stellar space velocities are broadly comparable; it is not monotonic in distance. Our own examples show this immediately: Barnard's Star is given the largest proper motion, 10.3"/yr at 5.9629 ly, while Proxima - which we then call "the nearest star" at 4.2465 ly - moves only 3.85"/yr. Sirius, at 8.6 ly, moves 1.34"/yr, an eighth of Barnard's despite being far nearer than most fast movers. A defender needs one counterexample and the paragraph hands him one.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "large proper motions are found almost exclusively among the nearest stars, because proper motion is transverse velocity divided by distance and stellar space velocities are broadly comparable".

holes.quoted_phrase: Henderson's 0.98 arcsec for Alpha Centauri
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:48. The TLDR credits 0″.98 to Henderson, which is neither his published figure nor what our own refutation says. Rowbotham's text reads "The parallax thus assigned α Centauri, is so very nearly a whole second in amount (0″.98)" - a value carried in from his secondary source, not from Henderson's announcement. Our own refutation section 2 (line 203) states, on ESA's authority, "Henderson published one arcsecond for α Centauri against a modern 0.75″", and the ESA page confirms "He reported a parallax of one arc second for the star Alpha Centauri"; Henderson's 1839 paper is usually cited nearer 1.16″. The reader therefore gets two different numbers for the same man, with the wrong one in the field the harness says outranks paragraph nine. The substantive point - that the source prints measurements - is untouched.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "the 0.98 arcsec his own source assigns to Alpha Centauri".

holes.quoted_phrase: Two more items (5 and 37/264)
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:329. The structural tally in section 7 counts items 37 and 264 in two categories, so the cluster of six adds up to seven: two are the duplicate pair (37, 264); "Two more items (5 and 37/264)" are true-with-scope; two (8, 240) are unsourced; one (103) is faithful. 2+2+2+1 = 7. The paragraph's whole argument is that the list was assembled carelessly, which makes an arithmetic slip inside it unusually cheap to quote back at us.
holes.recommendation: Replace "Two more items (5 and 37/264) are true statements with their scope intact" with "Three of the six (5, 37 and 264) are true statements with their scope intact".

holes.quoted_phrase: misattributes the whole objection to Tycho Brahe
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:387-388. We say Dubay "misattributes" the no-parallax objection to Tycho Brahe, but Tycho did make that argument and our own steelman and refutation section 3 spend two paragraphs crediting him with it. Dubay's proof 19 opens "Tycho Brahe famously argued against the heliocentric theory in his time, positing that if the Earth revolved around the Sun, the change in relative position of the stars after 6 months orbital motion could not fail to be seen" - historically correct. The real fault is the one the same sentence goes on to name: the omission of the stellar-angular-diameter premise that made Tycho's version work and that diffraction later dissolved. Calling a correct attribution a misattribution is a self-contradiction inside one entry, and it blunts the criticism sitting beside it.
holes.recommendation: Replace "misattributes the whole objection to Tycho Brahe without mentioning" with "rests the whole objection on Tycho Brahe without mentioning".

holes.quoted_phrase: a later reduction of his own data moved it further out, to 0.360″
holes.description: scripts/_b6_A05.py:204-205. Two small problems. First, 0.360″ is not a re-reduction of the 1838 data: the record gives Bessel's 1838 result as a centre point of 313.6 +/- 13.6 mas and his best later value, 360.2 +/- 12.1 mas, as coming from observations made in 1849 - new data. Second, it sits inside the paragraph reconstructing what "a well-informed sceptic in 1849 could reasonably have said", so a figure derived from that same year's observations is doing anachronistic work in a passage whose entire point is dating what was available when. We apply exactly that standard to Rowbotham three paragraphs later, which makes the slip worth fixing even at minor severity.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "and his own later series, observed in 1849, moved the centre value further out still, to 0.360″", and relocate the clause to a following sentence beginning "Convergence was slow even afterwards:".

citation_failures: FAILED - scripts/_b6_A05.py sources[10] and [11] (Graney & Grayson, arXiv 1003.4918; Graney, Church Life Journal) for the claim "a single star as wide as Saturn's orbit". "Saturn" does not occur in the arXiv paper; the Church Life Journal article gives "well larger than the whole orbit of the Earth". The paper's other uses DO check out: Galileo's 4" average fixed star, Hevelius's Sirius at 6", Cassini's Sirius at 5", and Airy 1835 on diffraction rings.

PARTIAL - scripts/_b6_A05.py sources[6] (ESA, "A history of astrometry, Part II"). It does NOT state Struve's 1837 Vega value of 0.125" - it says only that the 1837 data "were not considered highly reliable". The source label as written over-credits the page.

reviews.summary: The verdict REFUTED holds and most of the entry is well sourced, but its central charge is wrong: we say Rowbotham introduces the three-foot base line as "the result of actual experiment" and then supplies no experiment, when the apparatus is described in full seven pages earlier in the same chapter (pp. 79-81: two six-foot bored tubes "one yard asunder" on a wooden frame, parallel axes, two observers, knock signals, a reported time lag). That false claim appears six times, including the TLDR and the verdict sentence, and the true answer is stronger than the one we published - the instrument is roughly ten orders of magnitude too coarse to see the angle in dispute, so what its "distinct period of time" measures is the misalignment of his own tubes. Second, drift_type="reversed" renders as "The item states the opposite of its source" above six items that do no such thing; the reversal is imported from our own cluster title and from Dubay's proof 19, and the block's own item-by-item tally assigns zero items to it. Also: "as wide as Saturn's orbit" appears in neither cited Graney source (the figure is Earth's orbit), and the 1881 publisher is Simpkin, Marshall & Co., not Day.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: PASS, and this is the target's strongest feature. I put the list fragments ("Atmospheric coupling unexplained", "No wind drag from 67,000 mph orbit", "No visible rotation of atmosphere or clouds") beside Rowbotham's own sentences in the 1881 third edition, ch. III, and both halves of the rule are satisfied. The source's sentence — verified word-for-word at sacred-texts za21.htm, p. 74: "Hence we are compelled to conclude that if the earth revolves, the atmosphere revolves also, and in the same direction" — is the reverse of the fragment's premise, and drift_type="reversed" is the right call. Our refutation answers the source, not the fragment: it opens "Start where Rowbotham starts, because it is not where the list puts him", quotes his concession, and puts the weight on the arithmetic (a ~10 m/s stratum riding a ~465 m/s carrier) and on the hemispheric sign reversal, which is what actually engages his claim that everything suspended in the air "must of necessity partake of its eastward motion" (also verified verbatim, p. 74). The second clause is honoured too: the circulating items (jet streams, calm belts, superrotation, airglow) are each answered rather than waved off as misquotation. Two qualifications, neither of which flips the verdict. (1) The compression note's self-assessment is now stale — it says "The refutation opens by answering the fragment", which was true of the draft it was written against on 2026-08-05 and is false of the current text; that is hole 5. (2) The `drifted=True` verdict is honest and load-bearing, not an avoidance: the note names the specific inserted figure (67,000 mph, orbital, absent from an argument about axial rotation) rather than asserting drift generically.

holes.quoted_phrase: with a latitude-dependent precession matching f = 2Ωsinφ
holes.description: Wrong by a factor of two, and it conflates two different quantities in a paragraph whose whole job is to show we know the physics. The Coriolis parameter is f = 2Ωsinφ, correctly stated earlier in the same refutation ("The strength of the deflection is f = 2Ωsinφ"). The precession rate of a Foucault pendulum's plane of swing is Ωsinφ — half of f. Confirmed against the standard statement of the pendulum's precession rate and rotation period (Wikipedia, Foucault pendulum: rate = Ω sin φ, full turn in ~32 h at the latitude of Paris; the 2Ωsinφ figure would give ~16 h, which is not what the Paris pendulum did). This is the single most screenshot-able error in the entry: a defender does not need to know any meteorology to use it, only the pendulum formula, and it sits in the paragraph headed "Routine measurement" where we are asserting our own rigour.
holes.recommendation: Foucault demonstrated rotation directly in Paris on 3 February 1851, and the demonstration is quantitative: the plane of swing precesses at Ωsinφ — half the Coriolis parameter — so a full turn takes about 32 hours at the latitude of Paris, slows towards the equator, and never completes there at all.

holes.quoted_phrase: All thirteen items descend from these pages
holes.description: A universal attribution claim that our own compression block contradicts on the same page, and that fails on at least two of the thirteen. Item 54 is "No wind drag from 67,000 mph orbit"; the compression note says of it, correctly, that the figure and the mechanism are "a figure and a mechanism absent from his atmospheric argument, which concerns axial rotation only." Item 271 is "Lightning frequency sun path" — a diurnal-electrical claim with no counterpart anywhere in Rowbotham's ch. III atmosphere pages (pp. 73-77), and it is also the one item of the thirteen that the refutation never addresses at all, not even to mark it underspecified as it properly does for item 241, airglow. This is the exact failure logged in corrections.json for ARG-R06 on 2026-08-02: cluster-level attribution applied to every item in the cluster without checking each against the source. A critic assembling "this site contradicts itself" gets the gloss and the compression note from the same rendered entry.
holes.recommendation: Eleven of the thirteen items are recognisable descendants of these pages, and Rowbotham's chain of reasoning is more careful than most of his successors'. Two are not: item 54 imports a 67,000 mph orbital figure into an argument that is about axial rotation only, and item 271, Lightning frequency sun path, has no counterpart here or elsewhere in the chapter and is carried in this cluster on subject-matter proximity alone. He grants that a rotating Earth would carry its atmosphere with it — his grinding-stone experiment is offered as proof that it would.

holes.quoted_phrase: Nothing needs to grip it.
holes.description: The weakest link in the entry, and it is weak because our own steelman two paragraphs earlier supplies the counterexample. We tell the reader that Venus's atmosphere is gravitationally bound, formed with the planet, and nonetheless circulates roughly sixty times faster than the body beneath it (verified: Horinouchi et al., Science, 24 April 2020, via ISAS/JAXA, which states the atmosphere "rotates 60 times as fast as its planetary rotation") — and that identifying the momentum pump took a dedicated orbiter. Gravitational binding plus common origin therefore does not by itself deliver co-rotation, which is precisely the point Rowbotham pressed and precisely what the flat sentence denies. Our own straw_man block states the position better than the refutation does ("friction and pressure gradients redistributing momentum inside an already co-rotating system"), so the fix is to bring the refutation up to the standard the straw_man block already sets. Related: `advocate.survives` is recorded as 2 with `preemptive=None`, but the recorded best_defense is exactly this objection, and under the harness a defence this live rates 3 and obliges a preemptive.
holes.recommendation: First, the mechanism is misidentified. The atmosphere is not held in step by friction against a rough surface. It is gravitationally bound and inherited the Earth's angular momentum at formation, and once a fluid shell is in solid-body co-rotation there is no relative motion for friction to act on, so nothing has to keep gripping it. What surface friction, mountain torque and pressure gradients do is redistribute momentum inside an already co-rotating system — an exchange large enough to measure, since it shows up as millisecond-scale variation in the length of the day. Venus shows what the alternative looks like when the redistribution runs the other way, and it is not what Rowbotham observed: he was right that co-rotation needs an account, and wrong that the account has to be a grip. (Set advocate.survives=3 and put this paragraph in preemptive.)

holes.quoted_phrase: Rowbotham devotes several pages of the 1865 edition to collecting newspaper complaints about Foucault's pendulum
holes.description: An uncited edition claim, and the edition looks wrong — the recurring trap this project has already logged three times (ARG-A05, ARG-B04, ARG-B01 in corrections.json, all Rowbotham, all 1849/1865 material that turned out to be 1881). The press-clipping treatment of Foucault's pendulum is verified in the enlarged third edition of 1881, ch. XIV, "Examination of the So-Called 'Proofs' of the Earth's Rotundity: The Supposed Manifestation of the Rotation of the Earth", pp. 305-312 (sacred-texts za52.htm), quoting the Liverpool Mercury of 17 and 23 May 1851, the Manchester Examiner supplement of 24 May 1851, Charles Maclaren in the Scotsman, and Punch of 10 May 1851. That chapter has no counterpart in the 1865 table of contents. The 1865 edition's only pendulum material I could reach is in Section II and concerns the length of the seconds pendulum at different latitudes (Derham in the Philosophical Transactions, Phillips's Million of Facts) — a gravity-variation argument, not the rotation demonstration — and the name Foucault did not appear in the retrieved portion. HONEST LIMIT: the 1865 Section XII miscellanea does carry a heading "Pendulum Experiments as Proofs of the Earth's Motion", and every full-text fetch of Gutenberg 69892 truncated before reaching it, so I cannot prove the 1865 edition lacks press quotations. What I can say is that our sentence has no citation, that the documented locus is 1881, and that repointing it at the verified locus costs nothing and removes the risk entirely.
holes.recommendation: Rowbotham devotes seven pages of the enlarged third edition to collecting press complaints about Foucault's pendulum — ch. XIV, pp. 305–312, quoting the Liverpool Mercury of 17 and 23 May 1851, the Manchester Examiner supplement of 24 May 1851, Charles Maclaren in the Scotsman, and Punch of 10 May 1851 — which tells us he understood how much rested on it.

holes.quoted_phrase: The refutation opens by answering the fragment
holes.description: Stale self-criticism, published. The compression note was written on 2026-08-05 against the pre-rewrite draft and tells the reader that our refutation commits an error it no longer commits. The current refutation opens "Start where Rowbotham starts, because it is not where the list puts him", quotes his co-rotation concession, and when it reaches Galileo explicitly labels the sealed cabin "a premise Rowbotham grants, so it is common ground rather than a rebuttal." Leaving the note as-is invites a defender to quote our own compression block as an admission that our refutation misses the target — and to be right about the words while wrong about the text. The fix should preserve the record that the draft was changed, rather than erasing it: on a page whose product is provenance, "we caught this and fixed it" is worth more than silence.
holes.recommendation: This bore on our own text, and the text was changed. An earlier draft opened by answering the fragment — Galileo’s sealed cabin, the air is inside the cabin, the atmosphere co-rotates — and Rowbotham agreed with every word of it. The refutation now opens from his own sentence and presents the Galileo material as shared ground. The parts that answer him are the arithmetic, a 10 m/s stratum riding a 465 m/s carrier, and the hemispheric reversal of the Coriolis deflection that his own citation of Ross’s north-east and south-east trades hands us.

holes.quoted_phrase: reasonable thing for a self-taught experimenter in 1865 to try
holes.description: Contradicts our own corrected dating in the same argument. The grinding-stone experiment is Experiment 4 of the enlarged third edition, ch. III, p. 73 (verified at sacred-texts za21.htm); neither "grinding stone" nor "phosphorus" appears in the retrieved text of the 1865 first book edition, and clusters.py already carries the corrected originator year 1881 for exactly this reason, with the change logged in corrections.json on 2026-08-05. The advocate block was not updated with the rest, so the entry now dates the same experiment to two different editions in two adjacent fields.
holes.recommendation: reasonable thing for a self-taught experimenter to try, and it is his own addition to the enlarged third edition of 1881

holes.quoted_phrase: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/The_Systeme_of_the_World:_in_Four_Dialogues
holes.description: Two load-bearing primary-source quotations — Salviati on the imperceptibility of shared motion, and Galileo's pre-emptive answer to the vertical-shot experiment — rest entirely on a wiki page. Exact-phrase searches for both quotations return that page as the top result, so I have no reason to doubt the wording, but the domain is cache-only and could not be fetched this run, which means neither quotation was verified against a text this cycle. On every other source in this entry we link a scan or the issuing institution; this is the one place where a hostile reader can say we traced a 1661 translation to a wiki. Low reader impact, but it is the site's own method applied unevenly.
holes.recommendation: Galileo, The Systeme of the World: in Four Dialogues, Second Dialogue — Thomas Salusbury trans., in Mathematical Collections and Translations, Tome I (London, 1661); relativity principle and the vertical-shot answer. Link a page-image scan of the 1661 Salusbury as the citation of record and demote the Wikiquote page to a finding aid.

reviews.summary: The verdict (REFUTED) holds and the hedge rule passes cleanly — this is one of the better-aimed entries on the site, and every Rowbotham sentence in the passage block checks out word-for-word against the 1881 third edition, including the one the previous audit could not confirm. Four majors nonetheless: the Foucault pendulum's precession is given as f = 2Ωsinφ when it is Ωsinφ, a factor-of-two error in the paragraph asserting our own rigour; the gloss claims "All thirteen items descend from these pages" when our own compression block says item 54's orbital figure does not and item 271 (lightning) is neither traceable to Rowbotham nor addressed anywhere in the refutation; "Nothing needs to grip it" is contradicted by our own Venus paragraph, which is also the recorded best_defense and is under-rated at survives=2; and the Foucault press-clippings are credited to the 1865 edition when the verified locus is the 1881 third edition, ch. XIV, pp. 305-312 — the fourth instance of the Rowbotham edition trap. All four are single-sentence patches.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Split result. The declared source IS reached and IS quoted accurately: I fetched the Taliaferro text at bertie.ccsu.edu and confirmed both load-bearing sentences verbatim — I.4 "if it were flat, the stars would rise and set for all people together and at the same time" and I.7 "as far as the appearances of the stars are concerned, nothing would perhaps keep things from being in accordance with this simpler conjecture" — along with the chapter titles (the host page prints I.7 as "That the Earth Does Not an any Way Move Locally", an obvious transcription slip for "in any Way"; our normalisation is fine). Our refutation genuinely answers Ptolemy at his own strength and openly agrees with him, so it is NOT a case of beating the fragment. The failure is the mirror image and the rule's schema already has a name for it that we did not use. Three of the four items sampled in `list_phrasing` — 34 "Day–night cycle from firmament rotation", 39 "Precession from dome rotation", 210 "Seasonal stars via dome" — have no relationship to the Almagest whatsoever, were never traced to any source, and are here compared against a source that is not theirs. `drift_type="force_upgraded"` is defensible for item 32 and the retrograde/precession-as-observation items; it is meaningless for the three dome items, where no wording of Ptolemy's is preserved because none was ever taken. The honest handling is to split the block: `force_upgraded` for the Ptolemaic-appearance items, and `assessed="no_source"` recorded separately for the dome items, with a note saying what was searched. The block instead papers over the gap with a sentence asserting that those items "credit him" with a firmament — an attribution the list never makes (see hole 5). So: rule applied, source reached, but the comparison is vacuous for 3 of the 4 items it samples and the third `assessed` state was available and unused.
reviews.summary: A22 is well-researched and mostly accurate — the Ptolemy quotes are verbatim, the equation-of-time, libration, Foucault, Bessel and aberration numbers check out, and the "roughly ninety items" figure is exactly right (90 STANDARD PHYSICS items across the corpus). But the TLDR concedes far more than the body does: it states that all twenty items are true, which hands the movement its firmament and dome mechanisms (items 34, 39, 210) as conceded truths, and the body itself only says "most". Two hard errors follow: the Foucault precession is given as 2Ωsinφ (it is Ωsinφ; 2Ωsinφ is the Coriolis parameter and is double the 11.3°/hr we correctly quote), and the refutation's claim that aberration is "the first observation a stationary Earth cannot accommodate" is contradicted three fields later by our own advocate block. The entry also asserts Ptolemy as originator of all twenty items — rendered on the page as "first published by Claudius Ptolemy" and counted in the site's headline traceability statistic — with no documented chain and with the dome items affirmatively not his. Finally, the ~460-word passage is flagged pd=True, but what is quoted is R. Catesby Taliaferro's 1952 Encyclopaedia Britannica translation, which is in copyright; the flag routes the quote around our own 60-word fair-use test.
citation_failures: scripts/deep_batch2.py A22 passage: pd=True is wrong for the text actually quoted. The Almagest is public domain; the English rendering is R. Catesby Taliaferro's, published 1952 by Encyclopaedia Britannica (confirmed via archive.org/details/almagest00ptol metadata: 1952, Chicago: Encyclopaedia Britannica, translator R. Catesby Taliaferro). Our locator names the translator, so the entry knows this. ~460 words of an in-copyright 1952 translation are published under a flag that exempts the passage from the 60-word cap in tests/test_provenance.py:176.

scripts/deep_batch2.py A22 sources: the Penn State ASTRO 801 link is cited accurately for what its label claims (I confirmed it says retrograde motion is 'a perspective effect caused when Earth passes a slower moving outer planet' and 'the planet is described as being at opposition'), but it does NOT support the adjacent and much sharper claim that Ptolemy locked each superior planet's epicycle to a one-year period with its radius parallel to the Earth-Sun line. That claim — the strongest paragraph in the refutation — currently carries no citation at all.

scripts/deep_batch2.py A22 refutation: 'the modern value is 0.28718″' for 61 Cygni is a Hipparcos-era figure quoted to five significant figures. Gaia gives 285.9949 ± 0.0599 mas (A) and 286.0054 ± 0.0289 mas (B), i.e. 0.2860″. Bessel's own 0.3136″ ± 0.0136″ is confirmed correct (313.6 ± 13.6 mas).

holes.quoted_phrase: every one of them is true
holes.description: The TLDR states that all twenty items in the cluster are true. Items 34 ('Day–night cycle from firmament rotation'), 39 ('Precession from dome rotation') and 210 ('Seasonal stars via dome') are not observations of the sky at all — they are dome-mechanism claims, and they are false, not merely non-discriminating. Item 254 ('Analemma lamp artifact') asserts an anomaly, which our own straw_man field says is 'treating a fully explained consequence of axial tilt plus orbital eccentricity as an anomaly'. Item 35 ('Lunar phases explainable without orbit') is likewise a model claim, not an observation. The entry contradicts itself: the refutation body says only that 'most are simply correct', and the compression block says flatly that Ptolemy has neither firmament nor dome and 'refutes the cosmology it belongs to'. This is the highest-visibility field on the argument and it is where a defender will quote us: a flat-earth debunk whose summary line concedes that the day–night cycle comes from firmament rotation. Note the phrase is split across two Python string literals in the source — 'and every one ' + 'of them is true.' — so search for 'of them is true' when locating it.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'and every one of them is true' with: 'and most of them are simply true. Three are not observations at all: items 34, 39 and 210 explain the day–night cycle, precession and the seasonal stars by the rotation of a firmament or dome, and that mechanism is false rather than merely non-discriminating — it is refuted by the southern celestial pole at ARG-B08.'

holes.quoted_phrase: matching 2Ωsinφ at the latitude of Paris
holes.description: Factual physics error. A Foucault pendulum's plane precesses at Ω sin φ, not 2Ω sin φ. 2Ω sin φ is the Coriolis parameter f and is exactly twice the pendulum rate. Our own numbers prove the formula wrong in the same sentence: 15.041°/hr × sin 48.87° = 11.33°/hr, which matches the '11.3° per hour' we quote; 2Ω sin φ would give 22.7°/hr. Confirmed against Wikipedia's Foucault pendulum article, which gives 'ω = Ω sin φ' and the same 28 kg bob, 67 m wire and 11.3°/hr for the Panthéon (those three are correct as written). This is the single cheapest shot available to a physically literate defender: our marquee rotation experiment, stated with a formula that disagrees with our own number by a factor of two.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'matching 2Ωsinφ at the latitude of Paris' with 'matching Ωsinφ at the latitude of Paris'.

holes.quoted_phrase: the first observation a stationary Earth cannot accommodate
holes.description: Self-contradiction inside the entry. The refutation asserts that stellar aberration 'is the first observation a stationary Earth cannot accommodate'. The advocate block, three fields later, says the opposite in our own voice: 'a Tychonic arrangement with the stars carried around annually could reproduce both. It can be made to, and van der Kamp attempted exactly this by reinterpreting aberration as parallax.' Both cannot stand. A neo-Tychonic model with an annually revolving stellar sphere does reproduce aberration and parallax kinematically — that is why the honest argument is about the cost of the stipulation, not about impossibility, and the preemptive already makes that argument well. As written the refutation overstates and the advocate block then withdraws the overstatement, which is worse than not making it.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'and it is the first observation a stationary Earth cannot accommodate' with 'and it is the first observation no stationary-Earth model reproduces without stipulating an annual motion of the entire stellar sphere, applied to every star at once and for no independent reason — the move van der Kamp attempted and Bouw abandoned.'

holes.quoted_phrase: originator="Claudius Ptolemy (via the modern movement)"
holes.description: Provenance overreach, and it moves a published figure. render.py:94 turns this field into the line 'first published by Claudius Ptolemy' at the head of the argument, and build.py:136 counts all twenty items toward the site's headline 'N of 461 items trace to a named originator' statistic.
