No chain from the Almagest to any of these twenty list items is cited anywhere in the entry, and for items 34, 39 and 210 the attribution is affirmatively wrong — our own compression note says Ptolemy has neither firmament nor dome. The parenthetical hedge '(via the modern movement)' is discarded on render, so the reader sees an unqualified authorship claim. This is the exact failure mode already logged four times in corrections.json (entries 2, 3, 7, 8): attribution asserted from the shape of the genre rather than checked against the primary text. Entry 11 (E13) is the precedent for the fix — a claim of ours was withdrawn and the published figures moved with it.
holes.recommendation: Replace the A22 cluster record's attribution fields with: originator=None, originator_work=None, year=None, real_source="Ptolemy, Almagest I.4 and I.7 — the appearances these items cite, and the chapter that declares them non-discriminating", and change the note to: "The observations are true and ancient, and the Almagest is where the non-discrimination point is first stated. No chain from Ptolemy to any of these twenty items has been traced, and three of them (firmament, dome) descend from a cosmology Ptolemy refutes in I.4, so the cluster is recorded as untraced and Ptolemy appears as counter-witness, not author." Recompute the traceability headline; the shift is 20 items."

holes.quoted_phrase: credit him with a “firmament” and a “dome.”
holes.description: Located in scripts/_hedge_audit_batch_a.py, HEDGE_A['A22'] note, which deep.py:275-280 merges into the A22 entry. The sentence asserts that items 34, 39 and 210 'credit him' — Ptolemy — with a firmament and a dome. The item texts are 'Day–night cycle from firmament rotation.', 'Precession from dome rotation.' and 'Seasonal stars via dome.'; none names Ptolemy or any authority. The only thing crediting Ptolemy is our own cluster record. So the compression block — the machinery whose whole purpose is to stop us attributing to a source things the source does not say — is itself attributing to the list an attribution the list does not make. It is also what allows the block to record a single drift_type against a source three of its four sampled items have no connection to, instead of using the `assessed="no_source"` state that deep.py's docstring provides for exactly this case.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'Items 34, 39 and 210 credit him with a “firmament” and a “dome.” Ptolemy has neither.' with: 'Items 34, 39 and 210 invoke a “firmament” and a “dome.” They name no authority, and no chain has been traced from any of them to any source; the Almagest is not it. Recorded separately as no_source: searched the Almagest I.1–I.7 (Taliaferro) for firmament and dome language and found none, and found instead the I.4 argument that disposes of the flat option. He does not merely omit the dome, he refutes the cosmology it belongs to.'

holes.quoted_phrase: The celestial sphere does appear to rotate about the observer.
holes.description: We concede our strongest counterpoint away. The refutation grants that the apparent rotation of the celestial sphere (item 32) is non-discriminating. That is true for a stationary spherical Earth under a full celestial sphere — Ptolemy's case — but three items in this very cluster propose a rotating dome over a flat Earth, and against that model the observation is decisively discriminating: southern observers see circumpolar trails about a *southern* pole, which no single-plane dome model reproduces. Our own B08 record says so in terms: 'Southern-hemisphere circumpolar star trails around a southern pole are impossible on any single-plane model. This is the item the flat model most clearly gets wrong.' A22 never mentions the southern pole and does not list B08 in `related` (currently A10, A17, A05, A04, R01). The result is that the cluster carrying the dome items is the one place we decline to use the argument that kills the dome.
holes.recommendation: After 'The celestial sphere does appear to rotate about the observer.' insert: 'It appears to rotate about two centres, and that detail decides three of the items in this cluster. Southern observers watch circumpolar trails close around a southern pole no northern observer can see; a single rotating dome over a single plane has one centre and cannot produce two. Against Ptolemy's stationary sphere the observation is non-discriminating, exactly as he says. Against the dome invoked by items 34, 39 and 210 it is fatal, and it is handled in full at ARG-B08.' Add "B08" to `related`.

holes.quoted_phrase: work="WRK-PTOLEMY-ALMAGEST", pd=True
holes.description: The passage runs to roughly 460 words and is flagged pd=True, which exempts it from the fair-use cap at tests/test_provenance.py:176 ('pd or len(quote.split()) <= 60'). The Almagest is public domain; the text we are quoting is not. Our own locator says '(trans. R. Catesby Taliaferro)', and archive.org/details/almagest00ptol gives that edition as 1952, Chicago: Encyclopaedia Britannica — a 1952 US publication whose English rendering is a separately copyrightable work still in term. works.py:161-166 compounds this by recording the work as year='c. 150 CE', pd=True with imprint 'Alexandria.', which is the ancient work's status, not the quoted text's. A22 is the only argument using this work, so the fix is local.
holes.recommendation: Set pd=False and replace the quote with a 42-word excerpt: '[I.4] … if it were flat, the stars would rise and set for all people together and at the same time. …\n\n[I.7] … as far as the appearances of the stars are concerned, nothing would perhaps keep things from being in accordance with this simpler conjecture …' Move the surrounding narrative (eclipse hours scaling with distance, mountains rising from the sea, clouds left behind) into the gloss as our own prose. In works.py set pd=False and imprint="Alexandria, c. 150 CE. Quoted here from R. Catesby Taliaferro's English translation, Great Books of the Western World vol. 16, Encyclopaedia Britannica, 1952 — the Greek is public domain, this rendering is not."

holes.quoted_phrase: broken by measurement, not argument: the phases of Venus
holes.description: The TLDR defines the equivalence narrowly — 'a rotating sky and a rotating Earth predict the identical appearance' — and then names four measurements that broke it. Only one of the four bears on rotation. Foucault's pendulum (1851) measures the Earth's spin. The phases of Venus (1610) settle planetary ordering, stellar aberration (1729) and stellar parallax (1838) settle the Earth's annual motion; a geocentrist who keeps the whole cosmos turning daily concedes nothing about rotation from any of the three. Worse, the refutation body itself concedes that the first of the four does not touch the list's model: 'this refutes Ptolemy, not Tycho … and the list's geocentric bulk is Tychonian, so it survives this particular test.' The TLDR therefore advertises as a decisive break something the body says the opponent survives.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'The equivalence was real until it was broken by measurement, not argument: the phases of Venus (1610), stellar aberration (1729), stellar parallax (1838) and Foucault's pendulum (1851).' with: 'The equivalence was real until measurement broke it — and the measurement that reaches rotation specifically is Foucault's pendulum (1851), which needs no sky at all. The phases of Venus (1610), stellar aberration (1729) and stellar parallax (1838) broke the companion equivalence, the one about the Earth's annual motion, and they are what forced the geocentric side back from Ptolemy to Tycho.'

holes.quoted_phrase: what Ptolemy meant by
holes.description: Conceptual slip, and it misattributes a doctrine. The TLDR says the observational equivalence of the two models is 'precisely what Ptolemy meant by saving the appearances — and he says so himself in Almagest I.7.' Saving the appearances means constructing a geometry that reproduces the observations; the indistinguishability of two such geometries is a consequence, not the meaning. And the formula belongs to the Platonic tradition transmitted by Simplicius, not to Ptolemy — who in I.7 argues as a physical realist, conceding that the stars cannot decide and then rejecting a turning Earth on mechanical grounds (clouds and thrown objects left behind), which is the opposite of instrumentalism. What he actually says in I.7 is the non-discrimination point, and that is all we need. Phrase is split across string literals: search 'what Ptolemy meant by'.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'which is precisely what Ptolemy meant by saving the appearances — and he says so himself in Almagest I.7' with: 'and Ptolemy grants exactly this in Almagest I.7 — as far as the appearances of the stars go, nothing would keep things from being in accordance with the simpler conjecture that the Earth turns. He then rejects a turning Earth anyway, on mechanical grounds, and that is the one part of the chapter that is wrong.'

holes.quoted_phrase: the epicycle's period is locked to one year
holes.description: The sharpest historical claim in the entry — that Ptolemy fixed each superior planet's epicycle to a one-year period with its radius parallel to the Earth–Sun line, a correlation the heliocentric model derives rather than imposes — carries no citation. The Penn State ASTRO 801 link sits in the same paragraph's source list but covers only the opposition/perspective point; I fetched it and it makes no mention of the epicycle period or any Earth–Sun alignment. On a page whose product is provenance, the load-bearing claim in the best paragraph should not be the uncited one. A verifiable source exists and I checked it: Fitzpatrick's 'Ptolemy's Model of the Solar System' states that the radius vectors connecting the epicycle centres to the planets 'should always all point in the same direction as the vector connecting the earth to the sun'.
holes.recommendation: Add to `sources`: dict(label="Fitzpatrick, “Ptolemy's Model of the Solar System” (UT Austin) — for the superior planets the epicycle radius vectors “always all point in the same direction as the vector connecting the earth to the sun”, with a one-year period", url="https://farside.ph.utexas.edu/books/Syntaxis/Almagest/node3.html")

holes.quoted_phrase: on his fourth page
holes.description: Rhetorical flourish that is literally false and trivially checkable. The flat-Earth clause is in Book I chapter 4, not on page 4. In the Taliaferro translation the Book I preface and chapters 1–3 precede it; chapter 4 begins several pages in. On a site that has already logged three corrections for edition and pagination errors (corrections.json entries 1, 6, 7), an unnecessary page claim is a gift to a checker.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'refutes the list's headline claim on his fourth page' with 'refutes the list's headline claim in his fourth chapter'.

holes.description: Stale figure quoted to five significant figures. Gaia gives 61 Cygni A at 285.9949 ± 0.0599 mas and B at 286.0054 ± 0.0289 mas, i.e. 0.2860″; 0.28718″ is the Hipparcos-era value. Bessel's own 0.3136″ ± 0.0136″ is confirmed correct (313.6 ± 13.6 mas, published 1838). The five-digit precision is what makes the mismatch worth fixing — at two digits nobody would look.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'the modern value is 0.28718″' with 'the modern Gaia value is 0.2860″'.

holes.quoted_phrase: Galileo observed Venus through its full cycle
holes.description: Date compression. Galileo's Venus observations ran from the autumn of 1610 to February 1611; the gibbous and near-full phases that make the argument were observed from December 1610 into 1611, so a *full cycle* was not observed within 1610. The Royal Belgian Institute for Space Aeronomy page cited in our own sources gives 'During the autumn of 1610' through 'February 1611'. Dating the discovery to 1610 is standard usage; saying the full cycle was observed in 1610 is not.
holes.recommendation: Replace '1610: Galileo observed Venus through its full cycle of phases, including gibbous and near-full.' with '1610–11: Galileo followed Venus from the autumn of 1610 to February 1611 through a full cycle of phases, including gibbous and near-full.'

reviews.hedge_rule_note: See hedge_rule_ok field.
citation_failures: De Morgan, A Budget of Paradoxes — cited in the passage gloss and in straw_man.detail as commentary on the 1849 pamphlet's TITLE PAGE. It is not. The entry is headed 'Zetetic Astronomy: Earth not a globe. 1857 (Broadsheet)' and addresses Rowbotham's 1849 Trowbridge LECTURE ADVERTISEMENT, issued under the name S. Goulden, whose wording differs from the title page we quote: 'A paper on the above subjects was read before the Council and Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, Somerset House, Strand, London (Sir John F. W. Herschel, President), Friday, Dec. 8, 1848.' De Morgan also hedges — 'I suspect that the above is Mr. S. Goulden's way of representing the following occurrence' — and his account confirms that a few of the lecturer's transmitted arguments WERE read aloud at the meeting. Source: Budget of Paradoxes/L, en.wikisource.org.

Etymology of 'level' — the cited entry supports the first half of our claim (mid-14c., name of a tool, Old French livel, Latin libella, diminutive of libra) but contradicts the second half. Etymonline gives the adjective 'having an even surface' from early 15c. and 'lying in the same horizontal plane (as something else)' from the 1550s. Our sentence 'It never meant "planar"' is false, and it contradicts our own steelman paragraph conceding that 'in ordinary English a level line is a straight horizontal one.'
reviews.summary: The verdict (REFUTED) holds and the argumentative architecture is the strongest in the batch — concede the premise, define the term from the trade that owns it, quantify the equivocation, then answer the unfalsifiability charge in a dedicated section. Every number I could check is right (Nile elevations, curvature at 30 m / 1 km / 800 km, arcsecond-per-division, WGS 84, Panama 20 cm, PSMSL, NGS, Newton's 689:692), every Carpenter and Dubay quotation is verbatim, and the item-384 reattribution to Carpenter 1885 survives an independent full-text check of the 1865 edition. But the page's marquee provenance gotcha is misattributed: De Morgan's Budget of Paradoxes entry answers an 1857 broadsheet reprinting Rowbotham's 1849 Trowbridge lecture advertisement, not the pamphlet's title page, and he hedged with "I suspect" while confirming that a reading did occur — we dropped the hedge and named the wrong document, in two separate fields, on a site whose product is provenance. Beyond that: the etymological claim "level never meant planar" is false and contradicts our own steelman; "Newton was wrong in the third digit" and "within a few tenths" both understate a 30 per cent error and contradict section 6(a), which admits it honestly; and "The sea stands 21.4 km higher at the equator" uses "higher" in precisely the sense the page has just spent two sections denying.

holes.quoted_phrase: The title page contains a documented misrepresentation.
holes.description: We attribute De Morgan's Budget of Paradoxes rebuttal to the 1849 pamphlet's title page. It is not about that document. De Morgan's entry is headed 'Zetetic Astronomy: Earth not a globe. 1857 (Broadsheet)' and quotes Rowbotham's 1849 Trowbridge lecture advertisement, issued under the name S. Goulden: 'A paper on the above subjects was read before the Council and Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, Somerset House, Strand, London (Sir John F. W. Herschel, President), Friday, Dec. 8, 1848' — different wording from the title-page sentence we quote from Schadewald. Two further problems in the same paragraph. (a) We drop De Morgan's hedge: his sentence reads 'I suspect that the above is Mr. S. Goulden's way of representing the following occurrence', and our text converts it to the flat 'is not what happened'. (b) Our own quoted evidence undercuts our claim: De Morgan says the Secretary 'then read a few of the arguments that had been transmitted by the lecturer', so a reading DID occur on 8 December 1848 and the pamphlet's offence is inflation, not fabrication. On a page whose product is provenance, a defender who opens Budget of Paradoxes/L finds an 1857 heading, a different sentence and a hedge we deleted. (Sources checked: en.wikisource.org/wiki/Budget_of_Paradoxes/L; cantab.net Schadewald ch. 1.)
holes.recommendation: The Royal Astronomical Society claim, and what De Morgan actually said. The title page describes the pamphlet as “the substance of a paper read before the Royal Astronomical Society on the evening of Dec. 8, 1848” (transcribed by Schadewald; we have not seen the sheet itself). Augustus De Morgan, the Society's Secretary at the time, answered a near-identical claim printed on Rowbotham's 1849 Trowbridge lecture advertisement, issued under the name S. Goulden — “A paper on the above subjects was read before the Council and Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, Somerset House, Strand, London (Sir John F. W. Herschel, President), Friday, Dec. 8, 1848” — which he reprinted in A Budget of Paradoxes under the heading Zetetic Astronomy: Earth not a globe. 1857 (Broadsheet). De Morgan wrote: “No account of such a paper appears in the Notice for that month: I suspect that the above is Mr. S. Goulden's way of representing the following occurrence: Dec. 8, 1848, the Secretary of the Astronomical Society (De Morgan by name) said, at the close of the proceedings,—‘Now, gentlemen, if you will promise not to tell the Council, I will read something for your amusement:’ and he then read a few of the arguments that had been transmitted by the lecturer.” Note what this does and does not establish. Something was read: a few transmitted arguments, read out by the Secretary on his own initiative after the close of business, expressly not to the Council. Describing that as a paper read before the Society — still less before its Council, with the President named — converts an after-hours amusement into an institutional hearing. De Morgan's target is the handbill; the same claim, shorter, sits on the pamphlet's title page in the same year.

holes.quoted_phrase: founding document itself: the 1849 pamphlet's title page claims its contents
holes.description: The same misattribution recurs in a second field, and here it is load-bearing: it is offered as one of three documented misrepresentations. De Morgan never addressed the pamphlet's title page; he addressed the 1849 lecture advertisement (name S. Goulden), reprinted in his entry on an 1857 broadsheet, and he hedged. Fixing the gloss without fixing this leaves the error in circulation.
holes.recommendation: A third misrepresentation is institutional rather than scientific. Rowbotham's 1849 Trowbridge lecture advertisement, issued under the name S. Goulden, announced that "A paper on the above subjects was read before the Council and Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, Somerset House, Strand, London (Sir John F. W. Herschel, President), Friday, Dec. 8, 1848", and the 1849 pamphlet's title page carries the same claim in shorter form. De Morgan, the Society's own Secretary, reprinted the advertisement in A Budget of Paradoxes and recorded that no account of such a paper appears in that month's Notice; he suspected it to be a restatement of his own after-hours reading of a few of the arguments the lecturer had transmitted, prefaced by "if you will promise not to tell the Council". A reading happened. A hearing did not.

holes.quoted_phrase: It never meant “planar” and was never derived from geometry
holes.description: False, and it contradicts our own steelman two fields earlier. Etymonline gives the adjective 'level' as 'having an even surface' from early 15c. and 'lying in the same horizontal plane (as something else)' from the 1550s — three centuries before Rowbotham. Our steelman concedes exactly this ('In ordinary English a level line is a straight horizontal one') and calls the complaint fair. A defender needs one dictionary lookup to catch us asserting in the refutation what we grant in the steelman, on the single lexical point the whole section turns on. The true and sufficient claim is about priority, not about non-existence.
holes.recommendation: It began as the name of the instrument that finds the direction of gravity, not as a term of geometry; the planar senses are later derivations from it — the adjective “having an even surface” is attested only from the early fifteenth century, and “lying in the same horizontal plane” from the 1550s, two centuries after the tool. An argument that runs “we say sea level, not sea curve” leans on the derived sense while presenting it as the original one, and the original one names a gravity instrument.

holes.quoted_phrase: Newton was wrong in the third digit and right in the physics
holes.description: Wrong by two orders of magnitude of precision, and it contradicts section 6(a) of our own refutation. Newton's flattening is 3/692 = 1/230.7, i.e. f = 0.004335; the modern value is 1/298.257223563, f = 0.003353. The disagreement is in the FIRST significant figure of f (4 against 3) and is about 29 per cent. Section 6(a) states this correctly and honestly — 'a real disagreement with 1/230 that later theory ... had to earn its way out of' — so the page says two incompatible things about the same number, and the flattering version is the one in the steelman's payoff sentence, which is where the KERNEL cashes out. (APS, 'How Newton Derived the Shape of the Earth', verified for 689:692 and 1-to-230.7.)
holes.recommendation: Newton was about 30 per cent out on the magnitude and right on the physics, which is the ordinary condition of a first-principles prediction: 1/230.7 against the modern 1/298.257223563, with almost the whole gap traceable to his assumption of uniform density, which Clairaut later relaxed.

holes.quoted_phrase: The observed value sits within a few tenths of Newton's 1687 estimate.
holes.description: Vague where it needs to be exact, and misleading in the direction that flatters us. 1/230 against 1/298.257 is a 29 per cent error in the flattening; 'within a few tenths' reads to any ordinary reader as near-agreement, and there is no unit under which it is a fair description. It sits in section 4(i), the most-read part of the refutation, and it is contradicted by section 6(a) of the same document, which correctly calls the gap 'a real disagreement'. Section 6(a) is the better text and the page should say the same thing in both places.
holes.recommendation: Newton's 1687 estimate of 1/230 is some 30 per cent larger than the measured 1/298.257 — the sign, the cause and the mechanism were right, the magnitude was not, and the shortfall was later traced to his assumption that the Earth is of uniform density.

holes.quoted_phrase: does the same work by inventing a spokesman
holes.description: An unsupported attribution of fabrication to a named, long-dead person, which our own harness classes as major ('Distinguish "was wrong" from "was lying". Unsupported bad-faith attribution is major even when the person is long dead'). Carpenter's proof 90 reports an exchange he does not source; that it is unverifiable does not establish that he made it up, and we have no evidence either way. The criticism that actually lands — unnamed astronomer, unsourced exchange, and a formulation no geodesist would use — is already in the next clause and does all the work without the accusation. This is also the same class of error already logged in corrections.json for ARG-D07 (the Dzyan sentence), so it is a recurrence, not a novelty.
holes.recommendation: Proof 90 does the same work through an unverifiable authority: "Is water level, or is it not?" was a question once asked of an astronomer. "Practically, yes; theoretically, no," was the reply. Carpenter names no astronomer, no date and no occasion, so the exchange cannot be checked; and the answer he reports is not the answer geodesy gives, since on the technical definition water is level, simply and without qualification. Whether or not someone once said this, the concession it stages is not one the discipline makes.

holes.quoted_phrase: The sea stands 21.4 km higher at the equator.
holes.description: We use 'higher' in exactly the sense the page has just spent two sections denying. By the definition the refutation adopts — orthometric height, referred to the geoid — the equatorial sea is not higher than the polar sea at all: both lie on the same equipotential, and that is the whole point of the paragraph the heading introduces. The TLDR gets it right ('further from the centre at the equator than at the poles'), which shows the distinction was understood; the heading then hands a defender the line 'you equivocate on height in your own headline while accusing me of equivocating on level'.
holes.recommendation: (i) The sea surface stands 21.4 km further from the Earth's centre at the equator than at the poles — and it is not, on that account, “higher”.

holes.quoted_phrase: the sixth experiment (fig. 9)
holes.description: A specificity the only reachable source does not support. Schadewald introduces the New Bedford passage with 'The pamphlet describes six experiments with a surveyor's theodolite. For example:' — he neither numbers the quoted experiment nor says it is the last of the six. 'Fig. 9' is the pamphlet's figure number, not an experiment number, and there is no reason to assume one figure per experiment. On a page that corrects other people's locators, our own locator should claim only what the source gives us, particularly for a document we state we could not read.
holes.recommendation: title page, and one of the six theodolite experiments (illustrated as fig. 9). No transcription or scan of the 16-page pamphlet could be reached; the body sentence is quoted from Schadewald, The Plane Truth, ch. 1, which reproduces it verbatim as an example and does not say which of the six it is

holes.quoted_phrase: Rowbotham's Old Bedford Canal trials, which are where his 1849 water sentence comes from
holes.description: Contradicted by the quotation we print three fields above. The 1849 sentence Schadewald reproduces names a different waterway: 'there is an artificial river called the "New Bedford;" it is upwards of 20 miles in length' — the Hundred Foot Drain, which runs parallel to the Old Bedford, not the Old Bedford on which the famous 1838/1839 trials and the 1870 Wallace wager were run (Earth Not a Globe ch. II opens 'In the county of Cambridge there is an artificial river or canal, called the "Old Bedford"'). Either the 1849 sentence is not from the Old Bedford trials, or Rowbotham's own accounts differ between 1849 and 1865 — which is itself worth saying, since Schadewald notes 'his later accounts are contradictory'. Asserting the identification as settled, in the same document that prints the contrary evidence, is a cheap catch for a defender.
holes.recommendation: Rowbotham's Bedford Level trials are ARG-B03: that cluster covers the two-point near-water sightline that produces a false null, Wallace's three-point 1870 repeat and Oldham's 1901 replication. Note that the 1849 sentence quoted above names the New Bedford river, while the celebrated trials and the 1865 and 1881 books use the Old Bedford — one of several points on which, as Schadewald observes, Rowbotham's own accounts of what he did in the Fens do not agree with each other.

holes.quoted_phrase: The 8-inches-per-mile-squared figure is the flat model's own arithmetic
holes.description: Wrong as stated, and refuted by our own next sentence. Eight inches per mile squared is the drop predicted by a sphere of radius 6,371 km; the flat model predicts no drop at all. We then say, correctly, that Rowbotham took the figure from the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on Levelling — i.e. from the spherical model — which makes 'the flat model's own arithmetic' a claim about origin that our following sentence contradicts. (Verified: the 1865 Gutenberg text of Earth Not a Globe reprints the Britannica passage, including 'the curve of the Earth being the true level, and the tangent to it the apparent level' and 'it is raised eight inches very nearly above the Earth's surface at one mile's distance; four times as much, or 32 inches, at the distance of two miles'.)
holes.recommendation: The 8-inches-per-mile-squared figure is the spherical model's arithmetic, adopted wholesale by the flat-earth argument as its own yardstick, and it is a prediction with a threshold.

holes.quoted_phrase: A level surface is one of constant gravitational potential
holes.description: Wrong in the one place it most matters. The geoid is a surface of constant GEOPOTENTIAL — gravitational potential plus the centrifugal potential of rotation. A surface of constant purely gravitational potential on a rotating Earth is not the sea surface and is not oblate, so as written the TLDR removes the very term that produces the bulge the next clause credits to rotation. The refutation gets it right ('an equipotential surface of the gravity field'), which is standard geodetic usage; the TLDR does not, and readers may never expand past it.
holes.recommendation: A level surface is one of constant gravity potential — gravitation plus the centrifugal effect of the Earth's rotation — perpendicular to gravity everywhere, and on a rotating Earth that surface is curved:

holes.quoted_phrase: (Baltimore, 1885), not Rowbotham and not Dubay
holes.description: The edition is not stated, and this entry's central provenance claim rests on proof numbers taken from it. The Gutenberg #55387 title page reads '5th Edition: 6th Thousand ... BALTIMORE: Printed and Published by the Author, No. 71 Chew Street, 1885' (the Library of Congress flat-earth guide catalogues it as '[6th ed.] Baltimore, 1885. 39 p.'). Proof numbering in a fifth edition need not match a first, so 'Carpenter 1885, proof 4' and 'proof 18' should be pinned to the edition we actually read. Given that corrections.json already logs three edition-dating failures (A05, B04, B01 itself), leaving the edition unstated is the recurrence of a known failure class rather than a nicety. The 1885 dating itself is safe — Carpenter's introduction announces Rowbotham's death of 23 December 1884 — and I found no earlier printed source for the Nile claim, so the substantive finding stands.
holes.recommendation: (Baltimore: printed and published by the author, 1885 — the Project Gutenberg text is the “5th Edition: 6th Thousand”, and the proof numbers cited here are that edition's), not Rowbotham and not Dubay

holes.quoted_phrase: Two further hardening moves if this argument recurs.
holes.description: The preemptive answers the advocate's weakest demand and leaves its strongest one standing. The defence's sharpest line is not 'show me a photograph' but 'every direct measurement anyone has ever made of a water surface with an instrument in their hands returns a plane' — and the preemptive answers it with the Lapland and Peru arcs, which measured latitude with zenith sectors on land and are not measurements of a water surface at all. We own two direct instrumental measurements of standing water that return curvature and neither is named: Wallace's three-point 1870 repeat on the Bedford Level (already ours, at ARG-B03) and the levelling networks run between tide gauges, which is the same measurement at continental scale and is the evidentiary basis of every published orthometric height.
holes.recommendation: Three further hardening moves if this argument recurs. First, meet the "it's all models with the radius baked in" charge with pre-satellite, pre-model measurements: the Lapland and Peru arcs (1735-40) measured a degree of latitude with theodolites and zenith sectors and found the degree longer near the pole, which is oblateness measured directly, a century and a half before anyone had a datum to assume. Second, answer the "instrument in hand on water" demand on its own ground, because it is the strongest form of the objection and the arcs do not touch it: Wallace's three-point 1870 repeat on the Bedford Level was a direct instrumental measurement of a standing-water surface and it returned the curvature (ARG-B03), and every national levelling network run between tide gauges is that same measurement at continental scale, which is why published orthometric heights exist at all. Third, decline the photograph demand explicitly rather than by omission - a photograph of a lake is an optical measurement and belongs to ARG-B04, where refraction is the controlling term; B01 rests on gravimetry, levelling and tide-gauge data precisely because those do not depend on light paths at all. Do not answer a hydrostatic argument with a picture.

holes.quoted_phrase: none of them optical and none of them dependent on a photograph
holes.description: An overclaim that is cheap to exploit and unnecessary. The historical determination of the flattening rests on the Lapland and Peru arcs, whose latitude determinations were made with zenith sectors — optical astronomy — and our own advocate preemptive recommends citing exactly those arcs as the pre-satellite answer. The point actually being made is that none of the four depends on a long horizontal sightline through the atmosphere, where refraction is the controlling term; say that instead.
holes.recommendation: and it has been measured four independent ways, none of them a long horizontal sightline through the atmosphere and none dependent on a photograph.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Hedge rule passes, and this is one of the better-executed cases on the page. The refutation is aimed at Rowbotham's actual procedure, not at the fragment "Lighthouse visibility." I verified against sacred-texts za14.htm that he really does subtract an observer horizon before squaring ("Deducting 6 miles from 30 ... would be 24 miles. The square of 24, multiplied by 8 inches, shows a declination of 384 feet"; and separately "Allowing 16 feet for the altitude of the observer ... 5 miles must be taken from the 30 miles, as the distance of the horizon"), that he concedes and quantifies refraction ("one-twelfth the altitude of the object observed"), and that he prints the Cape Bonavista deduction (13 ft off 491 ft, making 478 ft). All present, all as we characterise them. The Britannica "Levelling" extract with the one-seventh mean and the one-fifth/one-fifteenth variability is genuinely in his own chapter. drift_type=hedge_dropped is right and drifted=true is used honestly, not evasively. Two gaps rather than failures: (1) the compression block's source_wording splices the "Allowing 16 feet ... 30 miles" quotation, which belongs to the Spurn Point coal-fire example, into the lighthouse-table discussion, where Rowbotham in fact uses the 10-foot standard and a 4-mile horizon (reconstructible from his own printed results: Egero 28-4=24, 8x24^2=384 ft, less 154 ft of light = the 230 ft Dubay prints; Bonavista 35-4=31, 8x31^2=641 ft, less 150 = 491); (2) the block misses the single cleanest hedge_dropped in the lineage, Rowbotham's calm-water condition on the telescope claim being dropped by Carpenter's proof 63 and by the TFES wiki. Neither makes the refutation land on the fragment.
reviews.summary: B04 is well sourced and the MISLEADING verdict holds; every citation I could reach checked out verbatim (Rowbotham 1881 ch. II and ch. XIV, Carpenter proofs 5/7/36/63, Dubay's 200 Proofs numbering including the absence of Cape Hatteras, the 2018 Dubay blog post, Bowditch ch. 4 §§406-407, NPS Cape Hatteras, Cape Agulhas, Young, the Chicago hidden-height figures, the TFES wiki sentence, AOGHS on Kermac No. 16). Three findings need fixing: the TLDR concedes that these sightings are "real, correctly reported" while the body's longest section argues that most of the lighthouse numbers are catalogue ranges nobody ever observed; the gloss asserts that none of Carpenter's four proofs is in Rowbotham, when Rowbotham 1881 ch. XIV already contains proof 63's telescope claim (hedged to calm water, which is itself the best hedge_dropped instance in the cluster and we miss it); and refutation §3 calls Rowbotham's 491 feet "the curvature term" when it is the curvature term less the light's own 150 feet, which makes the 70-foot and five-times figures wrong in the very paragraph where we correct his arithmetic.
citation_failures: Bislin, "Rainy Lake Experiment: Refraction Measurements" — we describe "targets 0.37-1.6 m above the water". The page states the Bedford target centres were "set exactly 1.85 m above the lake water level" and its target table gives heights of 1.67-10.54 m. The k range (about 0.19 to 0.41) and the distances (1.1-9.5 km) and the lifts (~0.5 m at 5.4 km, ~1 m at 9.5 km) all verify; the height range does not.

Bowditch, American Practical Navigator, ch. 4 §§406-407 — the section exists, is titled Navigational Publications / Light Lists and Finding Range and Bearing of a Light at Sighting, defines nominal, luminous and geographic range, states geographic range as the sum of the two horizon distances, and carries the "Abnormal refraction patterns might change this range" sentence verbatim. It does not print the 1.17*sqrt(h) coefficient or the specific 14.3 / 2.6 / 6.4 / 9.8 nm figures our source label attributes to it; those come from the horizon-distance table.

UNCHECKED (not failures): USCG Light List 2024 PDF (the "loom (glow) of a powerful light" sentence); Young, "An Introduction to Mirages" (the ~4 km inferior-mirage horizon against 13-14 km); Young, "Looming, Towering, Stooping, and Sinking"; Bislin "Eight Inches per Miles squared" and "Deriving Equations for Atmospheric Refraction"; Metabunk zoom thread; flatearth.ws horizon-distance; Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 7; and the negative search of the 1865 Gutenberg text through p. 83, which I could not re-run without full-text tooling and which our own wording already hedges correctly.

holes.quoted_phrase: Most of these sightings are real, correctly reported, and further than the popular arithmetic allows
holes.description: The TLDR concedes more than the body will support, and the body says the opposite in its longest section. Refutation §5 is headed "most of the lighthouse items never reach the refraction question, because the numbers are not sightings" and says of Cape Agulhas "Nobody has ever stood on a deck and seen that light at fifty miles" and "All three of the proof's numbers are wrong"; of Cape Hatteras, "Carpenter's 40 miles is not a published figure then or now". The module docstring is blunter still: "HALF THE CLUSTER FAILS BEFORE REFRACTION IS REACHED ... Nobody ever observed those lights at those ranges." A reader who sees only the TLDR is told the reports are sound and only the inference fails; a critic who reads both can quote us against ourselves, and the phrase "correctly reported" is exactly what §5 spends four hundred words denying for the named cases. This is the holistic cross-claim-consistency failure, sitting in the first sentence a reader meets.
holes.recommendation: Some of these sightings are real, correctly reported, and further than the popular arithmetic allows — concede those without a fight, because the arithmetic is wrong twice over. Check first, though, whether you are looking at a sighting at all: the lighthouse figures are catalogue ranges out of a light list, fixed by lamp brightness rather than by the horizon, and half this cluster fails on that before refraction is reached.

holes.quoted_phrase: Four of his hundred proofs are in this cluster and none of them is in Rowbotham.
holes.description: False as to proof 63, and on a provenance site a false negative about ancestry is the error class corrections.json already logs three times (C02, B01, R06). Rowbotham 1881 ch. XIV (sacred-texts za33.htm) contains the telescope claim directly: "But even on the sea, when the water is very calm, if a vessel is observed until it is just 'hull down,' a powerful telescope turned upon it will restore the hull to sight." The same chapter reports the Nab light-ship hull "through a good telescope, plainly visible" from 32 inches at eight miles. Worse, the correction is against our own interest twice over: it strengthens the lineage, and Rowbotham's version carries a condition Carpenter drops. Rowbotham also writes "In the case of a ship's hull a telescope fails to restore it, however powerful it may be" when the sea is running; Carpenter's proof 63 states the effect unconditionally and the TFES wiki still does ("a good telescope with sufficient zoom will change the observer's perspective and bring the ship's hull back in full view" — verified verbatim). That is a hedge_dropped on a falsifiable claim, the best specimen in the cluster, and neither the gloss nor the compression note mentions it.
holes.recommendation: Four of his hundred proofs are in this cluster. The Cape Hatteras figure and the two Chesapeake cases are his own and are nowhere in Rowbotham; the telescope claim is not. Rowbotham had already written it, with a condition attached: “even on the sea, when the water is very calm, if a vessel is observed until it is just ‘hull down,’ a powerful telescope turned upon it will restore the hull to sight” (ch. XIV), while in a running sea “a telescope fails to restore it, however powerful it may be”. Proof 63 states the same effect with the condition removed, and the Flat Earth Society wiki still repeats it that way. The hedge that was dropped here is the one that made the claim survivable.

holes.quoted_phrase: about a seventh of the 491-foot curvature term, some 70 feet
holes.description: 491 feet is not the curvature term. It is the curvature drop less the light's own altitude, which is how every figure in Rowbotham's table is built, and his own printed results prove it: Egero, 28 statute miles less a 4-mile observer horizon is 24; 8 in x 24^2 = 384 ft; 384 less the light's 154 ft = 230 ft, which is exactly the depression Dubay's proof 83 reprints. Bonavista: 35 less 4 is 31; 8 in x 31^2 = 641 ft; 641 less 150 = the 491 he prints. Cordonan and Port Nicholson reconstruct the same way. So the curvature term is about 641 feet, one-seventh of it is about 90 feet rather than 70, a one-fifth day takes about 130 rather than "more than 90", and the sentence four lines later, "the allowance he made was five times too small", should be about seven times. Getting the arithmetic wrong in the paragraph headed "The source contains the correction. This is the finding." is the most expensive place on the page to get it wrong. (Related: the gloss's "Allowing 16 feet ... 5 miles must be taken from the 30 miles" is genuine but belongs to the Spurn Point coal-fire example, not to the lighthouse table, where he uses the 10-foot standard and the 4-mile horizon reconstructed above.)
holes.recommendation: on Cape Bonavista he deducts 13 feet from a curvature term of about 641 feet — his printed 491 is that 641 less the light's own 150 feet, as the rest of his table confirms: Egerö, 28 miles less a 4-mile horizon, squared, times 8 inches, is 384 feet, and 384 less 154 is the 230 he gives — where the encyclopaedia's own mean would take about a seventh of the 641, some 90 feet, and a strong-refraction day nearer 130. Change the following sentence to read: the allowance he made was about seven times too small and applied to the wrong variable.

holes.quoted_phrase: Radio-path engineering uses the same construction with
holes.description: Symbol collision inside a single sentence, and it lands on the one attack surface our own advocate section identifies. The sentence defines the effective radius as R' = R/(1 - k) with the geodetic k of 0.13-0.14, then says radio engineering uses "the same construction with k = 4/3". Under the formula just given, k = 4/3 yields a negative radius. The radio k-factor is conventionally defined as the effective-radius multiplier itself, so radio's k = 4/3 corresponds to a refraction coefficient of about 0.25 in the geodetic convention. Our own cited source (Bislin, "Deriving Equations for Atmospheric Refraction") keeps the two apart, using k for the coefficient and a for the multiplier. The advocate block predicts precisely this line of attack — "a coefficient you are free to tune ... that is not a prediction, it is a spare parameter" — so leaving an undeclared change of definition in the paragraph that introduces the coefficient is a gift.
holes.recommendation: Radio-path engineering uses the same device with a larger allowance, and with a different convention worth naming: the radio k-factor is defined as the multiplier itself rather than as the refraction coefficient, so its median value of 4/3 corresponds to a coefficient of about 0.25 in the geodetic notation used above. That is why ITU-R P.530 has designers draw straight lines over a 4/3-radius Earth.

holes.quoted_phrase: the same 7/6 effective-radius rule surveyors and radio engineers use today
holes.description: Radio engineers do not use the 7/6 rule; they use 4/3, as our own refutation §2 says three paragraphs later. What surveyors and radio engineers share is the effective-Earth-radius device, not the value. In the TLDR this is a flat misstatement of who uses what, and it is the sentence carrying the whole "the source printed the correction himself" finding, so it is the sentence most likely to be quoted back at us.
holes.recommendation: the same effective-Earth-radius device surveyors and radio engineers still use — 7/6 for surveying, 4/3 for radio paths

holes.quoted_phrase: The square of 24, multiplied by 8 inches, shows a declination of 384 feet.
holes.description: Our quotation begins one sentence too late, and the omission hides the source's own care — the exact failure the hedge rule exists to prevent, committed by us in our own quoting. The preceding sentence at sacred-texts za14.htm reads: "Deducting 6 miles from 30, the distance from the horizon to Holyhead, on the one hand, and to Dublin Bay on the other, would be 24 miles." Without it a reader cannot tell where 24 came from, and Rowbotham appears to be naively squaring a distance — which directly contradicts the gloss two inches below, where we credit him with subtracting the observer's horizon first and call it "the correct geometric procedure". The one sentence that evidences our own central concession to him is the one we cut.
holes.recommendation: Deducting 6 miles from 30, the distance from the horizon to Holyhead, on the one hand, and to Dublin Bay on the other, would be 24 miles. The square of 24, multiplied by 8 inches, shows a declination of 384 feet.

holes.quoted_phrase: the page does not yet do it as a numbered item
holes.description: The advocate block rates the defence 4 and, under the harness, that obliges a concrete text change. Items (a) and (b) of the preemptive are satisfied — the Rainy Lake and Chicago numbers are in §7, the range definitions are in §5. Item (c) is not: the preemptive itself states that the page does not carry the falsification list, and it does not. So the closing demand of the best defence — "Name in advance one observation of a light or a ship that your model forbids, and that I could go and make" — is answered on the page only by a note to ourselves saying we should answer it. A reader who reaches the advocate block finds us conceding the gap rather than closing it.
holes.recommendation:
Add as refutation §12, and delete clause (c) from the preemptive once it is in:

12. What would refute us. Four observations this model forbids and a flat plane permits, each cheap enough to attempt in an afternoon. (i) A ship's hull recovered by magnification alone at a fixed eye height — Carpenter's proof 63 asserts exactly this; the controlled form is to photograph, zoom by two and photograph again, then enlarge the first frame by two and compare the gap between waterline and horizon. (ii) A light whose visible range does not change when the observer's eye is raised, in conditions where lamp brightness is not the limit. (iii) A distant target that sinks, stretches, or doubles into an inverted image with no temperature structure in the air to produce it. (iv) Any distant object occluded from the top downward rather than from the waterline upward. None has ever been produced, and the first one is the cheapest experiment on this page.

holes.quoted_phrase: which concedes that he does not know what the theory he is refuting predicts
holes.description: An inference about a long-dead man's state of knowledge, stated as fact, on a reading his words do not compel. Carpenter's parenthesis "(one way or the other!)" reads at least as naturally as a hedge against being argued with about the sign — whichever direction you care to compute it, the theory demands 112 ft 8 in and you observe none — as it does as an admission of ignorance. The harness's charitable-interpretation rule asks us to distinguish what a person said from what we infer they believed, and the substantive point survives without the psychology: the prediction is determinate, and a ship's rail is not a level. Keeping the inference costs us the moral high ground on a page whose complaint about the other side is that it attributes to sources what the sources do not say.
holes.recommendation: demands a change in apparent elevation “one way or the other!” — a hedge against argument about the sign, where the prediction is in fact determinate in one direction: approaching a light, it rises relative to the horizon.

holes.quoted_phrase: Across Rainy Lake, targets 0.37
holes.description: The height range does not match the cited page. Bislin's "Rainy Lake Experiment: Refraction Measurements" states that "the Bedford target centers were set exactly 1.85 m above the lake water level" and its target table lists heights of 1.67-10.54 m at ranges of 1095-9459 m. Nothing on the page describes targets 0.37-1.6 m above the water; 1.6 m is a target-plate vertical size, not a height above water. Everything else in the sentence verifies — the k range of about 0.19 to 0.41 across sessions (0.187 and 0.270 from the computer model, 0.41 as the strongest observed at the Tangent targets), the 1.1-9.5 km distances, the ~0.5 m lift at 5.4 km and ~1 m at 9.5 km. This matters because §7 is the paragraph carrying the "k is measured, not fitted" answer to the spare-parameter charge, so its numbers have to be exactly right. The same range appears in the source label and should change with it.
holes.recommendation: Across Rainy Lake, targets set 1.85 m above the lake surface at ranges from 1.1 to 6.4 km, together with a 10.5 m target at 9.5 km, were surveyed against GNSS-fixed positions

holes.quoted_phrase: ch. 4 §§406–407 — nominal, luminous and geographic range
holes.description: The section reference is right and the quoted sentence is right — Bowditch ch. 4 (Navigational Publications) §406 Light Lists and §407 Finding Range and Bearing of a Light at Sighting do define nominal, luminous and geographic range, do state geographic range as the sum of the observer's and the light's horizon distances, and do contain "Abnormal refraction patterns might change this range; therefore, one cannot exactly predict the range at which a light will be seen" verbatim. But the label goes on to attribute the 1.17√h coefficient and the 14.3 / 2.6 / 6.4 / 9.8 nm figures to those sections, and they are not printed there; they come from the horizon-distance table and from our own arithmetic. Small, but this is a page that audits other people's citations.
holes.recommendation: Bowditch, American Practical Navigator, ch. 4 §§406–407 — nominal, luminous and geographic range; geographic range stated as the sum of the observer's and the light's horizon distances; “abnormal refraction patterns might change this range”. The figures below (150 ft → 14.3 nm; 5 ft → 2.6; 30 ft → 6.4; 70 ft → 9.8) are computed from Bowditch's 1.17√h horizon-distance table, not printed in §§406–407

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Hedge rule passes. I put Carpenter's own sentences beside the list fragments. All four quoted proofs (3, 40, 41, 51) are verbatim-correct against Project Gutenberg #55387 (Baltimore 1885), and the refutation answers Carpenter's actual case in Carpenter's order — the meaning of "level", Suez, the balanced back-and-fore sight, Parliament's datum line — before it touches any modern item. The compression block is honestly assessed: it says plainly that Carpenter is BLUNTER than the list ("this is a cutting proof that Earth is not a globe" vs "Railroads negligible curvature"), so drifted=True is recorded for scope rather than strength, and drifted is not being used to dodge work. drift_type="scope_widened" is right as far as it goes. One refinement: a second drift rides along with the first and is not named. Carpenter's proofs are claims about ENGINEERING PRACTICE ("no allowance is made"), which is checkable and, in his cases, true. Several modern list items — "Microwave links flat", "Undersea cables straight", "Highways horizon" — are claims about PHYSICAL GEOMETRY, which is a different kind of assertion and false. That is category_shifted running alongside scope_widened. The enum forces a single value, and the harness explicitly permits saying so rather than forcing the box; the note should record it.

holes.quoted_phrase: allows engineers to plot direct wave paths as straight lines rather than calculating path curvature explicitly
holes.description: This string is inside quotation marks and introduced as the ITU's own words ("The ITU's own handbook is explicit about what the trick is for"), but it does not occur in ITU-R Handbook R-HDB-54. The handbook, §3.3 'Diffraction fading and path clearance', reads: 'To avoid having to calculate the path curvature when designing a link, the effective Earth radius can be used instead of the actual Earth radius. In this modified geometry, the difference between the path of the direct wave and the Earth's curvature becomes constant and the path of the direct wave can be plotted as a straight line, helping to identify possible obstructions by the terrain profile or Earth's surface.' The substance of our claim is correct; the quotation is a paraphrase wearing quotation marks. On a site whose entire product is that claims degrade in transmission, publishing our own paraphrase as a verbatim quote is the single most discreditable error available to us, and it is trivially found by anyone who Ctrl-Fs the cited PDF.
holes.recommendation: Replace the quoted clause and its frame with: The ITU’s own handbook says why the trick exists: “To avoid having to calculate the path curvature when designing a link, the effective Earth radius can be used instead of the actual Earth radius. In this modified geometry … the path of the direct wave can be plotted as a straight line.” That is the same move as balanced backsights — curvature folded into the coordinate frame so the drawing looks straight.

holes.quoted_phrase: Four of the hundred are about engineering practice
holes.description: Undercount, and it contradicts our own compression note in the same entry. Carpenter's engineering-practice proofs are at least seven: 3 (surveyors, railroads, tunnels, canals), 25 and 26 (Atlantic cable survey and soundings), 40 (Suez), 41 (the 'true level' contradiction), 51 (Parliament's Standing Order) and 67 ('Seven-hundred miles is said to be the length of the great Canal, in China. Certain it is that, when this canal was formed, no "allowance" was made for "curvature."'). Our own compression note already lists 'the Atlantic cable soundings' among his engineering proofs, so the entry says four in one field and more than four in another. Proof 67 matters beyond arithmetic: it is Carpenter's longest-baseline canal claim, seven times the Suez baseline, and we answer only the 100-mile canal. A defender's first move is 'you picked the short one.'
holes.recommendation: Replace with: Seven of the hundred are about engineering practice — proofs 3, 25, 26, 40, 41, 51 and 67 — and they are the ancestor of the whole modern cluster. And add to the Suez paragraph: Carpenter’s proof 67 makes the same claim about the Grand Canal of China at seven times the baseline. The arithmetic only gets worse for it: a 700-mile chord sits about 24 km below the water surface at its midpoint, which is not an allowance any engineer has ever been asked to make.

holes.quoted_phrase: condensing Samuel Rowbotham's sprawling
holes.description: Unsourced genealogical claim, and our own corrections.json contradicts it twice. Correction 9 (ARG-B01) established that Carpenter's proof 4, the Nile river-grade item, has no Rowbotham ancestor at all; I re-verified today that 'Nile' does not occur in the 1865 Zetetic Astronomy (Gutenberg #69892). Correction 3 (ARG-C02) established that Carpenter's scriptural content is his own rather than the genre's. Carpenter also had his own prior books, named on his 1885 title page ('Common Sense' on Astronomy, London 1866; Proctor's Planet Earth; Wallace's Wonderful Water), which is where much of the material actually comes from. On a page whose product is provenance, 'condenses Rowbotham' is a derivation claim asserted without a citation, and it is the kind of line a critic uses to compile 'this site contradicts itself'.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: it condenses the Rowbotham tradition — much of it already reworked in Carpenter’s own earlier books, named on his title page — into a hundred one-line items, each closing with the same formula. Not everything in it is Rowbotham’s: proof 4, the Nile river-grade item, has no counterpart in Earth Not a Globe.

holes.quoted_phrase: although vertical, are 1.4 inches (36 mm) farther apart at the top than the bottom
holes.description: A verbatim quotation with no entry in `sources`. It is Wikipedia's Humber Bridge sentence, and Wikipedia's own reference for it is a tourism page (Visit Grimsby), not the bridge board or a design document. Two paragraphs of ours apply a stricter standard in the same breath: the MTA sentence is sourced to the operator, and Akashi Kaikyo is explicitly withheld because 'we found no operator or primary documentation of a curvature figure for it'. Applying the Akashi standard to Humber would exclude it on the same grounds. The physics checks out independently (155.5 m towers, 1,410 m apart, h*d/R = 34 mm), so the number is fine; the sourcing is not.
holes.recommendation: Replace the Humber sentence with: The Humber Bridge is widely reported to show the same effect — towers 1,410 m apart and 36 mm further apart at the top — but we have found no bridge-board or design-document source for that figure, only secondary ones, so we rest nothing on it. The geometry is checkable without it: 155.5 m towers 1,410 m apart, each plumb, diverge by h×d/R ≈ 34 mm.

holes.quoted_phrase: survives=2
holes.description: Under-rated, and the under-rating is doing work: survives<3 lets `preemptive` stay None. The best_defense we wrote ourselves contains two points our text never answers. (i) 'the 4/3 effective-earth factor ... its value is elastic - under ducting it runs to infinity, so the parameter can be set to whatever makes the link budget work.' This is the sharpest thing on the page, because k = infinity IS the flat case, and nothing in our RF paragraph says why k is a measured atmospheric quantity rather than a fitted one. (ii) 'The Gotthard figure is agreement between two survey networks reduced using the same ellipsoidal model' - and our Gotthard paragraph does assert 'requires the surface control to be reduced on an ellipsoid, with deflection of the vertical accounted for' with no citation supporting it (the tunnel-online article we cite says nothing about the reference frame). A defence that names an uncited step in our own argument is a 3, not a 2.
holes.recommendation:
Set survives=3 and add as `preemptive`:

Is the radius assumed rather than measured? No, and the RF case shows why. k is not a free parameter: it is fixed by the measured vertical gradient of refractivity, and ITU-R P.530 makes designers clear the path at the k value exceeded 99.99% of the time — the sub-refractive tail, where k drops below 1 and the bulge gets worse. A fudge factor tuned to make links close would be set generously, not adversarially. And the direction of the error is checkable: build a 50 km hop to flat-Earth geometry and it fades out, which is an observation, not a model. The same applies to Gotthard: two independently propagated networks meeting to 8 cm over 57 km is a closure test, and a reduction carrying a wrong figure for the Earth would show up as misclosure rather than as agreement.

holes.quoted_phrase: projections built to make geodesics look straight
holes.description: Wrong projection family. The projection built to make geodesics straight is the gnomonic, which is used for great-circle route planning but is not what submarine-cable route charts are drawn on. Cable and marine charts are Mercator or Mercator-derived, and Mercator's defining property is that it straightens rhumb lines, not geodesics — on Mercator a great circle appears as a curve. So the sentence explains an appearance by a mechanism that does not produce it. Any reader with a navigation background lands on this immediately, and it sits in the paragraph where we are otherwise at our strongest.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: and they look “straight” on a cable map only in the sense that any schematic route line does — on the Mercator charts these maps use, a true great circle is drawn as a curve, and the straight-looking line is a drafting convention, not a measurement.

holes.quoted_phrase: re-check against the k value exceeded 99.99% of the time, requiring roughly one full first-Fresnel-zone clearance over the highest obstacle
holes.description: The 99.99% figure is right (P.530-15 Step 2: 'obtain the value of ke(99.99%) from Fig. 2'), but the 1.0 F1 criterion belongs to Step 1, the median k = 4/3 case. At ke(99.99%) the recommendation asks for 0.6 F1 in temperate and tropical climates for paths over about 30 km, or 0.3 F1 where the obstruction is extended along the path; the designer then takes the larger of the two antenna heights. As written the clause reads as if 1.0 F1 applies at the 99.99% step.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: then re-check against the k value exceeded 99.99% of the time, where the criterion tightens to roughly 0.6 of the first Fresnel zone (0.3 over an extended obstruction); the designer takes whichever of the two steps demands the taller antenna.

holes.quoted_phrase: dedicating it to the astronomer Richard Proctor as “A Challenge to the Johns Hopkins University.”
holes.description: Two separate pieces of front matter fused into one. Gutenberg #55387 reproduces the dedication as 'Dedicated to RICHARD A. PROCTOR, Esq. / "The Greatest Astronomer of the Age."'; 'A Challenge to the JOHNS HOPKINS University' is a separate title-page banner. As written we attribute to the dedication a phrase that is not in it. Schadewald/Behrend, The Plane Truth ch. 5, records that Carpenter posted first-edition copies to Proctor, the Smithsonian and Gilman of Johns Hopkins in 1885, which is the fact the sentence is reaching for.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: dedicating it to the astronomer Richard A. Proctor as “The Greatest Astronomer of the Age” and running a separate title-page banner, “A Challenge to the JOHNS HOPKINS University”; he posted copies of the first edition to Proctor and to Gilman of Johns Hopkins.

holes.quoted_phrase: Voliva reprinted Carpenter's hundred proofs under his own Zion, Illinois imprint in 1929
holes.description: The publisher was the Christian Catholic Apostolic Church, per Schadewald/Behrend, The Plane Truth ch. 8: 'The Christian Catholic Apostolic Church reprinted Carpenter's One Hundred Proofs that the Earth Is Not a Globe in 1929.' Voliva led that church, so nothing substantive changes, but this is the bolded sentence in the gloss and the only transmission link we assert between 1885 and 2015; on this page the named publisher of a reprint is the kind of detail that should be exact.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: Voliva’s Christian Catholic Apostolic Church, in Zion, Illinois, reprinted Carpenter’s hundred proofs in 1929

citation_failures: FAILED (wording, not substance): ITU-R Handbook R-HDB-54, quoted in the refutation as 'allows engineers to plot direct wave paths as straight lines rather than calculating path curvature explicitly'. That string is not in the handbook. §3.3 reads 'To avoid having to calculate the path curvature when designing a link, the effective Earth radius can be used instead of the actual Earth radius. In this modified geometry, the difference between the path of the direct wave and the Earth's curvature becomes constant and the path of the direct wave can be plotted as a straight line...'. Our claim is true; our quotation marks are not.

UNCHECKED, not failed: the two NOAA Manual NOS NGS 3 quotations - 'would be parallel to the equipotential surface if the gravity field, at each setup, also defined a plane. This is not the case, however, since the gravity field defines a curved surface' and 'can be reduced by making the backsight and foresight distances in each setup nearly equal. If setups are thus balanced, within a tolerance, correction for curvature need not normally be made while leveling.' The PDF retrieval returned §3.1.2 and confirmed the SUBSTANCE (curvature error defined as the line of sight not being parallel to an equipotential surface; balanced backsight/foresight distances cancelling it because the error goes as distance squared; tables supplied for unbalanced setups) but the retrieval layer refused verbatim reproduction and then reported both exact strings absent - an unreliable negative from a truncated fetch. Given that the ITU quotation in the same entry turned out to be a paraphrase in quotation marks, a human should open NOAA_Manual_NOS_NGS_0003.pdf §3.1 and confirm both strings character by character before this is treated as clean.

UNCHECKED: 'Agreement at the centimetre level over 57 km requires the surface control to be reduced on an ellipsoid, with deflection of the vertical accounted for'. The cited tunnel-online article confirms 57 km, 8 cm transverse and 1 cm vertical, but says nothing about the reference frame or deflection of the vertical. The claim is almost certainly right and there is published Gotthard survey literature on it, but it currently has no supporting citation - and our own advocate attacks precisely this step.
reviews.summary: B05's verdict (REFUTED) holds and the hedge rule passes cleanly: Carpenter's proofs 3, 40, 41 and 51 are quoted verbatim-correct against Gutenberg #55387, the refutation answers his case in his order before touching any modern item, and the compression block honestly records that Carpenter is blunter than the list rather than hiding behind drifted=false. The Rowbotham 'back-and-fore sight' passage and the Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Levelling' quotation are both genuinely in the 1865 edition (Gutenberg #69892 title page confirms 1865), so the edition trap that caught A05, B01 and B04 does not recur here. The MTA Verrazzano quote, the Gotthard 8 cm/1 cm figures, the WGS 84 constants, the ke(99.99%) reference in P.530-15, the NGS 'no change in potential energy' phrasing, the Dubay 7/8 to Carpenter 3/40 mapping and every piece of arithmetic I recomputed (528 m Suez sagitta, 37 m earth bulge, 25 m Fresnel radius, 16 mm turbine divergence, 3 mm span departure) all check out. One major hole: the ITU handbook 'quotation' is our paraphrase inside quotation marks, which is the one error class this project cannot afford. Five moderates: the engineering-proof count is wrong and contradicts our own compression note while omitting Carpenter's 700-mile Grand Canal proof 67; the 'condensing Rowbotham' derivation is unsourced and cuts against two entries in our own corrections.json; the Humber Bridge quote has no source and would fail the standard we apply to Akashi Kaikyo two clauses later; advocate survives=2 suppresses a preemptive that the k-elasticity and model-internal-consistency objections genuinely earn; and the undersea-cable projection sentence names the wrong projection family. Localized edits throughout - nothing structural.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: Reached the named source in full: Rob Skiba, "The Bible and the Still Flat Earth" (c 2015-2016 by Rob Skiba), PDF at s3.amazonaws.com/mychurchwebsite/c4890/. Both sentences quoted in our compression block are verbatim and in context, he does discuss Joshua 10:13, Habakkuk 3:11, Isaiah 38:8, Psalm 19 and Ecclesiastes 1:5, and he nowhere concedes an observer-appearance reading. So the factual half of the compression block checks out. The hedge rule still fails, in its mirrored form. The list items are bare verse labels ("Joshua 10:13 sun stood still."); the source asserts far MORE than that - "there is growing evidence within the scientific community revealing that the earth is not rotating either. It is quite stationary in every respect." That second sentence is a claim about what a pendulum and a ring-laser gyro will read. Our refutation answers only the hermeneutic version - five numbered sections, not one measurement, verdict UNFALSIFIABLE - i.e. it is aimed at the fragment, which is the weaker text, while the compression block simultaneously asserts that "the treatment above is therefore aimed at the source's own claim". It is not. Note also that the drift here has no home in the seven-value enum: this is de-escalation (source flat, list bare label), the reverse of hedge_dropped, and "none" is the wrong label for it even though "drifted=false" is defensible in the narrow sense that the list does not overstate. Recording that as an enum gap rather than forcing it into a box, per the harness. One further item cuts the same way: item 450, "Prophetic visions framed from an Earth-fixed vantage", is itself an observer-frame framing - the very reading the note says the source "never entertained".

holes.quoted_phrase:
Proof-texts on a moving Sun",
    originator="Rob Skiba", originator_work="biblical-cosmology teaching", year="2015"
holes.description: The cluster credits the sun-motion proof-text corpus to Rob Skiba, 2015, and render.py line 94 prints that field as "first published by Rob Skiba". That is false, and it is refuted by a document this very entry cites. Cardinal Bellarmine's letter to Foscarini of 12 April 1615 deploys Ecclesiastes 1:5 exactly as a proof that the sun really moves and the earth stands still ("The sun also riseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose"), arguing that unlike a passenger watching the shore, "no wise man has any need to correct the error" (inters.org/Bellarmino-Letter-Foscarini). Galileo's Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina, which our own section 4 quotes at length, is a reply to that genre. In the modern geocentric lineage the same bloc is standard long before Skiba: Gerardus Bouw's Geocentricity Primer (1999, rev. 2004, bbc-cromwell.org/Geocentricity/primer.pdf) runs Joshua 10:12-13, Isaiah 38:8 and Psalm 19:4-6 as evidence that the sun's motion is real and not apparent, and Schadewald's survey "The Flat-Earth Bible" (Bulletin of the Tychonian Society 44, July 1987) already documents the corpus, as Elert's 1999 digest of it shows (hypertextbook.com/eworld/geocentric/, section "The mobility of the sun": Joshua 10:12-13, Habakkuk 3:11, Ecclesiastes 1:5, Psalm 19:4-6). This is the same failure class as the 2026-08-02 correction it replaced: an attribution asserted from the shape of the genre rather than checked against earlier primary texts. It is worse than that one in one respect - the Method tab tells readers to treat attributions on arguments "still marked cluster depth" as provisional, and C02 has a full DEEP entry, so it is presented as audited. It is also the C02 correction the Method tab holds up as a success story.
holes.recommendation:
Replace the two fields with:
    originator="Gerardus Bouw", originator_work="Geocentricity (and A Geocentricity Primer)", year="1992",
and replace the note with: note="Outside the testable domain. Attribution corrected twice. Carpenter's 1885 pamphlet contains exactly ONE scriptural proof (#50, on immovability and the stretched-out earth) and never mentions Joshua, Habakkuk or Ecclesiastes; the 2026-08-02 reattribution to Rob Skiba (2015) was also wrong, in the other direction. This proof-text bloc is not modern. Bellarmine cites Ecclesiastes 1:5 against Copernicus on 12 April 1615, and Galileo's Letter to Christina answers that argument the same year. Bouw's Geocentricity is the earliest work inside this review's own person set to run the full modern set - Joshua 10:12-13, Isaiah 38:8, Psalm 19:4-6 - as proofs of a physically moving sun; Schadewald had documented the corpus by 1987. Skiba (2015) and the online 'more than 200' compilations are distributors of it, not its origin, and are where these sixteen items were drawn from."

holes.quoted_phrase: The treatment above is therefore aimed at the source’s own claim
holes.description: The compression block states that the treatment answers the source's own claim, "a stationary Earth asserted as fact, not a reading offered as devotion." It does not. The source sentence the block itself quotes - "there is growing evidence within the scientific community revealing that the earth is not rotating either. It is quite stationary in every respect" (Skiba, The Bible and the Still Flat Earth, verified verbatim in the PDF) - is a falsifiable physical claim. The refutation engages it nowhere: section 1 is about language, 2 declines the interpretive question, 3 is about method consistency, 4 quotes Galileo, 5 declines Joshua 10, and the verdict says "the claim as stated cannot be confirmed or refuted by measurement." The steelman's why_it_doesnt_save_claim names gyroscopes, pendulums and ring interferometers and then never delivers any. So we publish a sentence claiming we answered the source at the source's strength, immediately below a quotation showing the source making a stronger, testable claim we declined. A defender reads that as either evasion or carelessness, and on the hedge rule it is the fragment-not-the-source failure with the polarity reversed.
holes.recommendation: Replace that sentence and the caveat that follows it with: "That produces a split we have to state plainly, because it cuts against the verdict. The sixteen list items are bare verse labels, and as stated they are claims about how to read a text, which no instrument settles — that is what UNFALSIFIABLE records here. The named source does not stop there. The earth is not rotating either is a claim about what a Foucault pendulum and a ring-laser gyroscope will read, and claims of that kind are answered rather than declined: see ARG-A06 and ARG-A07. The verdict on this page is therefore scoped to the sixteen items, not to everything their source says. The drift runs the unusual way round: the list carries less assertion than the paragraphs it was drawn from, and the part it dropped is the falsifiable part." Then add the same scoping clause to the refutation's Verdict paragraph, after "...is not the kind of thing measurement addresses.": "It is a verdict on these sixteen items as the list states them. Where the authors they come from go further and assert that the Earth does not rotate, that is a different claim in a different domain, and this review answers it at ARG-A06 and ARG-A07."

holes.quoted_phrase: The standard compilation files Isaiah 40:22 under “Earth is a Disk/Circle”
holes.description: Section 3 is the only part of the treatment that claims to establish anything, and its evidence is quoted verbatim from a source we never name, never link, and do not list in sources[]. Our own hedge-audit file says so outright: scripts/_hedge_audit_batch_c.py, docstring, records that the headings "Sun Moves, not the Earth", "Earth is a Disk/Circle, not a ball", "Earth has 4 Corners/Quarters", "Earth has Pillars, and hangs on nothing" come from the worldslastchance.com "more than 200" compilation and "are the ones our C02 refutation already quotes verbatim without citing them." On a page whose product is provenance, an unattributed "the standard compilation" is not acceptable, and it is the exact move we criticise. It is also unnecessary: every verse used as an example is in the 461-item list itself - 414 Isaiah 40:22 circle of Earth, 420 Revelation 7:1 four corners, 415 1 Sam 2:8 pillars set world, 410 Psalm 75:3 pillars of Earth, 412 Job 26:7 hangs on nothing - so the internal-conflict point can be made from our own corpus with item numbers a reader can check, instead of from an anonymous third party. As written, a defender's reply is ready-made: none of your four example verses is one of the sixteen items on this page.
holes.recommendation: Replace the paragraph with: "It does not deliver consistent results, and the list under review shows it without any help from us. Item 414 enters Isaiah 40:22, the circle of the Earth. Item 420 enters Revelation 7:1, the four corners. Items 410 and 415 enter the pillars of Psalm 75:3 and 1 Samuel 2:8. Item 412 enters Job 26:7, the Earth hung upon nothing. Those are four different shapes and two incompatible supports, entered as five separate confirmations of one physical model. The compilations these items are drawn from do the same thing under explicit headings — World’s Last Chance’s “more than 200” set files one heading as “Earth has Pillars, and hangs on nothing”, which states both at once. A method that returns circle, four corners, pillars and hangs-upon-nothing as independent confirmations of one model is not filtering anything. It is counting." Add to sources[]: dict(label="World's Last Chance, 'more than 200 proofs' scriptural compilation - section headings quoted above", url="https://www.worldslastchance.com/biblical-christian-beliefs/200-proofs-earth-is-not-a-spinning-ball.html").

holes.quoted_phrase: Skiba states the conclusion
holes.description: The whole hedge verdict rests on Skiba, "The Bible and the Still Flat Earth", and the compression note quotes him by name - but that document appears in neither C02's sources[] (Carpenter x2, Galileo x2, USNO, HMNAO) nor works.py. PER-SKIBA's only work record is WRK-SKIBA-2018, Testing the Globe (2018), and scripts/_hedge_audit_batch_c.py states plainly that the 2018 book "was not obtained; the assessment rests on his own PDF essay, not the book." So the reader is shown a named quotation with no way to check it, supported by a work record for a different, unread book, dated three years after the year on the cluster card. The PDF is reachable and was read in full for this review.
holes.recommendation: Add to C02 sources[]: dict(label="Rob Skiba, The Bible and the Still Flat Earth (c. 2015-2016) - the essay quoted in the compression block; PDF", url="https://s3.amazonaws.com/mychurchwebsite/c4890/the_bible_and_the_still_flat_earth_rob_skiba.pdf"). Add a WRK-SKIBA-2015 record for it in works.py (author PER-SKIBA, year 2015, pd=False) and add it to PER-SKIBA's works list, with a note on WRK-SKIBA-2018 that the book itself has not been obtained and no claim on this site rests on it.

holes.quoted_phrase: two Psalm 19 items sit in this cluster
holes.description: Wrong count and wrong characterisation, in the one paragraph where we are being scrupulous about our own coverage.
