There are four Psalm 19 items in C02, not two: 70 (Psalm 19 sun's tabernacle), 149 (Psalm 19:4-6 sun's course), 417 (Psalm 19 line through Earth), 435 (Psalm 19 heavens declare glory). And the claim that the compilations file "those verses" away from sun-motion is false for two of them: Psalm 19:4-6, the sun as a bridegroom running his circuit from one end of heaven to the other, is a first-rank sun-motion proof-text, cited as exactly that in Bouw's Geocentricity Primer ch. 1 (bbc-cromwell.org/Geocentricity/primer.pdf) and listed under "The mobility of the sun" in Elert's 1999 digest of Schadewald (hypertextbook.com/eworld/geocentric/). Two further items are genuinely off-theme and go unmentioned: 418, Ecclesiastes 1:6 wind circuits, is about the wind rather than the sun, and 450, prophetic visions framed from an Earth-fixed vantage, is an observer-frame framing - the reading the same note says the source "never entertained".
holes.recommendation: Replace the caveat with: "Two caveats we record rather than resolve. Four Psalm 19 items sit in this cluster — 70, 149, 417 and 435 — and they do not all belong to the same argument: Psalm 19:4–6, the sun running his circuit from one end of heaven to the other, is a sun-motion proof-text of long standing and is used as one by Bouw, while 417 and 435 are filed in the compilations under the firmament and the “line” of creation. And two items sit oddly in a sun-motion cluster at all: 418 is Ecclesiastes 1:6, which is about the wind, and 450 frames prophetic visions as taken from an Earth-fixed vantage — which is the observer-perspective reading the named source declines to take. Cluster boundaries are ours, and these are the places ours are weakest."

holes.quoted_phrase: could not be made if the Earth were a globe … we have a store
holes.description: The ellipsis in our Proof 50 quotation removes the single sentence our own straw_man block relies on. The full text reads: "...and which are, therefore, said by the astronomer to be absurd and contrary to what he knows to be true! This is the groundwork of modern infidelity. But, since every one of many, many allusions to the Earth and the heavenly bodies in the Scriptures can be demonstrated to be absolutely true to nature, and we read of the Earth being 'stretched out' 'above the waters,' as 'standing in the water and out of the water,' of its being 'established that it cannot be moved,' we have a store..." (Project Gutenberg 55387, verified). The straw_man field asserts that Carpenter "frames the astronomer's position as 'the groundwork of modern infidelity'" - which is accurate - but a reader checking it against the quote directly above cannot find the phrase. The text is public domain and pd=True, so there is no reason to elide it, and restoring it also puts the immovability and stretched-out-earth wording on the page, which is what the gloss claims Proof 50 gestures at.
holes.recommendation: Restore the elided text so the quote reads unbroken: "...but hundreds of allusions there are in its pages which could not be made if the Earth were a globe, and which are, therefore, said by the astronomer to be absurd and contrary to what he knows to be true! This is the groundwork of modern infidelity. But, since every one of many, many allusions to the Earth and the heavenly bodies in the Scriptures can be demonstrated to be absolutely true to nature, and we read of the Earth being \"stretched out\" \"above the waters,\" as \"standing in the water and out of the water,\" of its being \"established that it cannot be moved,\" we have a store from which to take all the proofs we need, but we will just put down one proof-the Scriptural proof-that Earth is not a globe."

holes.quoted_phrase: Quoting Cardinal Baronius, he wrote
holes.description: Galileo does not name Baronius. The Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina attributes the line to "an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree" (verified verbatim in the Ohio State translation we cite: "I would say here something that was heard from an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree: 'That the intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes.'"). The identification with Baronio is a standard editorial gloss, not Galileo's text. Every other Galileo phrase we quote checked out verbatim - "in discussions of physical problems we ought to begin not from the authority of scriptural passages but from sense-experiences and necessary demonstrations", "but casually", and "proceed alike from the divine Word" - so this is the one loose thread in an otherwise clean citation, and on a page about provenance it is worth two words.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Quoting a line he attributes only to “an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree” — Cardinal Baronio, by long editorial consensus — he wrote:"

citation_failures: UNCHECKED, not failed: worldslastchance.com returned HTTP 429 on the direct fetch, so the six section headings our refutation quotes verbatim were not re-verified against the live page in this pass. They are corroborated only by our own scripts/_hedge_audit_batch_c.py docstring, which is not an independent source. Re-verify before publishing the fix to hole 3.

UNCHECKED: Rob Skiba, Testing the Globe (2018) - WRK-SKIBA-2018, the only work record attached to PER-SKIBA - was not obtained in this pass or in the original hedge audit. No claim in C02 should rest on it.

PARTIAL: the Ohio State PDF of the Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina appears to be an abridgement - Joshua is not mentioned in it anywhere, though the full letter's closing discussion of Joshua 10 is its best-known section. All four phrases C02 quotes from it were verified verbatim in the file we cite, so no C02 claim is affected, but the source label should not be read as pointing to the complete letter.

VERIFIED: Carpenter, One Hundred Proofs, Gutenberg 55387 - Proofs 38, 39 and 50 quoted accurately; Joshua, Habakkuk, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Psalm and Genesis all return zero occurrences; "groundwork of modern infidelity" is in Proof 50; only Proof 50 mentions the Bible or Scripture.

VERIFIED: Skiba, The Bible and the Still Flat Earth - both compression-block sentences verbatim and in context; c. 2015-2016; discusses Joshua 10:13, Habakkuk 3:11, Isaiah 38:8, Psalm 19, Ecclesiastes 1:5; no phenomenological concession anywhere. Quotation is 48 words, inside the 60-word in-copyright cap.

VERIFIED: Bellarmine to Foscarini, 12 April 1615, citing Ecclesiastes 1:5 as proof of a really-moving sun (inters.org). Bouw, A Geocentricity Primer, 1999 rev. 2004, running Joshua 10:12-13, Isaiah 38:8 and Psalm 19:4-6 as proofs. Elert 1999 digesting Schadewald, "The Flat-Earth Bible", Bulletin of the Tychonian Society 44, July 1987, under the heading "The mobility of the sun".
reviews.summary: C02's verdict (UNFALSIFIABLE) survives, its steelman is genuinely KERNEL-tier, and its handling of religion is disciplined - it adjudicates nothing theological and says so repeatedly. But two critical faults sit in the two most load-bearing places. First, the hedge rule fails in mirrored form: the compression block quotes Skiba asserting that the Earth "is not rotating either... quite stationary in every respect" - a falsifiable physical claim, verified verbatim in his 2015 PDF - and then asserts that our treatment "is therefore aimed at the source's own claim", when the refutation declines all physical engagement and answers only the bare verse labels. We answered the weaker fragment and published a sentence saying we had not. Second, the 2026-08-02 reattribution of this cluster to "Rob Skiba, 2015" is itself wrong, and wrong in the same way the Carpenter attribution it replaced was: Bellarmine deploys Ecclesiastes 1:5 against Copernicus on 12 April 1615, Galileo's Letter to Christina - which this very entry quotes - answers that argument, Schadewald documented the corpus in 1987 and Bouw ran the full modern set as proofs by 1992/1999. render.py prints that field as "first published by Rob Skiba", and the Method tab's provisional-attribution caveat does not cover C02 because C02 has a full DEEP entry. Below those: section 3, the only part of the treatment that claims to establish anything, quotes an unnamed compilation verbatim with no citation, while every example verse it uses is in our own corpus with an item number; the Skiba PDF the hedge verdict rests on is in no source list or work record; and the "two Psalm 19 items" caveat miscounts four as two and mischaracterises Psalm 19:4-6. Also noted, not filed as a hole: review/triage.json still records C02's originator as William Carpenter, which build.py does not read but a future editor might.

reviews.hedge_rule_note:
The refutation is aimed at the source, not the fragment. It grants the solid-firmament reading at full strength (Seely's WTJ 53 wording, verified verbatim at thedivinecouncil.com/seelypt1.pdf: "The historical-grammatical meaning of raqia' in Gen 1:6-8 is very clearly a literally solid firmament") and answers the description-to-prediction step, which is the load-bearing move in Skiba's own document. The compression block also does the rarer, harder thing correctly: it considers hedge_dropped, rejects it, and says why. drifted=true with drift_type=unsourced_addition is the right call for items 424/425/439 and is not an evasion.

BUT the evidence sentence used to justify rejecting hedge_dropped is itself de-hedged by us. Skiba's actual sentence, verified in the quoted PDF, is: "So much for the notion that the sky/heaven above us consists of just gaseous air. We apparently have a hard canopy somewhere, very high above us." Our compression note renders this as "a man who writes that the sky consists of a hard canopy high above us" — "apparently" and "somewhere" are dropped. That is the exact compression operation the project exists to document, performed by us, inside the block whose job is to catch it. It does not flip the drift verdict (the document's title and thrust do assert a still, flat earth), so hedge_rule_ok stays true, but the sentence must be requoted accurately or the finding is self-refuting.

holes.quoted_phrase: and we have no evidence that he did
holes.description: We assert we have no evidence Skiba took the proof-text set from Schadewald. The evidence is inside the very document we quote as our passage. Skiba's "The Bible and the Still Flat Earth" (the 2015-2016 PDF at the URL in our own sources list) names Schadewald and block-quotes him at length: "Regardless, an online article, titled 'The Flat-Earth Bible,' written by Robert J. Schadewald, (c) 1987, 1995, states some things worth quoting here (I recommend you actually read the entire article too):" — followed by roughly five to six paragraphs of Schadewald, including "The vault of heaven is a crucial concept" and the NEB Isaiah 40:22 rendering "sits throned on the vaulted roof of earth", and carrying Job 37:18, Isaiah 40:22, Psalm 19:1, Psalm 102:25, Job 9:8, Job 22:14, Isaiah 42:5, 44:24, 45:12, 48:13 inside the quoted block. This is the same failure class as corrections.json entries 3, 8 and 9 (attribution asserted from the shape of the genre rather than checked against the primary text) running in the negative direction: we disclaimed a derivation that the primary source documents in plain sight. On a page whose product is provenance, throwing away a signed, dated, openly credited transmission is the most damaging error available. Note the finding is not plagiarism — Skiba credits Schadewald by name and tells readers to go read the whole article — and the replacement must say so.
holes.recommendation: Replace the sentence We do not claim Skiba took it from Schadewald, and we have no evidence that he did. What is established is that the list predates his teaching by twenty-eight years and that its first modern compiler was a debunker. with: Skiba takes it from Schadewald, and says so. The teaching document quoted above introduces “an online article, titled ‘The Flat-Earth Bible,’ written by Robert J. Schadewald, © 1987, 1995”, block-quotes several paragraphs of it, and tells the reader “I recommend you actually read the entire article too”. Job 37:18, Isaiah 40:22, Psalm 19:1, Job 9:8 and Isaiah 44:24 all reach the page inside that quotation. This is not concealment and nothing here suggests it was: the citation is open, credited and dated. It is something rarer and more useful — a fully documented link in a transmission chain, in which a distributor's proof-text set is lifted, with attribution, from a critic who assembled it to argue the opposite.
holes.recommendation_note: Also update scripts/clusters.py C04 real_source (see separate hole) and consider a line in claude/source-genealogy.md.

holes.quoted_phrase: Three of the nine items cannot be located in the named source.
holes.description: The heading is wrong on its own criterion, and the criterion is applied inconsistently across the nine items. "The named source" is used throughout the gloss to mean Skiba's teaching document ("Skiba's teaching document does not cite Tobit"). Checked against that document: item 439's Psalm 104 IS in it — Skiba quotes Psalm 104:1-9 in full and bolds verse 2 ("stretchest out the heavens like a curtain"), verse 3 ("layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters") and verse 5 ("laid the foundations of the earth"). Item 425's 1 Enoch IS in it — "Things get even worse if we accept the Book of Enoch as having any measure of credibility, because as far as I'm concerned, that book knocks a home run out of the park for the Flat Earthers." Only item 424 (Tobit) is absent from Skiba, from Schadewald, and from the Worlds Last Chance compilation. Meanwhile item 426 ("Jubilees lights for Earth") is equally absent from all three — Skiba's document does not cite Jubilees, Schadewald does not, and the WLC list does not — yet our sources list passes it with "(item 426 checks out)" on the strength of Jubilees 2:8-10 saying what the item says. So one criterion (is it in Skiba) condemns three items including 426, and a different criterion (does the named scripture say it) condemns two and clears 426. We ran a different test on each item and reported one count.
holes.recommendation: Replace the heading and its first clause with: 2. On the list's fidelity, four findings and only one of them is an absence. One item is unlocatable in every source we could read: Tobit 13 dome heaven (item 424). Tobit 13 is a hymn of thanksgiving and a vision of Jerusalem rebuilt in sapphire and gold; it contains no dome, no vault, no firmament and no description of the sky's structure at all, and it appears in neither Skiba's document, nor Schadewald's essay, nor the standard circulating compilation. Two more items are present in the source but misdescribe the text they name. Psalm 104 firmament supporting lights (item 439): Skiba does quote this psalm — verses 1–9, with verses 2, 3 and 5 emphasised — but the word firmament does not occur in Psalm 104 in the KJV and no verse of it places any light in anything; the standard compilation likewise files Psalm 104:1–9 under the heading “Where is the sun?”, quoting the curtain, not a firmament. 1 Enoch concentric heavens (item 425): Skiba does invoke the Book of Enoch, but 1 Enoch's astronomical cosmology is a portal cosmology — “I saw six portals in which the sun rises, and six portals in which the sun sets” (1 Enoch 72:3) — not a scheme of nested heavens; that schema belongs to 2 Enoch. And one item we had passed should be recorded alongside them: Jubilees lights for Earth (item 426) states what Jubilees 2:8–10 states, but Jubilees is cited by neither Skiba, nor Schadewald, nor the standard compilation, so on the same test it is as unattached to the named originator as Tobit is. Also correct section 6, which repeats the old count: "In short: three of the nine items cannot be located in the named source".

holes.quoted_phrase: endorses Augustine's reading of the firmament as the region of the air where clouds gather, calling it
holes.description: Misattributed quotation. The words "worthy of all commendation, as neither contrary to faith nor difficult to be proved" are Augustine's, not Aquinas's. Summa Theologiae I q.68 a.1 reads: "Augustine, in fact (Gen. ad lit. ii, 4), recommends it thus: 'I consider this view of the question worthy of all commendation, as neither contrary to faith nor difficult to be proved and believed.'" Aquinas is reporting Augustine's self-commendation, and in the body of the article he canvasses both the starry-heaven and the atmospheric readings under Augustine's rule about not adhering too firmly to any one of them — "endorses" is stronger than the article supports. We also silently truncate the quotation ("and believed" dropped without ellipsis). A defender with a copy of the Summa gets a free hit here, and it is precisely the citation-attribution error class that fills corrections.json.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: Aquinas, canvassing the opinions in Summa Theologiae I q.68 a.1, sets the starry-heaven reading beside Augustine's reading of the firmament as the region of the air where clouds gather, and records that “Augustine, in fact, recommends it thus: ‘I consider this view of the question worthy of all commendation, as neither contrary to faith nor difficult to be proved and believed’” — working throughout under Augustine's rule that one should hold a particular explanation “only in such measure as to be ready to abandon it, if it be proved with certainty to be false.” He does not settle the question; that a thirteenth-century doctor could leave it open is itself the point.

holes.quoted_phrase: does not overstate a man who writes that the sky consists of a hard canopy high above us.
holes.description: The one sentence we use as evidence that Skiba states the claim at full strength is itself de-hedged in our paraphrase. His actual sentence in the quoted document is: "So much for the notion that the sky/heaven above us consists of just gaseous air. We apparently have a hard canopy somewhere, very high above us." We drop "apparently" and "somewhere" — two hedges — and then cite the result as proof that no hedge was dropped. The conclusion may well survive on other grounds (the document is titled "The Bible and the Still Flat Earth" and asserts a stationary enclosed earth), but the demonstration as written performs the operation it is denying, inside the block whose entire function is to catch that operation. Highest-embarrassment finding on the page after the Schadewald one.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: Item 72, “Firmament as real structure”, is close to what Skiba asserts, though not identical to it: his sentence is “We apparently have a hard canopy somewhere, very high above us” — two hedges, on the certainty and on the location, both of which the item drops. What the item does not do is manufacture a claim its author declined to make: the document's title is The Bible and the Still Flat Earth, its surrounding paragraphs assert a stationary enclosed earth, and Skiba's disclaimer is about his own authority rather than the reading's strength. So the drift on this item is real but small, and it is not the drift that matters here. We record it rather than smoothing it over, because a page that criticises compression cannot compress its own evidence.

holes.quoted_phrase: its first modern compiler was a debunker
holes.description: Unsupported, and contradicted by a source we cite ourselves. Younker and Davidson, "The Myth of the Solid Heavenly Dome", AUSS 49:1 (2011) 125-147 — in our sources list — trace the solid/metal-sky reading and its supporting texts to nineteenth-century scholarship, naming John Pye-Smith (1839), Tayler Lewis and Charles Wycliffe Goodwin, and locating the modern conflation with Washington Irving and Letronne. Schiaparelli's Astronomy in the Old Testament (Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1905) is a book-length compilation of the same Old Testament cosmology material. Seely's own 1991 WTJ study rests on a long prior literature. "Assembled in print in July 1987" is defensible for the specific flat-earth-facing set including 1 Enoch; "its first modern compiler" is not, and it is the kind of rhetorically attractive line corrections.json entry 7 was written about.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: the compiler in the transmission chain that reaches this list was a debunker. The underlying scholarly reading is far older — Younker and Davidson trace it to Pye-Smith in 1839, and Schiaparelli's Astronomy in the Old Testament (Clarendon, 1905) had compiled the same Old Testament cosmology texts eight decades before Schadewald. What Schadewald did was assemble them for a geocentrist readership, in the flat-earth-facing form the modern movement uses, twenty-eight years before Skiba quoted him.

holes.quoted_phrase: The ancient Hebrew sky really was solid
holes.description: The TLDR asserts as fact about the world the exact proposition the whole entry exists to distinguish from a fact about a text. "The ancient Hebrew sky really was solid" states that the sky over the ancient Near East was, in fact, solid — which is false, and which is the description-to-reality slide that section 2 of the refutation names as the argument's fatal step. Seely's finding, correctly stated, is about what the Hebrews pictured, not about the sky. Reader impact is at maximum: this is the first clause a reader meets and many will never expand. Any hostile reader who pastes this page into an AI and says "debunk this debunk" gets this sentence first.
holes.recommendation: Replace the opening clause with: The ancient Hebrews really did picture the sky as solid, and mainstream biblical scholarship says so — Skiba did not invent that, and anyone who tells him he did is the one out of step with the journals.

holes.quoted_phrase: The ancient Near Eastern sky was solid.
holes.description: Same defect as the TLDR, in the concession that opens the refutation. It is immediately followed by "That is mainstream biblical scholarship", which a charitable reader will use to repair the sentence, so the impact is lower — but the sentence is bolded-adjacent, sits at the head of the section, and asserts the physical claim rather than the scholarly one. Since the argument turns entirely on keeping "the text describes X" apart from "X is the case", our own concession must not collapse them.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: The ancient Near Eastern picture of the sky was of something solid, and the writers of Genesis shared it.

holes.quoted_phrase: real_source=None, verdict="UNFALSIFIABLE", note="Outside the testable domain."
holes.description: With the Schadewald citation now documented inside Skiba's own teaching document, real_source=None is a claim of ours that has been falsified. The field elsewhere in the dataset carries the genuine scholarly source a cluster's originator was drawing on (compare the A-lane rows, e.g. "Michelson & Morley 1887, Am. J. Sci. 34:333"). C04's originator quotes, by name and with a copyright date, an essay by the president of the NCSE board. Leaving it None discards the best-evidenced provenance link in lane C.
holes.recommendation: Change the C04 record in scripts/clusters.py to: real_source="Robert Schadewald, 'The Flat-Earth Bible', Bulletin of the Tychonian Society 44 (July 1987), 27-39 - quoted by name and at length in Skiba's teaching document", verdict="UNFALSIFIABLE", note="Outside the testable domain. The proof-text set is quoted, with attribution, from a critic who assembled it to argue the texts are ancient."

holes.quoted_phrase: What Skiba actually uses from that psalm is verse 2
holes.description: Incomplete. Skiba quotes Psalm 104:1-9 and emphasises three verses, not two: verse 2 (curtain), verse 3 (beams in the waters) and verse 5 ("laid the foundations of the earth, that it should not be removed for ever"). Verse 5 matters because our own corpus already files it as item 62 in ARG-C01. A defender can say we described his use of the psalm and left out the verse we ourselves treat as load-bearing elsewhere.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: What Skiba actually uses from that psalm is verses 1–9, with three phrases emphasised: verse 2, the heavens stretched out “like a curtain”; verse 3, the beams of God's chambers laid in the waters; and verse 5, the foundations of the earth “that it should not be removed for ever” — which is the immovability material handled at ARG-C01, not a firmament

holes.quoted_phrase: later president of the National Center for Science Education
holes.description: Slightly overstated against the source we cite for it. The Wikipedia entry says he "served on the board of directors of the National Center for Science Education" from 1986 to 1992, "including two years as president" — that is president of the board, over a span that begins the year before the 1987 essay rather than clearly after it, and NCSE's executive was Eugenie Scott. "Later president of" reads as heading the organisation subsequently.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: who sat on the board of the National Center for Science Education from 1986 to 1992 and served two of those years as its board president

citation_failures: scripts/_b7_C04.py refutation section 3 — 'worthy of all commendation, as neither contrary to faith nor difficult to be proved' attributed to Aquinas ('calling it'). Verified at newadvent.org/summa/1068.htm: the words are Augustine's, quoted by Aquinas ('Augustine, in fact (Gen. ad lit. ii, 4), recommends it thus'), and the quotation is truncated ('and believed' dropped without ellipsis).

scripts/_b7_C04.py gloss — 'its first modern compiler was a debunker'. No citation supports a first-compiler claim, and Younker & Davidson (already in our sources list) name Pye-Smith 1839, Tayler Lewis and Goodwin as earlier; Schiaparelli, Astronomy in the Old Testament (Clarendon, 1905) is an earlier book-length compilation.

scripts/_b7_C04.py gloss — 'We do not claim Skiba took it from Schadewald, and we have no evidence that he did'. Refuted by the source cited two fields above it in the same entry: the Skiba PDF names and block-quotes Schadewald's 'The Flat-Earth Bible'.

scripts/_b7_C04.py sources — '(item 426 checks out)' on the Jubilees entry. Jubilees 2:8-10 does say what item 426 says, but Jubilees is cited by none of the three sources we used to condemn Tobit (Skiba's document, Schadewald 1987, the Worlds Last Chance compilation). The pass uses a different test from the one applied to the other items.

UNCHECKED, not failed: Paul H. Seely, 'The Geographical Meaning of Earth and Seas in Genesis 1:10', WTJ 59 (1997) — galaxie.com serves only the first page or two behind a subscription. Title, author, journal, volume and 1997 date confirmed; the specific claim that Seely 'argued that too' (a flat, disc-shaped earth) could not be verified against the article text.

UNCHECKED, not failed: Younker & Davidson full text — digitalcommons.andrews.edu PDF returned 403. Citation, page range 125-147, the 19th-century-origins thesis and the spherical-Earth-inside-solid-spheres point were all confirmed instead via grisda.org's copy of the same article.

PARTIAL ACCESS caveat: the Skiba PDF is long and the fetch tool appears to render only part of it (it reports the Book of Enoch discussion as 'cut off'). All positive findings above (Schadewald quotation, Psalm 104:1-9, the 'apparently ... somewhere' sentence, the copyright line) are robust to truncation; the negative finding 'does not cite Tobit / does not cite Jubilees' is scoped accordingly and the entry's existing 'not located, not does-not-exist' discipline should be kept.
reviews.summary: C04 is one of the better-built entries on the site — the concession is genuine, the steelman reaches KERNEL tier, the verdict is honest, and the compression block does the rare thing of testing hedge_dropped and rejecting it with reasons. It is holed anyway, in one place badly. The gloss states "we have no evidence" that Skiba took the proof-text set from Schadewald; Skiba's own teaching document, the artefact we quote as our passage, names "an online article, titled 'The Flat-Earth Bible,' written by Robert J. Schadewald, © 1987, 1995", block-quotes several paragraphs of it, and recommends readers read the whole thing. We disclaimed the best-documented transmission link in lane C. Four further majors: "three of the nine items cannot be located in the named source" applies a different test to each item and mis-states the count (Psalm 104 and 1 Enoch are both in Skiba; Jubilees, which we pass, is in none of our three sources); "worthy of all commendation" is Augustine's phrase, not Aquinas's; the compression block strips "apparently" and "somewhere" from the one Skiba sentence it uses to prove no hedge was dropped; and "its first modern compiler was a debunker" is contradicted by Younker & Davidson, whom we cite. The TLDR's "The ancient Hebrew sky really was solid" asserts as fact the exact description-to-reality slide the entry exists to name. Verdict UNFALSIFIABLE holds and should not move.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: The refutation is aimed at the source, not the fragment: sections 5 and 6 answer Skiba's own resolution before the list's seven items are touched, and the compression block records both the item-level unsourced_addition (Psalm 61:2, item 164) and the load-bearing hedge_dropped (the caveat on the container) rather than forcing one box. That structure is right. The defect is the mirror of a hedge-rule failure rather than an instance of it: the "source wording" we set against the list is itself partly unverified. The sentence we print as Skiba's — "So, what you effectively end up with is a circle inscribed into a square" — could not be located in any Skiba text reachable by search, and the word "square" appears in his corpus only in a reader's comment on his own blog ("I have seen illustration with a circle sitting within a square", commenter Sandy, robschannel.com/the-four-corners-of-the-earth, 26 Feb 2017). His located wording is weaker and vaguer: "Isaiah's 'circle of the Earth' was INSCRIBED (i.e. cut into) something else that likely has four legitimate corners/ends" (same article), and "carved as a 'circle' with edge boarders inside something with four corners" (the 2015-16 PDF, verified). So we upgraded a vague container into a named polygon — a certainty upgrade of exactly the kind we prosecute the compiler for, running in the source's favour rather than against him, which is why it survived review. drifted=true is used honestly here, not as avoidance.

holes.quoted_phrase: So, what you effectively end up with is a circle inscribed into a square.
holes.description: This sentence is printed inside quotation marks as Rob Skiba's own words and cited to a named work, and it could not be located in any Skiba source. Checks run 2026-08-09: the cited PDF (s3.amazonaws.com/.../the_bible_and_the_still_flat_earth_rob_skiba.pdf) returns no occurrence of "square" in the extracted text (extraction truncated, so 'not located', not 'does not exist'); testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html contains no occurrence of "square" or "inscribed"; robschannel.com/the-four-corners-of-the-earth (26 Feb 2017) contains "square" exactly once and it is a reader's question from a commenter named Sandy, not Skiba, and the fetch confirms Skiba does not use the word anywhere in that article or in his replies; three web searches on the exact phrase return nothing. Skiba's actual wording is 'INSCRIBED (i.e. cut into) something else that likely has four legitimate corners/ends' and 'carved as a "circle" with edge boarders inside something with four corners' — both verified, neither of which names a square. The same fabricated string is reused in compression.source_wording as 'so, what you effectively end up with is a circle inscribed into a square'. On a site whose product is provenance, a quotation mark around a sentence the author did not write is the single worst failure available, and it is in the passage block a reader meets first.
holes.recommendation: Replace the passage quote with verified wording (46 words, inside the 60-word in-copyright cap): "In this case, it's quite easy to see how Isaiah's “circle of the Earth” was INSCRIBED (i.e. cut into) something else that likely has four legitimate corners/ends. … Now I'm not being dogmatic about any of this. I fully acknowledge this is pure speculation on my part." In compression.source_wording, replace the first clause with: "Skiba: Isaiah's “circle of the Earth” was “INSCRIBED (i.e. cut into) something else that likely has four legitimate corners/ends” — with the alternative that the corners “could be part of the ‘roof’ above the system”, flagged “I fully acknowledge this is pure speculation on my part.”"

holes.quoted_phrase: Rob Skiba resolves it with a square container he calls pure speculation
holes.description: Two errors compounded in the field readers see first and may never expand past. (1) 'square container' is our word, not his — see the critical hole above. (2) The 'pure speculation' caveat does not attach to the container at all. It is on testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html, and the paragraph it follows reads: 'Thus, if true, then the 4 corners don't necessarily have to be part of the “circle of the Earth” below, but rather they could be part of the “roof” above the system' — i.e. the disclaimer covers the corners-on-the-roof alternative and the visual depiction ('I'm just trying to think “outside the box” and doing the best I can with the information provided to depict this stuff visually'), not the inscribed-container model. As written the TLDR asserts a shape he did not name and a disclaimer he did not place there, and a defender who checks one page finds both.
holes.recommendation: "The contradiction belongs to the list rather than to the teacher credited with it: Rob Skiba resolves it by having the circle cut into a larger object that carries the corners — or by moving the corners to the roof above the system, which he flags as pure speculation — and the compiler kept the verses and dropped both."

holes.quoted_phrase: He calls the construction speculation, in those words.
holes.description: Same scope error as the TLDR, restated in the section that carries the verdict. Verified against testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html: the sentence 'Now I'm not being dogmatic about any of this. I fully acknowledge this is pure speculation on my part.' follows the corners-on-the-roof paragraph, on a page where the word 'square' does not occur. The compression block repeats the error at 'a square container the source describes and then labels, in terms, “pure speculation on my part”', and that sentence is the load-bearing one for the whole hedge_dropped finding — if the caveat sits on the roof alternative rather than the container, the finding is still true (a hedge was stripped in transit) but it is a different hedge on a different claim, and it has to be stated as the one he actually wrote.
holes.recommendation: In refutation section 5: "He calls the second of these — the corners belonging to the roof of the system rather than to the ground — pure speculation, in those words, on the page carrying his 3D model." In the compression note, replace "a square container the source describes and then labels, in terms, “pure speculation on my part”" with "a container the source describes and an alternative placement of the corners he labels, in terms, “pure speculation on my part”".

holes.quoted_phrase: two passages from it, joined by an ellipsis
holes.description: The locator states that both halves of the quote come from 'The Bible and the Still Flat Earth, the 2015–2016 teaching document'. They do not. The disclaimer half is documented on testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html ('Enoch's Domed World'), a separate page; the 'inscribed into something else' half is documented in two robschannel.com articles ('Circle Means CIRCLE – NOT Ball/Sphere/Globe!', 12 Aug 2016, and 'The Four Corners of the Earth', 26 Feb 2017). Neither page appears anywhere in the entry's sources list, although between them they supply the disclaimer, the inscribed-container wording and the east/west argument the steelman credits to Skiba. The Scope paragraph's claim 'Verified against Skiba's 2015–2016 document' is therefore false for the entry's most load-bearing quotation. What IS verified in the cited PDF, and should be kept: 'carved as a “circle” with edge boarders inside something with four corners'; 'As Robert J. Schadewald points out, the Hebrew word used here is “chug” (pronounced “khoog”)'; the '© 1987, 1995' line; and the printed Simanek URL (lhup.edu/~dsimanek/febible.htm).
holes.recommendation: Locator: "Two documents, joined by an ellipsis: “The Four Corners of the Earth”, robschannel.com, 26 February 2017, for the inscribed-container wording; and “Enoch's Domed World”, testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html, for the speculation disclaimer. The 2015–2016 teaching document supplies the summary sentence quoted in the gloss and the Schadewald attribution. The work record WRK-SKIBA-2018 catalogues the later 2018 book; same mismatch noted at ARG-C04." Add two entries to sources: {label: "Rob Skiba, “Enoch's Domed World” — the 3D model page carrying the corners-on-the-roof alternative and the disclaimer “I fully acknowledge this is pure speculation on my part”", url: "https://www.testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html"} and {label: "Rob Skiba, “The Four Corners of the Earth”, 26 February 2017 — the circle “INSCRIBED (i.e. cut into) something else that likely has four legitimate corners/ends”, and the east/west argument", url: "https://robschannel.com/the-four-corners-of-the-earth"}.

holes.quoted_phrase: The list cites both 'four corners' and 'the circle of the Earth' as proofs. They describe different shapes.
holes.description: The entry's own gloss says our cluster record is wrong — 'Our cluster record should say so; as written it attributes to a named living-memory figure an incoherence his own text pre-empts, and that is the kind of error this review exists to catch' — and the record in scripts/clusters.py has not been changed. It still reads originator="Rob Skiba" with a note that presents the contradiction flatly, and verdict_challenge is set to challenged=False. That note is what ships in data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.csv and .json against all seven items and is what a reader sees without expanding the deep entry. Diagnosing a defect in the published record and then leaving the published record unchanged is the same failure mode as the A10 and D07 corrections already logged: the fix was identified and not applied.
holes.recommendation: In scripts/clusters.py, C05: note="The list cites both 'four corners' and 'the circle of the Earth' as proofs of one object, with nothing to reconcile them. The verdict is on the compilation, not on Skiba: his own teaching answers the objection — the circle is cut into a larger object that carries the corners, or the corners belong to the roof above — a resolution he flags as speculation and the list did not carry." Set verdict_challenge to dict(challenged=True, proposed_verdict="SELF-CONTRADICTED (scoped to the compilation)", reasoning="The seven items as entered are self-contradictory; the teaching they are credited to is not. The verdict stands but must be scoped in the record, not only in the deep entry.")

holes.quoted_phrase: The transmission to Schadewald is documented here, not inferred.
holes.description: The direction is reversed in a bolded heading. The transmission runs from Schadewald to Skiba, as the paragraph's own body states two sentences later: 'The chain for item 414 runs Schadewald 1987 → Skiba 2015–16 → the list.' On a page whose product is provenance, a heading that states a derivation backwards is the kind of thing a hostile reader screenshots.
holes.recommendation: "The transmission from Schadewald is documented here, not inferred."

holes.quoted_phrase: Its numeric neighbours — 159 to 171 without exception — are esoteric-symbolism items assigned to D06, D07, D08 and D09
holes.description: 'Without exception' is falsified by our own data. Item 160, 'Axis mundi doctrine.', is assigned to ARG-D04, which is not in the enumerated set. Checked against data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.csv: 159 D06, 160 D04, 161 D06, 162 D06, 163 D08, 165-166 D07, 167 D09, 168-171 D07. The substantive point survives — D04 is an esoteric-symbolism family too — but the emphatic enumeration is wrong as printed, and the compression note repeats it as 'filed to families D06–D09'.
holes.recommendation: Gloss: "Its numeric neighbours — 159 to 171 without exception — are esoteric-symbolism items assigned to D04, D06, D07, D08 and D09". Compression note: replace "filed to families D06–D09" with "filed to families D04 and D06–D09".

holes.quoted_phrase: used it fourteen chapters earlier
holes.description: Arithmetic. Isaiah 22:18 is eighteen chapters before Isaiah 40:22, not fourteen. Verified: kaddûr (H1754) at Isaiah 22:18, biblehub interlinear. The philological point is unaffected, but this is precisely the free, checkable slip a defender leads with to suggest the rest was not checked either.
holes.recommendation: "used it eighteen chapters earlier"

holes.quoted_phrase: two of the four have circular support
holes.description: The sentence promises two and delivers one: only the corners case is then explained ('one Greek phrase from one book, counted three times'). 'Circular support' is also the wrong term for what is being described, which is duplication, not circularity — the corners items do not support each other, they are the same item entered three times. A defender reading closely gets a free 'they cannot count and they cannot name a fallacy' in a section whose whole point is arithmetic.
holes.recommendation: "Seven items are, at most, four distinct claims, and the largest of the four is one Greek phrase from one book, counted three times."

holes.quoted_phrase: is word for word the phrase Deuteronomy 22:12 uses for the four corners of a garment
holes.description: Overstated by one word. Isaiah 11:12 has 'arba' kanphôt hā'āreṣ; Deuteronomy 22:12 has 'arba' kanphôt kəsûtəkā. The shared string is 'arba' kanphôt — the governed noun differs, which is the entire point being made. 'Word for word' invites the reply that the two phrases are not in fact identical, and the steelman states it correctly ('uses the identical phrase — 'arba' kanpôt'), so the two fields disagree with each other.
holes.recommendation: "shares its first two words with Deuteronomy 22:12, where 'arba' kanpôt is used of the four corners of a garment"

citation_failures: FAILED — Skiba, 'The Bible and the Still Flat Earth' (2015-16 PDF) cited as the locator for the passage quote. Neither quoted sentence is located in it. 'square' returns zero occurrences in the extracted text; the 'pure speculation on my part' disclaimer is documented on testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html instead. (Extraction was truncated mid-sentence, so the defensible claim is 'not located', never 'does not exist' — the entry's own Scope rule.)

FAILED — 'So, what you effectively end up with is a circle inscribed into a square' attributed to Skiba in passage.quote and compression.source_wording. Not located in the 2015-16 PDF, in testingtheglobe.com/3dmodel.html, in robschannel.com/the-four-corners-of-the-earth (2017), in robschannel.com/circle-means-circle-not-ballsphereglobe (2016), or in three targeted web searches. The only occurrence of 'square' in Skiba's reachable corpus is a reader's comment.

FAILED (scope) — the 'pure speculation' caveat is cited as attaching to the container. On the page where it occurs it follows the paragraph proposing the corners 'could be part of the “roof” above the system'.

UNCHECKED — whether the 2015-16 PDF contains the disclaimer or the square beyond the truncation point. The PDF text extraction ended mid-sentence ('...it had come under serious criticism by some Renai[truncated]'), so the negative result covers only the extracted portion.

UNCHECKED — testingtheglobe.com/bible.html could not be fetched: it returns a 302 from https to http and WebFetch upgrades http back to https, producing a redirect loop. No bash/curl used, per instructions.

UNCHECKED — the gloss's list of Skiba's ends-of-the-earth texts (Job 28:24, Job 37:3, Job 38:13, Isaiah 43:6, Matthew 24:31). Their absence from all 461 list items IS verified against data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.csv (zero matches for each); their presence in Skiba's document is not, for the truncation reason above.

VERIFIED — Schadewald, 'The Flat-Earth Bible': 'Weaker Arguments' heading; 'Another less-than-conclusive argument…'; gonia 'can refer to regions rather than points'; 'The modern flat-earth model doesn't have literal corners.'; 'sits throned on the vaulted roof of earth [chuwg]'; Job 22:14 'walks to and fro on the vault of heaven [chuwg]'; the Morris paragraph and 'This divide and conquer strategy is poor scholarship and worse logic.' (confirmed to be about Henry Morris and about reading 'circle' as 'sphericity'); the editor's note that Schadewald 'was not defending the idea that the earth is flat'; Psalm 61, Isaiah 11:12 and Ezekiel 7:2 absent. Checked in both the Simanek and Behrend texts.
VERIFIED — Schadewald was NCSE board member 1986-1992, including two years as president; 'The Flat-Earth Bible' published in the Bulletin of the Tychonian Society, 1987.

VERIFIED — Skiba's 2015-16 PDF does contain: 'carved as a “circle” with edge boarders inside something with four corners'; 'As Robert J. Schadewald points out, the Hebrew word used here is “chug” (pronounced “khoog”)'; the '© 1987, 1995' copyright line; the printed Simanek URL; copyright line '© 2015 – 2016 by Rob Skiba'.

VERIFIED — Carpenter, One Hundred Proofs (Gutenberg 55387): 'Isaiah' 0, 'Proverbs' 0, 'corners' 0; 'circle of the Earth' occurs once, in proof 79, as an argument being answered ('it is only a circular disc that he has to do with, not a spherical mass'); proof 50 is the stretched-out/immovable proof, as we say.

VERIFIED — Revelation 7:1 τὰς τέσσαρας γωνίας τῆς γῆς with τοὺς τέσσαρας ἀνέμους τῆς γῆς in the same sentence; Revelation 20:8 ταῖς τέσσαρσιν γωνίαις τῆς γῆς, KJV 'the four quarters of the earth'; Isaiah 22:18 kaddûr H1754; chug three noun occurrences (Isa 40:22, Job 22:14, Prov 8:27).
VERIFIED — the CSV holds 461 items; Isaiah 11:12, Ezekiel 7:2, Job 28:24, Job 37:3, Job 38:13, Isaiah 43:6 and Matthew 24:31 appear in none of them.
reviews.summary: The argument's architecture is sound and the verdict holds — SELF-CONTRADICTED scoped to the compilation is right, the hedge rule was applied in the correct direction, the Schadewald→Skiba transmission is documented rather than inferred, and every philological and Carpenter claim I could check came back verified. But the passage block prints as a Skiba quotation a sentence I could not locate in any Skiba source, and the 'square container' it introduces is our word, not his: his located wording is 'something else that likely has four legitimate corners/ends'. Compounding it, the 'pure speculation' caveat that carries the entire hedge_dropped finding lives on a different page and attaches to a different claim — the corners belonging to the roof, not the container — and neither that page nor the 2017 article supplying the rest of the quote appears in sources. Fix the quote, the locator, the sources and the caveat's scope, apply the cluster-record correction the entry itself diagnoses and left unapplied, and the entry is one of the strongest on the site.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: The hedge rule is satisfied in structure. The refutation's substantive weight (sections 2, 5, 6 and the steelman) answers the source's own claim at the source's own strength: Bellarmine's Trent rule is stated in full and granted as a rule rather than dismissed as head-counting, and the sphericity answer is taken from the source's own sentence rather than imposed on him. Section 1 is aimed at the nine fragments, but that is legitimate under the rule's second clause - it is explicitly framed as a finding about the compilation, and the compression block publishes the gap as a finding instead of using it to dodge. drifted=true with drift_type=scope_widened is honest, not evasive: the note argues affirmatively that force_upgraded is ABSENT ("we are not manufacturing a drift where the wording is faithful"), which is the harder and more credible call, and it records a second, category_shifted drift for items 24 and 445 that the single-value enum could not hold. Two caveats. First, the drift enum fit is loose: what moved is not the breadth of the source's claim but the conclusion the evidence is offered for (geocentrism -> flat Earth); scope_widened is the nearest box and the note says so, which is what the harness asks for. Second, and more materially, one of the two source quotations the compression block rests on (the p. 455 "geocentric foundation laid down in Scripture" sentence) could not be verified this pass - see citation_failures - so the drift finding is sound in shape but its source-side anchor is currently unchecked, not confirmed.

holes.quoted_phrase: John Chrysostom says the Earth “turns not, but stands firm”
holes.description: A quotation is attributed by name to a named Church Father with no citation anywhere in the entry and no entry in `sources` - the exact defect the module docstring claims not to repeat from C02 ("Known defect in C02 NOT repeated: every quotation below traces to an entry in `sources`"). It is also not locatable. I searched Chrysostom, Homily 12 on the Statues / to the People of Antioch (newadvent.org/fathers/190112.htm), which is the standard locus for his statements on the Earth's fixity: the phrase does not occur there. I searched scripturecatholic.com/geocentrism, which collects the patristic geocentrism quotations this argument circulates on, and it carries five Chrysostom quotations, none of them this one. Two further web searches on the phrase returned nothing. The nearest real Chrysostom sentence is "the earth is fixed, but the waters are continually in motion" (Homily 12 on the Statues). I cannot prove the phrase exists nowhere in Chrysostom's corpus, but on this site's own standard an unciteable quotation attributed to a named person is a fabricated citation until it is sourced, and it sits in the steelman where a defender checking our generosity will look first.
holes.recommendation: Replace with the verified line: `John Chrysostom says the Earth “is fixed, but the waters are continually in motion”` and add to `sources`: dict(label="John Chrysostom, Homilies on the Statues (to the People of Antioch), Homily XII — “the earth is fixed, but the waters are continually in motion”", url="https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/190112.htm")

holes.quoted_phrase: every authority in the dossier held that the Earth is a sphere
holes.description: This is the topic sentence of `why_it_doesnt_save_claim` and the load-bearing claim of the whole entry, and it is stated at a strength that our own cited sources contradict on two counts. (1) Basil of Caesarea is the first authority the steelman leads with, and our own source entry five - Hexaemeron Homily 9 §1, newadvent.org/fathers/32019.htm - records that he declines to settle the Earth's shape: verified verbatim this pass, "If it be spherical or cylindrical, if it resemble a disc and is equally rounded in all parts, or if it has the for[m] of a winnowing basket and is hollow in the middle". An authority in our own dossier who explicitly refuses to say the Earth is a sphere is a counterexample to "every", and we cite him in the sources list without ever using him. (2) The sentence also drops the source's own hedge. Sungenis's claim, quoted verbatim in our own passage block, is scoped: "Every other Father who wrote at length on cosmological issues stated his belief... that the Earth was a sphere" - other than Lactantius, and restricted to those who wrote at length on cosmology. Our restatement is unqualified and universal. Refuting a fragment is the failure the hedge rule names; overstating a source in our own favour is the same failure with the sign flipped, and it is the single sentence a well-informed defender attacks first.
holes.recommendation:
Replace with: `every Father in the source's own sphericity dossier — and, at the strength he states it, every Father who wrote at length on cosmological issues — held that the Earth is a sphere`. Then append to the end of that paragraph: `

holes.quoted_phrase: originator_work="Galileo Was Wrong, Vol. III", year="2006"
holes.description: Our own gloss states, in section 2, that this is "not a citation that can exist" - and I confirmed the basis of that from the scan's own copyright page this pass (previous five editions in two volumes 2005-2010; sixth edition in three volumes January 2013; the volume held is Vol. II, seventh edition, 2013, Catholic Apologetics International Publishing). The record is nevertheless unchanged, the gloss's own recommendation is unapplied, and the string appears ten times in the published export data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.csv (and in the JSON). The same pairing sits on ARG-D15, which the gloss also names. `real_source` is likewise still None, against the gloss's own instruction that it should carry Bellarmine's letter - which I verified independently this pass (inters.org/copernicanism-bellarmine-foscarini: 12 April 1615, "the Council [of Trent] prohibits interpreting Scripture against the common consensus of the Holy Fathers", "you will find all agreeing on the literal interpretation that the sun is in heaven and turns around the earth", "whether the church can tolerate giving Scripture a meaning contrary to the Holy Fathers and to all the Greek and Latin commentators"). The result is that a site whose product is provenance publishes, as machine-readable data, a citation it elsewhere declares impossible. This also carries the R06 error class forward: nine items are attributed cluster-wide to a work none of them has been checked against, and our own compression note concedes items 443 and 444 have no counterpart in the volume we could read.
holes.recommendation: In scripts/clusters.py, replace the C07 and D15 lines with: `originator_work="Galileo Was Wrong, Vol. III (2013 three-volume edition)", year="2013",` and for C07 set `real_source="Robert Bellarmine to Paolo Antonio Foscarini, 12 April 1615",`. holes.quoted_phrase: Appeal to authority; also historically contested.
holes.description: This note is not internal metadata: render.py line 141 renders `a["basis"]` as the collapsed one-line summary of section 3, the Refutation, so it is one of the first things a reader of this cluster sees. "Also historically contested" reads as disputing the historical claim - and the body does the opposite, deliberately and as its best move: section 1 says the items "are geocentric claims, and they are accurate ones: the tradition did hold that the Earth stands still at the centre", and the steelman says "Anybody who tells this cluster that the Fathers were quietly heliocentric is simply wrong". Our own advocate block identifies "you conceded the content and then marked it NOT DEMONSTRATED" as the defender's second-strongest point and answers it by conceding the history first; the visible one-liner hands that ground straight back and makes the page look as though it is both granting and denying the same fact.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: `The history is granted: the tradition did teach a stationary, central Earth. What is missing is the step from what it taught to what is the case — and every authority cited held that Earth to be a sphere.`

holes.quoted_phrase: Every one is about rest or centrality.
holes.description: False by the entry's own account, and self-contradicting within the same refutation. Section 4 says four paragraphs later: "Item 24, ‘Church consistency with Scripture’, does not assert anything about the Earth." An item that asserts nothing about the Earth is not "about rest or centrality". Item 124 is worse: the gloss itself notes that "‘Early Church fathers.’ is the entire text of item 124" - a bare noun phrase that is about nothing at all. Item 428, "Scholastics harmonize Aristotle", is not about rest or centrality either. The sentence is the pivot of the section's whole move, so a defender who spots the contradiction gets to discard the opening of the refutation at no cost, and the fix costs us nothing because the weaker claim - not one of the nine is about shape - is the one that actually does the work.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: `Seven of the nine are about rest or centrality; the remaining two, items 24 and 124, assert nothing about the Earth at all and are taken up in section 4.`

holes.quoted_phrase: “occupies the centre of the universe, its natural place”
holes.description: Presented in quotation marks with a citation to Hexaemeron Homily 1 §10, but it is not a verbatim string. Basil's text (Blomfield Jackson, verified this pass via newadvent.org/fathers/32011.htm and ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf208.viii.ii.html) reads: "It is not... without reason or by chance that the earth occupies the centre of the universe. It is its natural and necessary position." Two sentences have been welded into one quotation with a comma and "natural and necessary position" silently rewritten to "natural place". The second Basil quotation in the same sentence is verbatim and correct. There is a context problem behind it as well: §10 is Basil rehearsing the Greek natural philosophers' reasoning - "Placed, they say, in the middle of the universe..." - and he goes on to tell his hearers not to be entangled in it. On a site that exists to catch drifted quotations in other people's work, a stitched paraphrase inside quotation marks is the wrong kind of error to be carrying.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: `“occupies the centre of the universe”, that this is “its natural and necessary position”` and change the introduction of the sentence from `Basil of Caesarea, preaching in the 370s, says` to `Basil of Caesarea, preaching in the 370s, sets out the natural philosophers' reasoning without demur: the Earth`

holes.quoted_phrase: Two men, both marginal, both answered by their contemporaries.
holes.description: The second half is unsupported for Lactantius. Cosmas was answered by John Philoponus in his own century - verified, and stated in the preceding sentence. Nothing in this entry, in its sources, or in anything I could find supports a contemporary refutation of Lactantius's flat-Earth polemic in Divine Institutes III; the judgement we do have is the source's own retrospective one, that he was "not a highly esteemed patristic witness", which is a later assessment and not a contemporary answer. It is a small, checkable, gratuitous overreach in a section whose rhetorical force comes precisely from being checkable.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: `Two men, both marginal — and Cosmas answered inside his own century by John Philoponus.`

I-II are the scientific case (Vol. II is chs. 7-13); Vol. III is the church-history volume.`

reviews.summary: C07 is one of the better arguments on the site - the steelman is genuine KERNEL tier (it grants that Bellarmine is applying Trent's interpretive rule rather than counting heads, then shows the strong version is out of the list's own remit), the hedge rule is honoured, the compression block argues affirmatively that force_upgraded is absent rather than manufacturing a drift, and eleven of its independently checkable citations verified verbatim including Bellarmine, Aquinas, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, the Trent catechism, the 1820 Settele decree and the Carpenter word-search. Three things nevertheless need fixing before it is safe. A quotation is attributed by name to John Chrysostom with no source entry and no locatable original - the exact defect the module docstring claims not to have repeated from C02. The load-bearing sentence of why_it_doesnt_save_claim, "every authority in the dossier held that the Earth is a sphere", overstates both the source (whose claim is scoped to Fathers "who wrote at length on cosmological issues") and our own evidence (Basil, whom the steelman leads with, explicitly declines to settle the Earth's shape in a passage we cite in our own sources and never use). And the entry diagnoses three errors in our own records - the impossible "Vol. III, 2006" citation, the wrong works-tab imprint, the null real_source - without applying any of the fixes, so the site still publishes the impossible citation ten times in its CSV export and the wrong bibliography on the Works tab. Verdict NOT DEMONSTRATED holds; nothing found disturbs it.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: The refutation answers the sources, not the fragments: §1 works from the Arabic Kitab sirr al-khaliqa and the Latin vulgate on their own terms, §3 from the Kybalion's own chapters, §§4-5 from Plato/Kepler/Titius-Bode, and Atkinson is introduced as the PROXIMATE source rather than as an authority on Hermeticism. So hedge_rule_ok = true. But the hedge discipline fails twice inward. (a) The compression block, whose whole job is to set list wording beside source wording, asserts that item 161 reproduces the Kybalion axiom "word for word" while quoting, four lines above in its own list_phrasing field, the actual item text "Hermetic as above so below." — a five-word fragment that drops the doubling. (b) The TLDR compresses our own carefully-distinguished §1 back into the error §1 was written to avoid, reading the Latin's gerundive purpose clause and its closing "operatione Solis" line into the Arabic recension, which has neither. Both are our own compression degrading our own source-reading in exactly the direction the project documents in other people.
reviews.summary: D06 is well-sourced and its UNFALSIFIABLE verdict holds — every Kybalion quotation checks verbatim against Gutenberg #14209 and sacred-texts, the Emerald Tablet datings (Kraus 813-833, Weisser 750-800, Ruska earlier), the Latin "ad preparanda miracula rei unius", Blavatsky Isis Unveiled I.35, Kepler 1596/1619, the Timaeus solids, Phaedo 108d-e and Coon 1971/Grant 1972 all verify. But the TLDR carries two errors — it attributes the Latin's purpose clause and closing line to the Arabic, which our own §1 says it should not, and it still says the 1908 pamphlet "put the slogan into modern circulation", the precise overcredit corrections.json retracted on 2026-08-07 — and the entry asserts three times that item 161 reproduces the Kybalion axiom verbatim when item 161 reads only "Hermetic as above so below." Separately, the published dataset assigns items 198/204/206 an originator (Atkinson, 1908) that this very writeup refutes.

(Gregory's Latin original is 1702, but the passage Wikipedia quotes is the 1715 English, and the mismatch is unexplained in our text.)
Item 204 ('Toroid sacred geometry nested') is dated to a 'recent stratum' with no citation anywhere in the sources list — the only dating claim in the entry with no source behind it.

paulwestonglastonbury.com — supports Coon January 1971 and Grant 1972, but hedges Grant as 'the first published reference I'm aware of'; our text states it flatly as 'the earliest publication of the idea'.

V grain-of-dust and 'our own little solar system', ch. VIII three Great Planes); Wikipedia Emerald Tablet (Arabic literal translation, Latin vulgate, Kraus/Weisser/Ruska datings, Hugo of Santalla c. 1145-1151 'not widely circulated', anonymous 12th-c. vulgate, sulphur-mercury theory, Hortulanus); Wikipedia As above so below (Blavatsky earliest free-standing occurrences); theosociety.org Isis Unveiled I p. 35 (the Blavatsky quotation, verbatim and in context); Wikipedia Mysterium Cosmographicum (<10%, 'virtually the first attempt since Copernicus', Sun-as-Father Trinity); Wikipedia Harmonice Mundi (16:15 mi-to-fa, angular speeds from the Sun, third law); Wikipedia Titius–Bode (Neptune/Pluto failure, Icarus policy); SEP Plato's Timaeus (53b5-6 solids, dodecahedron 55c4-6 'used for the universe as a whole', spherical body); badancient.com (Phaedo 108d-e, quotation exact as we give it); Wikipedia Eratosthenes (1/50, 250,000 stadia, Syene/Alexandria).

holes.quoted_phrase: in both the Arabic and the Latin the correspondence clause is
holes.description: The TLDR says that in BOTH recensions the correspondence clause is subordinate to a purpose clause 'to accomplish the miracles of the one thing', and that 'the text closes by saying it has finished speaking about the operation of Sol'. Neither is true of the Arabic. The literal translation of the Kitab sirr al-khaliqa version (Wikipedia, Emerald Tablet) reads 'indeed, the uppermost is from the lowermost and the lowermost is from the uppermost, / [it] worked the wonders from one, (just) as all things come from one by means of one plan' — a coordinate past-tense declarative, not a purpose construction — and it closes 'this is my renown and therefore I am named Hermes the threefold with the wisdom.' The gerundive 'ad preparanda miracula rei unius' and the closing 'Completum est quod diximus de opere solis' are peculiar to the Latin vulgate. Our own refutation §1 makes exactly this distinction ('the comparison is peculiar to the translation'); the TLDR then collapses it. This is the entry's headline sentence, the field readers see first and may never expand past, and it attributes to a primary source a grammatical structure and a closing line the source does not have — the same failure class the hedge rule exists to catch, run inward on our own body text.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "The maxim is the licence for an alchemical operation, not a description of the sky. In the Latin vulgate the correspondence clause is subordinate to a purpose clause — ad preparanda miracula rei unius, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing — and that version signs off by saying it has finished speaking about the operation of Sol. The older Arabic does not compare the two realms at all: it derives one from the other, and says the wonders were worked from one."
holes.failure_scenario: A defender who reads Arabic, or who simply opens the Wikipedia page we cite, reads our first two lines and replies: 'You have read the Latin translator's grammar back into the Arabic and given the Arabic a closing line it does not contain — after spending a paragraph telling us the two differ. That is your own compression rule broken in your own summary.' The TLDR is the field with the widest readership in the entry.

holes.quoted_phrase: item 161 is its axiom, verbatim, in its
holes.description: Three places assert that the list reproduces the Kybalion's axiom word for word: refutation §3 ('item 161 is its axiom, verbatim, in its doubled form'), refutation §2 ('in the form item 161 reproduces'), and the compression note ('Item 161 reproduces his axiom accurately, word for word'). Item 161 in scripts/corpus.py reads, in full: 'Hermetic as above so below.' The Kybalion ch. II reads 'As above, so below; as below, so above.' (verified verbatim, sacred-texts kyb04 and Gutenberg #14209). The item is a five-word unpunctuated fragment that drops the second half of the doubling — and the doubling is precisely the feature we elsewhere identify as the Kybalion's own contribution, so the 'verbatim' claim is not decorative: it is the link that makes the Kybalion, rather than Blavatsky 1877 or any post-Renaissance English source, the proximate source of the cluster, and the advocate/preemptive block leans on it explicitly ('the text item 161 reproduces verbatim'). Worse, the compression block quotes the true item text in its own list_phrasing field four lines above the sentence that contradicts it, so the error is self-demonstrating to any reader of that block.
holes.recommendation: In §3 replace with: "item 161 is its axiom in compressed form — the Kybalion's doubled 'As above, so below; as below, so above.' arrives on the list as the bare 'Hermetic as above so below.' — and in chapter V it says:" In §2 replace 'in the form item 161 reproduces' with 'in the doubled form that item 161 compresses'. In the compression note replace 'Item 161 reproduces his axiom accurately, word for word; what changes is what the sentence is taken to be about.' with: "Item 161 keeps the axiom's sense but not its wording: the doubled form is cut back to 'Hermetic as above so below.' What changes far more than the words is what the sentence is taken to be about."
holes.failure_scenario: A defender opens the list at item 161, reads 'Hermetic as above so below.', and sets it beside our sentence 'item 161 is its axiom, verbatim, in its doubled form'. The word 'verbatim' is false on inspection, in the entry whose subject is other people's inaccurate quotation, and it is the sentence that pins the cluster to the Kybalion.

holes.quoted_phrase: The 1908 pamphlet that put the slogan into modern
holes.description: The TLDR still credits the Kybalion with putting the slogan into circulation. This is the exact claim retracted in review/corrections.json on 2026-08-07 ('Said the maxim was popularised in its modern form by a 1908 Chicago New Thought pamphlet... Overcredits the Kybalion... The Kybalion's contribution was to codify it as one of seven numbered Principles, not to popularise it'). The cluster note in scripts/clusters.py was fixed; the refutation §2 and the compression note both state the corrected position; the TLDR was not updated and now contradicts the entry's own §2, its own compression block, its own docstring, and a published correction. Verified this run: Isis Unveiled (1877) vol. I p. 35 carries 'As above, so it is below. That which has been, will return again. As in heaven, so on earth.' as a free-standing axiom, thirty-one years earlier.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'The 1908 pamphlet that put the slogan into modern circulation calls the Earth' with: "The 1908 pamphlet that fixed the slogan as one of seven numbered Principles — Blavatsky had already put it into English circulation in 1877 — calls the Earth"
holes.failure_scenario: A critic reads the retraction we publish on the Method tab, then reads the TLDR of the very argument the retraction was about, and finds the retracted wording still there in the most-read field. That converts a credibility asset into evidence that our corrections are cosmetic.

holes.quoted_phrase: It is not an Egyptian statement about the shape of the Earth.
holes.description: The published dataset contradicts this writeup on provenance, which is the site's entire product. data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.json (and the CSV) record ITEM-198 'Earth heart chakra symbolism.' with originator 'William Walker Atkinson (as Three Initiates)', originator_work 'The Kybalion', originator_year '1908' — while refutation §6 of this same argument states the idea is a 1971-onwards development (Coon January 1971, Grant 1972) that is 'not in the Hermetic corpus at all'. The same inheritance gives item 204 the 1908 attribution our §6 denies, and gives item 206 a named originator our §7 says we could not identify. Item records inherit the cluster originator with no override mechanism anywhere in scripts/, so the contradiction is generated automatically and is invisible unless someone reads both artefacts. This is holistic check 6 (provenance-chain integrity) failing on a cluster where we have already done the work to know better.
holes.recommendation: Append to the ARG-D06 note in scripts/clusters.py, after 'It is not an Egyptian statement about the shape of the Earth.': " Three items are grouped here by subject and do not descend from this source: 198 and 204 belong to a much later stratum (Glastonbury as planetary heart chakra, Coon 1971, first in print in Grant 1972), and 206 could not be traced to any source. The item-level originator field for those three should be read as the cluster's subject heading, not as a provenance claim."
holes.failure_scenario: Someone downloads the CSV, filters on originator='William Walker Atkinson', and finds a 1971 New Age site-mapping scheme attributed to a 1908 book — then reads our own page saying it is a 1971 scheme. The dataset is the artefact most likely to be quoted back at us, and here it asserts a derivation we have already refuted in prose.

holes.quoted_phrase: That is not an isolated turn of phrase. Six chapters on, in
holes.description: Chapter arithmetic error in the gloss, and it contradicts our own refutation. 'The Mental Universe' is chapter V, three chapters after chapter II, not six (TOC verified against Gutenberg #14209: I Hermetic Philosophy, II Seven Hermetic Principles, III Mental Transmutation, IV The All, V The Mental Universe... VIII Planes of Correspondence). 'Six chapters later' is correct for the earlier sentence in the same gloss, which points at the three Great Planes in chapter VIII — so the gloss uses the same interval for two different chapters. Refutation §3 gets it right ('in chapter V it says'). The error is live in the built page (docs/index.html).
holes.recommendation: Replace 'That is not an isolated turn of phrase. Six chapters on, in The Mental Universe, the book states its cosmology outright:' with: "That is not an isolated turn of phrase. Three chapters on, in The Mental Universe (ch. V), the book states its cosmology outright:"
holes.failure_scenario: A reader checks the citation, finds the passage in chapter V rather than chapter VIII, and notices that the same gloss says 'six chapters later' for two different chapters. Small, but it is a checkable slip in a passage gloss on a page that asks readers to check citations.

holes.quoted_phrase: Neither quantity is even definable without a
holes.description: Overstatement, and the strongest reply a geocentrist defender has to §§4-5. 'Neither quantity is even definable without a Sun-centred distance to define it' is false in the form given: heliocentric distances are perfectly definable in the neo-Tychonic model that Sungenis, Bouw and Bennett actually defend, in which the five planets do orbit the Sun and the Sun orbits the Earth — and our own ARG-A02 and ARG-R08 record precisely that. Under the Tychonic transformation the nested-solid spacing of 1596 and the harmonic ratios of 1619 map across intact, so a defender can accept every number in §§4-5 and lose nothing. The point that does survive is the one worth making: the pattern is organised around the Sun's position, not the Earth's, in every frame.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'Neither quantity is even definable without a Sun-centred distance to define it.' with: "Both quantities are indexed to the Sun, and changing frames does not change that. Even in the neo-Tychonic arrangement geocentrists actually defend — planets circling the Sun, Sun circling the Earth — the spacing and the harmonies are organised about the Sun's position, and the Earth enters as one more body indexed to it. A pattern can be admired in any frame; what it picks out as the centre of the pattern does not move with the frame."
holes.failure_scenario: A Tychonian replies: 'We agree the planets orbit the Sun. Kepler's solids and his harmonies transform straight into our model — you have refuted heliocentrism-denial, which nobody in this cluster holds.' Our sentence as written is simply wrong, and it is the pivot of two consecutive numbered sections.

holes.quoted_phrase: belongs to the same recent stratum
holes.description: Item 204 ('Toroid sacred geometry nested') is dated to a late stratum with no citation and no source anywhere in the sources list — the only dating claim in the entry with nothing behind it, in a paragraph that otherwise carries Coon 1971 and Grant 1972 to the month. §7 goes to some trouble to say we could not trace item 206 and are 'recording that rather than guessing'; §6 then guesses about 204. The compression note doubles the exposure by classifying 204 as unsourced_addition on the strength of that undocumented dating.
holes.recommendation: Replace 'Item 204, “Toroid sacred geometry nested”, belongs to the same recent stratum rather than to the Hermetic corpus.' with: "Item 204, “Toroid sacred geometry nested”, we could not place either. The toroidal-field motif is not in the Hermetic corpus and reads as belonging to the same late stratum, but we could not document a first appearance and are recording that rather than dating it."
holes.failure_scenario: A defender asks for the source of the toroid dating, gets nothing, and points out that the paragraph immediately following boasts about our refusal to guess on item 206 — inconsistent standards inside two adjacent sections.

holes.quoted_phrase: antecedents in Gregory 1702 and Wolff 1723
holes.description: Dates do not match the source we cite for them. The Titius–Bode Wikipedia article gives David Gregory's The Elements of Astronomy as 1715 (that is the edition carrying the quoted 'ten equal Parts' passage) and Christian Wolff as 1724. Gregory's Latin original of 1702 is a defensible date for the work, but the entry gives no signal that it is citing the Latin against a source that cites the English, and Wolff 1723 is unexplained either way.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "antecedents in Gregory's Elements of Astronomy (Latin 1702, English 1715) and Wolff 1724"
holes.failure_scenario: Someone follows our own citation and finds two different years than the two we printed. Trivial in isolation; corrosive on a page whose method claim is that we check the source rather than the summary.

holes.quoted_phrase: the earliest publication of the idea is Kenneth Grant
holes.description: Stated flatly where our source hedges. Paul Weston writes that Grant's The Magical Revival (1972) is 'the first published reference I'm aware of that specifically refers to global chakras and their locations, and giving Glastonbury as the heart'. We convert a single writer's 'that I'm aware of' into a bare superlative — the drop-the-hedge move this project exists to document, on the one paragraph in the entry where our evidence rests on a single self-published source.
