reviews.summary: The argument itself is sound and the hedge-rule handling is exemplary — R06 concedes the one sentence the source actually supplies, answers it with Kretschmann's two-edged objection, and quarantines the fifteen item titles as claims of unknown authorship. The verdict STANDARD PHYSICS holds. What fails is the citation apparatus wrapped around it: the archive scan R06 quotes is Volume II of the seventh edition (2013, chs 7–13), confirmed this run from its own front matter and already corrected for the identical scan in scripts/_b7_C07.py, yet the passage locator, sources label, straw_man scope statement, compression note and cluster record all still say “Vol. I (2006)” — which also means our headline finding (six untraceable titles) is scoped to a volume that was never searched, and states an impossible locator, since Vol. I has no chapter 10. Two substantive defects sit beside that: the TLDR and two body passages attribute the centrifugal effect to the metric's off-diagonal terms when it comes from g_tt (the entry gets this right in its own light-cylinder paragraph), and the light-cylinder argument uses superluminal coordinate speeds against geocentrism two sentences after telling the reader coordinate speeds are not bounded by c — the frame-dragging reply is unanswered in the body although the preemptive block already contains its correct form. Unchecked, not failed: the “weave pattern of a net” quotation, the p. 161 Lagrangian and the term counts could not be independently re-verified this run — the archive djvu.txt fetch returned a truncated view whose silence proves nothing — so those rest on our own earlier passes, and that limitation should stay visible in the text.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: The refutation is correctly aimed at the source rather than the fragment — the 2026-08-05 rewrite did that job, and the primary-source spadework behind it checks out: the Einstein/Infeld sentence really is at Vol. I, Introduction, p. 9, n. 22, with Poincare ("We do not have and cannot have any means of discovering whether or not we are carried along in a uniform motion of translation") and Bellarmine on the same page, exactly as the gloss says. So the hedge rule is not broken in the usual direction. It is broken in the mirror direction, which the harness treats as the same failure class: we make the source MORE modest than it is. Two specific errors. (1) We assert that Sungenis and Bennett name no instrument and that "Sungenis's own later restatements of the case reach for the same Einstein sentence without naming one." Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II ch. 10 carries a subsection headed "Global Positioning System: Claims and Responses" (p. 204 in its own table of contents), and Sungenis's 2010 reply to Phil Plait argues in terms: "Using the ECI frame (Earth Centered Inertial Frame) is much easier than the Solar Barycentric frame. If you don't believe me I suggest you ask the engineers who put up the GPS." That is item 46 and item 283 in the author's own hand. The compression block's drift_type="unsourced_addition" therefore over-claims: the addition is real for seismology, LiDAR, VOR and most of the rest, but not for the GPS/ECI items. (2) We publish the Einstein conditional as a drift ("arrives here unconditioned"). Einstein and Infeld answer their own conditional two sentences later — "Could we build a real relativistic physics valid in all CS ... ? This is indeed possible!" — so restoring the condition takes nothing away from the quotation, and the drift we recorded is not one. drifted=True still holds on the main count; the type and two of the supporting claims do not.

holes.quoted_phrase: They do not cite GPS. They do not cite WGS 84, ITRF, seismic hypocentres or a nautical almanac. In the whole of the passage this cluster rests on, no instrument is named at all, and Sungenis’s own later restatements of the case reach for the same Einstein sentence without naming one.
holes.description: Both flat sentences are false of the work, and the final clause is false outright. Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II ch. 10 contains a subsection headed "Global Positioning System: Claims and Responses" (p. 204 of its own contents list, archive.org scan ...Bennett4276), and the same volume discusses GPS signal timing and the Sagnac effect at length. More damagingly, Sungenis's 2010 reply to Phil Plait of Discover Magazine (isidore.co, Sungenis & DeLano folder) makes precisely the R08 argument while naming the instrument: "Using the ECI frame (Earth Centered Inertial Frame) is much easier than the Solar Barycentric frame. If you don't believe me I suggest you ask the engineers who put up the GPS." That is a later restatement of the case that names an instrument, which is what we say does not exist. Since this paragraph is the premise of the whole second half of the refutation ("The twenty-eight items are the list's addition, not the authors'") and of the compression verdict, a defender who owns the books discredits the section with one page reference. Same error class as corrections.json entries 4 and 11: asserting absence from a source on the strength of one passage.
holes.recommendation: They do not cite GPS in it, or WGS 84, ITRF, seismic hypocentres or a nautical almanac: in the whole of the passage this cluster rests on, no instrument is named at all. Elsewhere they do, and it should be said plainly. Vol. II, ch. 10 carries a subsection headed “Global Positioning System: Claims and Responses”, and Sungenis’s 2010 reply to Phil Plait of Discover argues that “Using the ECI frame (Earth Centered Inertial Frame) is much easier than the Solar Barycentric frame. If you don’t believe me I suggest you ask the engineers who put up the GPS.” So a handful of these items — the GPS and ECI ones — do have an ancestor in the authors’ own writing, and we withdraw any suggestion otherwise. What that sentence claims is ease of use. It does not claim fixity, and the twenty or so remaining artefacts are not in the books at all. The gap between “easier to compute in” and “therefore at rest” is the whole of this cluster, and it is the list that closes it, not Sungenis.

holes.quoted_phrase: and Sungenis’s own later restatements of the case reach for the Einstein quotation without naming a single instrument
holes.description: The published compression note carries the same falsified claim as the refutation, and here it is load-bearing for the drift verdict itself. drift_type is recorded as "unsourced_addition" for all 28 items; the GPS and ECI items are not unsourced additions, because Sungenis argues from the ECI frame and from GPS engineers by name in his 2010 Discover reply, and Vol. II ch. 10 devotes a subsection to GPS. drifted=True survives on the other ~24 items, but the type and the supporting sentence do not.
holes.recommendation: and Sungenis’s own later restatements name instruments only in the weaker form: his 2010 reply to Discover argues that the ECI frame “is much easier than the Solar Barycentric frame” and points at “the engineers who put up the GPS”, and Vol. II ch. 10 gives GPS a subsection of its own. So the GPS and ECI items are not additions — they descend from the authors, in a claim about computational ease. The addition is twofold: the other twenty-odd artefacts (seismology, LiDAR, VOR, drone RTK, volcano infrasound, great-circle math), which appear in no source we can find; and the inference, which converts ease of use into evidence of fixity and belongs to the list alone.

holes.quoted_phrase: it arrives on the list stripped of the clause that governs it
holes.description: The conditional does not do the work we ask of it. Einstein and Infeld pose the condition and then answer it affirmatively two sentences later: "Could we build a real relativistic physics valid in all CS; a physics in which there would be no place for absolute, but only for relative, motion? This is indeed possible!", after which they build general relativity. Restoring the condition therefore subtracts nothing from the quotation, and a defender who reads the next paragraph of The Evolution of Physics will say so. The genuinely correct point in this paragraph - that the sentence is about the form of laws under coordinate transformation, not about the Earth being at rest - is buried under a framing that is wrong.
holes.recommendation: The Einstein sentence, and what it is a claim about. The quotation is real and it is quoted accurately. It is also conditional in its original: Einstein and Infeld ask whether physical laws can be formulated for arbitrarily moving frames, and say that if so, the Ptolemy–Copernicus struggle “would then be quite meaningless.” We will not lean on that condition, because they discharge it themselves on the same page — “Could we build a real relativistic physics valid in all CS … ? This is indeed possible!” — and then build general relativity. The point is not that the condition fails. The point is what the discharged condition delivers: general covariance, a statement about the form in which laws may be written. It is not a statement that a rotating and a non-rotating frame are dynamically alike, and Einstein plainly did not hold that the Earth is at rest.

holes.quoted_phrase: The Einstein sentence is conditional in its original — if the laws can be written for arbitrary frames, the old struggle would then be meaningless — and arrives here unconditioned
holes.description: Published as one of the "two smaller drifts" supporting drifted=True. It is not a drift. Einstein and Infeld satisfy the antecedent themselves in the following sentences ("This is indeed possible!"), so an unconditioned rendering of the consequent is faithful to them. On a page whose product is provenance, a drift finding that dissolves on reading the next paragraph of the source is worse than no finding.
holes.recommendation: One smaller drift rides along: a permission is again doing the work of a proof, the pattern already recorded at R01. We had also recorded the Einstein sentence as arriving unconditioned; we withdraw that. The original is conditional, but Einstein and Infeld discharge the condition themselves in the next breath — “This is indeed possible!” — so the unconditioned rendering is faithful and there is no drift on that count.

holes.quoted_phrase: Farrell and Hu (J. Geodesy 98:102, 2024) note the ECEF frame rotates during signal propagation, and that neglecting it puts the computed satellite position in error by over 30 metres, with roughly 20 metres of user-position shift at mid-latitudes
holes.description: Two citation defects in one sentence. Author order is reversed: the paper is Wang Hu and Jay A. Farrell, "Derivation of the Sagnac (Earth-rotation) correction and analysis of its accuracy for GNSS applications", J. Geodesy 98:102 (2024) - our sources[] label repeats the error. And the figure "roughly 20 metres of user-position shift at mid-latitudes" is not in the paper; two independent reads of the article return only the >30 m satellite-position figure (which the paper itself attributes to Ashby 2004) and its own result, that Sagnac corrections introduce range errors below 7.57e-4 m. A specific number attributed to a named paper that the paper does not contain is the exact error class corrections.json exists for.
holes.recommendation: In receiver processing the same physics appears as the Sagnac correction: Hu and Farrell (J. Geodesy 98:102, 2024) derive it for moving receivers, noting that the ECEF frame rotates during signal propagation and that without correcting the Earth-rotation effects the computed satellite position can be in error by over 30 metres. Every one of these numbers is exactly zero on a stationary Earth.

holes.quoted_phrase: Kind 2 — the item is about a transformation that exists only because of rotation. ECI-ECEF transforms, navigation inertial Earth base, airliner FMS Earth grid, ephemeris time.
holes.description: Ephemeris time is misfiled, and the heading is false of it. Ephemeris Time was introduced precisely because the Earth's rotation is too irregular to keep time by, and its second was defined as 1/31,556,925.9747 of the tropical year 1900 - that is, from the Earth's orbital revolution, not its rotation. Filing it under "exists only because of rotation" is an error any astronomer spots, in a section whose persuasive force is entirely that we know these artefacts better than the compilers do. It also throws away the strongest reading of the item: the one timescale on the list that is genuinely Earth-defined is defined by the Earth going round the Sun.
holes.recommendation: Kind 2 — the item is about a transformation that exists only because of rotation. ECI-ECEF transforms, navigation inertial Earth base, airliner FMS Earth grid. [and add to Kind 5:] “Ephemeris time Earth-defined” inverts itself hardest of all. Ephemeris Time exists because the Earth’s rotation is too irregular to keep time by; its second was defined as 1/31,556,925.9747 of the tropical year 1900, which is to say from the Earth’s orbital revolution. The one timescale in these twenty-eight items that is genuinely “Earth-defined” is defined by the Earth going round the Sun.

holes.quoted_phrase: They sort into seven kinds
holes.description: They do not, quite. Items 30 ("Modern astronomy uses Earth-centered coordinates"), 231 ("Nav systems Earth-fixed") and 244 ("Satellite ground tracks Earth-based") are named in the list_phrasing but answered nowhere in the seven kinds or the honest remainder. Item 244 is the most costly omission, because it is the cleanest self-refutation in the whole cluster and it is visual: a low-Earth-orbit satellite's successive ground tracks step about 22.5 degrees of longitude westward each pass because the Earth turns that far beneath the orbit in ninety minutes. We claim exhaustive coverage of a 28-item cluster and deliver 25.
holes.recommendation:
They sort into eight kinds — [and add as a new paragraph before the honest remainder:]

Kind 8 — the artefact draws the rotation. “Satellite ground tracks Earth-based.” A low-Earth-orbit satellite’s successive ground tracks are displaced roughly 22.5° of longitude westward on each pass, because the Earth turns about that far beneath the orbit in the ninety minutes the satellite takes to come round. The sine-wave-and-shift figure printed on every mission page is a picture of the Earth’s rotation, drawn by the spacecraft. Set ω to zero and every pass retraces the last exactly. Two more items — “Modern astronomy uses Earth-centered coordinates” and “Nav systems Earth-fixed” — are the cluster’s thesis stated without an artefact, and are answered by everything above.

holes.quoted_phrase: No sky is involved, so the symmetry the defence needs does not obtain.
holes.description: This is in the advocate preemptive, answering a defence we ourselves rate survives=3, and it does not land against the defence as written. The defence is explicitly Machian - it says the surrounding matter supplies the centrifugal and Coriolis terms as genuine gravitational effects. Under exactly that premise, a ring laser measures rotation relative to the local inertial frame, and the local inertial frame is what the distant matter sets. So a rotating cosmos predicts the same ring-laser reading, and "no sky is involved" is a non-sequitur against it. Our third point (that a rotating cosmos must track omega's irregularities, in phase with El Nino and the core) is the one that works; leaving a refutable point in front of it invites the defender to stop reading at point two.
holes.recommendation: Second, the relative-rotation premise is answerable locally, though not as cheaply as it first looks: a ring laser gyroscope in a sealed windowless room returns the Earth’s rotation rate, and the G ring laser at Wettzell resolves it to better than one part in 10⁹. A Machian defender will reply that the local inertial frame is itself set by the distant matter, so the same instrument would read the same in a rotating cosmos — and on that much they are right. What the ring laser settles is narrower and still fatal to this cluster: whatever fixes the local inertial frame, the Earth-fixed frame demonstrably is not it, and the offset is a measured number obtained with no sky in view. Third, the rotating-cosmos route must track ω’s IRREGULARITIES …

holes.quoted_phrase: The second-largest cluster.
holes.description: False, and it contradicts a neighbouring cluster on the same rendered page. R08 has 28 of the 461 items and is the largest cluster in the corpus; A22 is second at 20. ARG-R06's note reads "The largest single cluster in the list" and R06 has 15 items, ranking fourth. Both strings render once each in docs/index.html, R08's as the summary line of the Refutation section, so a reader sees it before opening anything. This is holistic check 4 (a critic compiling our own statements into a self-contradiction) sitting in plain view.
holes.recommendation: The largest cluster in the list, 28 of 461 items.

holes.quoted_phrase: NGA Office of Geomatics — WGS 84: the four defining parameters, including ω = 7292115 × 10⁻¹¹ rad/s
holes.description: The sources block is strong on the engineering artefacts (WGS 84, IERS, Ashby, DE440, PREM all verified against the cited documents) but omits every source the argumentative core rests on. There is no entry for Einstein and Infeld, The Evolution of Physics - the work whose conditional the second paragraph of the refutation turns on and which a reader must consult to check the "condition restored" move. There is no entry for the Wettzell G ring laser, which carries the answer to the survives=3 advocate defence. And there is no entry for the specimen list itself, which ARG-C07 and ARG-E13 both cite; R08 quotes its heading ("435 Pieces of Evidence The Earth is Not A Spinning Ball") without linking it.
holes.recommendation: Add three entries to sources[]: dict(label="Einstein & Infeld, The Evolution of Physics (1938/1966), p. 212 — the conditional, and its discharge: 'This is indeed possible!'", url="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Evolution_of_Physics"); dict(label="Di Virgilio et al., 'Overcoming 1 part in 10⁹ of Earth angular rotation rate measurement with the G Wettzell data', arXiv:2208.09134 — Allan deviation below 1 part in 10⁹", url="https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.09134"); dict(label="The specimen list, '435 Pieces of Evidence The Earth is Not A Spinning Ball' — the 28 items as bare noun phrases", url="https://withthesun33.com/about-1").

holes.quoted_phrase: WGS84 is an Earth-centred model *of an oblate rotating spheroid*
holes.description: The asterisks are markdown and the renderer does not convert them; docs/index.html shows the literal characters "*of an oblate rotating spheroid*" in the Refutation summary line. Cosmetic, but it is on the reader's first screen of that section.
holes.recommendation: WGS84 is an Earth-centred model of an oblate rotating spheroid

citation_failures: Hu & Farrell, J. Geodesy 98:102 (2024) — author order reversed in both the body text and the sources[] label (paper is Wang Hu and Jay A. Farrell, not 'Farrell & Hu'), and the '~20 metres of user-position shift at mid-latitudes' figure does not appear in the paper. The >30 m satellite-position figure does appear, but as the paper's citation of Ashby 2004.

Refutation claim 'They do not cite GPS' — contradicted by the subsection heading 'Global Positioning System: Claims and Responses' in Galileo Was Wrong Vol. II ch. 10 (archive.org ...Bennett4276) and by Sungenis's 2010 reply to Phil Plait.
Refutation and compression claim that Sungenis's later restatements name no instrument — contradicted verbatim by the Plait reply ('ask the engineers who put up the GPS').
Refutation's implicit reading of Einstein & Infeld as leaving the conditional open — the source discharges it two sentences later ('This is indeed possible!').
reviews.summary: The 2026-08-05 rewrite did its job: the refutation answers the book's conventionalism before it touches the 28 artefacts, and the primary-source work behind the passage box checks out exactly (Vol. I, Introduction, p. 9, n. 22, with Poincare and Bellarmine on the same page, as claimed). The engineering evidence is also solid — WGS 84's four defining parameters and the TR8350.2 section 3.2.4 wording, Ashby's 207.4 ns and the path-dependence quote, the ERA rate constant, the USNO 'essentially unpredictable' line, PREM, DE440 and Karney all verified against the cited documents. But two claims about the source are false and both are load-bearing. We say Sungenis and Bennett name no instrument and that his later restatements reach for Einstein without naming one; Vol. II ch. 10 has a subsection headed 'Global Positioning System: Claims and Responses', and his 2010 reply to Phil Plait says 'ask the engineers who put up the GPS' while arguing for the ECI frame — so the GPS and ECI items are the authors', not the list's, and drift_type='unsourced_addition' over-claims. And we publish the Einstein conditional as a drift when Einstein and Infeld discharge it themselves two sentences later. The MISLEADING verdict and drifted=True survive; the paragraph that carries them does not.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: PER-* records carry no `compression` block, so there is no list fragment / source sentence pair to score literally. The analogous failure is present and it is the reason I set this false. Our `ignored` field characterises Rowbotham by silence on two points — refraction and the southern sky — where the primary text speaks on both, at length, with entries in his own General Index. That is the A10 failure wearing biography clothes: we answered a simplified Rowbotham rather than the one in the book we link in `sources`. The zetetic self-definition quoted in `formation` is the one place we do test against his own wording, and it checks out verbatim against ch. I (sacred-texts za04.htm).

holes.quoted_phrase: He took the pseudonym “Parallax” — naming himself after the measurement he spent his life denying.
holes.description: This is a claim we have already retracted in public and are still publishing. review/corrections.json, entry dated 2026-08-07 (found_by: agent writing ARG-A05, batch 6), withdraws exactly this line from scripts/clusters.py: Rowbotham was signing himself 'Parallax' by the end of 1849 (Schadewald, The Plane Truth ch. 1), thirty-two years before he wrote a word about stellar parallax, and in the generic optical sense — apparent shift with change of viewpoint — which is the engine of his own perspective theory. scripts/_b6_A05.py adds that even in 1881 he does not deny observed stellar parallax: he quotes Henderson's 0″.98 and Bessel's 0″.35 approvingly and reassigns the cause. The line survives in the biography, so the Method tab now prints a retraction of a sentence the People tab still asserts. It is also the rhetorical shape our own rules warn about: a pun that reads as a fact, and one that insinuates self-contradiction in a dead man's choice of name.
holes.recommendation: He took the pseudonym “Parallax” by the end of 1849 — thirty-two years before he wrote a word about stellar parallax — and in the generic optical sense of the term: the apparent shift of an object with a change of viewpoint. That is the mechanism his own theory of perspective runs on. He named himself after something he relied on, not after something he denied.

holes.quoted_phrase: He did not engage it.
holes.description: False against the edition we link in this record's own sources[]. The 3rd ed. General Index (sacred-texts za68.htm) carries “Stars, north and south, motion of [284]” and “Southern Cross [287]”. The section itself (za48.htm, heading “Motion of Stars North and South”) argues that “all the constellations of the south—pole star included—sweep over a great southern arc and across the meridian”, states flatly that “there is no southern pole, no south pole star, and no southern circumpolar constellations”, cites Sir James Clark Ross, von Spix and von Martius, and Humboldt by name on their first-sighting latitudes for the Southern Cross, and discounts contrary reports on the ground that observers “educated to believe that the earth is a globe … do not examine such matters critically”. He engaged it for pages. This is the single first move available to a well-informed defender, and it is fatal to a project whose product is 'we went and read the primary text' — we missed something listed in the book's index. It also breaks the biography rule that `ignored` must mean data available and not engaged.
holes.recommendation: He engaged it, and disqualified it. The 3rd edition's own General Index lists “Stars, north and south, motion of [284]” and “Southern Cross [287]”; in that section he denies that any southern pole, south pole star or southern circumpolar constellation exists, explains the Southern Cross away as a constellation that has simply not yet risen, and sets aside the reports of Ross, Humboldt and von Spix and von Martius on the ground that observers “educated to believe that the earth is a globe … do not examine such matters critically.” The failure is not that he never looked south. It is that when the observation could only come out one way, the observers stopped counting as witnesses.

holes.quoted_phrase: First, atmospheric refraction over water — described in the surveying literature he was quoting from, and the reason a near-water sightline over a canal is the single worst configuration in which to test for curvature.
holes.description: Filing refraction under `ignored` contradicts the primary text and our own ARG-B04. Rowbotham's General Index (za68.htm) has “Experiments showing that refraction does not account for the elevation of objects seen at a distance of several miles [31]-36” and “Refraction can only exist where the line of sight passes from one medium into another of different density [34]” — he ran experiments on it and stated a doctrine about it. scripts/_b6_B04.py says so in our own words: he “concedes refraction outright, quantifies it, applies it, and shows his working on Cape Bonavista”, deducting 13 feet by a one-twelfth-of-target-height rule. He did not ignore refraction; he underrated it and applied it to the wrong variable (refraction scales with the square of distance, not with target height), while reprinting the Encyclopædia Britannica coefficient — “about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth” — that would have given roughly five times more. As written, the field is both wrong and weaker than the true version.
holes.recommendation: First, atmospheric refraction over water — which he underrated rather than overlooked. He reprints the Encyclopædia Britannica “Levelling” article, which gives him the mechanism and the coefficient (“at a mean … about one-seventh of the curvature of the earth”), and then substitutes an allowance of his own, one-twelfth of the target's height — the wrong variable, since refraction scales with the square of the distance and not with the height of the object. Elsewhere he denies the mechanism outright: “refraction can only exist where the line of sight passes from one medium into another of different density” (3rd ed., p. 34), which the article he had just typeset contradicts. The consequence is that he tested for curvature in the one configuration — a sightline a few inches above still water — where the effect he had cut by a factor of five is largest.

holes.quoted_phrase: the single largest share by any one author
holes.description: Contradicted by our own published figures, on the same page. Counting scripts/../data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.json: Rowbotham 65 items; Robert Sungenis is credited on 134 (31 alone, 79 with Bennett, 24 with DeLano), and docs/index.html prints exactly that on the PER-SUNGENIS card — “Tychonian lineage · 24 distinct arguments · 134 of the 461 items” — with the same number reachable from the people table a few hundred pixels away. review/corrections.json also publishes the figure ('Sungenis 128 to 134'). A superlative that the site's own table refutes is a free win for a critic, and it is avoidable: Rowbotham genuinely is the largest sole-authored source and the largest in the zetetic lane.
holes.recommendation: 65 of the 461 items on the specimen list descend from him — the largest share traced to any single-authored source, and the largest in the zetetic lane. (Robert Sungenis is credited on more items in total, 134, but across three bylines: alone, with Bennett, and with DeLano.)

holes.quoted_phrase: he ran the canal experiment in the one geometry where refraction guarantees a false null and never varied it
holes.description: “Guarantees” overstates, and it contradicts the passage we ourselves quote in ARG-B04, where the Encyclopædia Britannica tells Rowbotham refraction is “extremely variable and uncertain” and “sometimes exceeds one-fifth, and at other times does not amount to one-fifteenth”. Near-water sightlines over the Old Bedford make a false null likely and unreproducible, not certain — which is precisely why Wallace's raised-sightline repeat and Oldham's three-pole repeat came out the other way. Overstating the mechanism hands a defender a real reply: if refraction guaranteed the null, Rowbotham's own repeats would never have varied, and they did.
holes.recommendation: he ran the canal experiment in the one geometry where refraction most often manufactures a false null — a sightline inches above still water, where the correction is largest and least stable — and never varied the geometry

holes.quoted_phrase: were in every nautical almanac he could have opened
holes.description: Not accurate about the artefact named. A nautical almanac gives ephemerides and tabulated star positions; it does not depict circumpolar trails or centres of rotation. The southern circumpolar motion was available to him in southern star charts, in navigators' narratives, and — as za48.htm shows — in the published accounts of Ross, Humboldt and von Spix and von Martius that he quotes himself. Naming the wrong artefact in a sentence whose whole force is 'this was available to him' is the kind of detail a defender checks first.
holes.recommendation: and were recorded in the southern star charts, navigators' narratives and published expedition accounts available to him — several of which he quotes

holes.quoted_phrase: Dubay quotes him by name in nine of 200 proofs and closes the list with him.
holes.description: Two specific quantitative claims with no source on the record: sources[] lists sacred-texts, Schadewald, the LoC guide and the Bedford Level Wikipedia article, and no Dubay edition anywhere. I could verify part of it and not the rest. The archive.org full text (200proofsearthisnotaspinningballericdubay) names Rowbotham in proofs 62, 63, 64, 65, 66 and 130, but every fetch truncated at about proof 132, so neither 'nine' nor 'closes the list with him' could be checked. Under the biography rules an unsourced specific is moderate; leaving a countable claim uncited on a page whose product is provenance is worse than the count being off.
holes.recommendation: Dubay names him in the text of his 200 Proofs — proofs 62–66 and 130 among them — and quotes Zetetic Astronomy directly. [And add to sources: dict(label=“Dubay, 200 Proofs Earth is Not a Spinning Ball — full text scan”, url=“https://archive.org/details/200proofsearthisnotaspinningballericdubay”). Restore the count 'nine' and the 'closes the list with him' claim only with a proof number attached.]

holes.quoted_phrase: his 8-inches-per-mile formula is correct arithmetic, honestly sourced.
holes.description: This is DEEPER, not KERNEL, and the KERNEL-tier fact is already established elsewhere in our own repo and missing here. scripts/_b6_B04.py documents that on the lighthouse table Rowbotham does the geometry properly — he subtracts the observer's own horizon distance before squaring (“Allowing 16 feet for the altitude of the observer … 5 miles must be taken from the 30 miles”), converts the light lists' nautical miles into statute miles each time, and applies an explicit refraction deduction with the working shown — and that every one of those steps is gone from the modern list items that descend from him. 'His arithmetic was borrowed and correct' is the easy version; 'the founder's procedure was more careful than his tradition's, and the tradition dropped the corrections he made' is the specific true thing that also points the other way, because it makes the degradation-in-transit thesis a fact about his own lineage.
holes.recommendation: His insistence on going and looking is, in the abstract, the correct instinct — and his 8-inches-per-mile formula is correct arithmetic, honestly sourced from the Encyclopædia Britannica article on Levelling. The sharpest thing in his favour is procedural. On the lighthouse table he does the geometry the way it should be done: he subtracts his own horizon distance before squaring (“Allowing 16 feet for the altitude of the observer … 5 miles must be taken from the 30 miles”), converts the light lists' nautical miles into statute miles every time, and applies a refraction deduction with the working shown. Almost every modern list descending from him has dropped all three steps. The founder was more careful than his tradition.

citation_failures: FAILED — 'He did not engage it' (southern sky): contradicted by the 3rd ed. we link in sources[]. General Index (https://sacred-texts.com/earth/za/za68.htm): 'Stars, north and south, motion of [284]', 'Southern Cross [287]', 'Stars of varied colours near the Southern Cross [194]'. Section text at https://sacred-texts.com/earth/za/za48.htm, heading 'Motion of Stars North and South'.

FAILED — refraction filed under `ignored`: contradicted by General Index entries 'Experiments showing that refraction does not account for the elevation of objects seen at a distance of several miles [31]-36' and 'Refraction can only exist where the line of sight passes from one medium into another of different density [34]' (za68.htm), and by our own ARG-B04 text.

FAILED — 'the single largest share by any one author': data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.json gives Rowbotham 65, Sungenis 134 across three bylines; docs/index.html prints '134 of the 461 items' on the PER-SUNGENIS card.
FAILED (already retracted) — 'naming himself after the measurement he spent his life denying': withdrawn in review/corrections.json 2026-08-07 and in scripts/_b6_A05.py; still live in people.py.

UNCHECKED — 'Dubay quotes him by name in nine of 200 proofs and closes the list with him.' No Dubay source on the record. archive.org item 200proofsearthisnotaspinningballericdubay (_djvu.txt) names Rowbotham in proofs 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 130, but every fetch truncated near proof 132; flatearth.ws/eric-dubay and flatearthinsanity.blogspot.com truncated at proofs 125 and 43 respectively. Count of nine and the closing claim not verified, not disproved.

UNCHECKED — WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1849 imprint 'By “Parallax” [pseud.]. Birmingham: W. Cornish. 16 pp.' Listed in this record's works[] but not re-verified this pass; ARG-B01 already records that the pamphlet is catalogued and not digitised anywhere reachable.

VERIFIED — zetetic self-definition: ch. I, https://sacred-texts.com/earth/za/za04.htm. 'The term Zetetic is derived from the Greek verb Zeteo; which means to search, or examine; to proceed only by inquiry; to take nothing for granted' and '“Theoretic,” the meaning of which is, speculative--imaginary--not tangible,--scheming, but not proving.' Our quotation is accurate; it stops before '—scheming, but not proving' without an ellipsis, which does not change the sense.

VERIFIED — Encyclopædia Britannica 'Levelling' as the source of the 8-inches figure: General Index entry 'Levelling, quotation from the Encyclopædia Britannica [34]' (za68.htm), corroborated by scripts/deep_batch1.py and scripts/_b6_B04.py which reproduce the extract.
VERIFIED — dates '1816 – 23 December 1884': en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Rowbotham; LoC name authority 'Parallax, 1816-1884' (id.loc.gov/authorities/names/no2007094903).
VERIFIED — '65 of the 461 items': recounted from data/flat-earth-origins-provenance.json.
VERIFIED — Wallace 1870 (sightline raised to 13 ft, mid-point marker) and Oldham 1901: consistent with the Bedford Level experiment source already cited on the record.
reviews.summary: PER-ROWBOTHAM has two critical holes and they are the same kind of failure. First, `formation` still prints the 'named himself after the measurement he spent his life denying' line that review/corrections.json publicly retracted on 2026-08-07 — our Method tab now retracts a sentence our People tab asserts. Second, `ignored` says of the southern sky 'He did not engage it', which is false against the very edition this record links: the 3rd ed. General Index lists 'Stars, north and south, motion of [284]' and 'Southern Cross [287]', and Rowbotham argues the point at length, citing Ross, Humboldt and von Spix and von Martius by name. The same field files refraction under 'ignored' when his own index shows experiments on it at pp. 31–36 and our ARG-B04 says in our own words that he conceded, quantified and applied it. Add a superlative in `legacy` that the site's own people table refutes (Rowbotham 65 vs Sungenis 134), and this needs a major rewrite of `formation`, `ignored`, `legacy` and the kernel. The bio's underlying thesis — a real method with a stopping rule — mostly survives, but 'It was stopped early' is the wrong diagnosis: he kept going and disqualified the witnesses instead. Advocate mode (rates 5): 'You missed what is in the index of the book you link, and your own corrections page refutes your own biography — why should I trust the rest?' The preemptive fix is the rewrite itself, plus naming the southern-sky section explicitly so the strongest evidence against him is shown to be evidence he saw and rejected.

reviews.hedge_rule_note: A biography has no list fragment, so the rule applies in its analogue form: are we characterising the person at the strength our source states, or at a hardened version of it? We harden. Bouw's obituary (Biblical Astronomer no. 84) says only "Through Walter's pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure and the Michelson-Morley experiments, Walter may truly be called the father of modern geocentricity." Two hedges — "pioneering work in pointing out" (not coining) and "may truly be called" — and we render them as the flat assertions "Coined 'Airy's failure'" (role line, always visible, no toggle) and "Bouw's obituary of him credits the coinage by name" (legacy). Our own scripts/works.py gets this right — it says "Earliest DOCUMENTED use of the phrase" and explicitly flags the 1968/1970 Airy Reconsidered precursor as unverified — so the honest form already exists in the codebase and people.py states the stronger claim anyway. That is hedge_dropped, committed by us, against our own cited source. Separately, van der Kamp himself in Biblical Astronomer no. 66 uses "Airy's failure" as if it were established vocabulary rather than his own label, which is weak but points the same way.
reviews.summary: Two critical holes. The `ignored` field says van der Kamp "passed over stellar aberration" — but De Labore Solis (1988), the only work on his card, is a book about stellar aberration, treating Bradley at pp. 27ff and proposing that "the starry sphere swings" instead of the Earth, and our own cluster A04 credits him as the originator of an aberration argument that renders on the same card under "Arguments originating here". And the legacy field's coinage credit is not in the obituary we cite for it. Three further majors: the role line hardens the same unsourced coinage claim, `ignored` claims "both nulls had been predicted in advance" when nothing predicted the Michelson-Morley null in advance, and `had` claims "both nulls were genuinely awkward for the aether physics of their own moment" when Airy's null was the result Fresnel's dominant partial-drag theory predicted — which contradicts our own ARG-A03 headline. The core attribution (24 items, six arguments, founder of the movement, underdetermination kernel) checks out and holds.
citation_failures: FAILED — Bouw's obituary, The Biblical Astronomer no. 84 (https://www.geocentricity.com/ba1/no084/obits.pdf), is cited in `legacy` as crediting van der Kamp with coining 'Airy's failure'. It contains no coinage credit. Its only Airy sentence is: 'Through Walter's pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure and the Michelson-Morley experiments, Walter may truly be called the father of modern geocentricity.' The 'father of modern geocentricity' half of our sentence is verified; the coinage half is not in the document.

FAILED — 'he read Popper and Dingle' (`formation`). Dingle verified: De Labore Solis quotes him at length on the twin paradox, pp. 58-59. Popper is not named in De Labore Solis on two separate targeted fetches, is not in Biblical Astronomer no. 66, and no other source is offered. The philosophers of science van der Kamp actually names are Dingle, Polanyi, Russell, Mach, Eddington and Herman Dooyeweerd.

FAILED (unsourced) — the kernel asserts Bouw 'conceded in print that the model is observationally equivalent to heliocentrism'. No source for it in PER-VANDERKAMP.sources. Worse, the site's supporting record scripts/works.py WRK-BOUW-1992 still carries url='https://creation.com/geocentric-gobbledegook' with the note 'Concedes the model is observationally equivalent to heliocentrism' — the exact citation review/corrections.json entry 1 (2026-08-02) retracted as being Faulkner reviewing Marshall Hall. The correction was applied to source-genealogy.md and not to works.py, so the retracted citation is still live in the build.

UNCHECKED, not failed — 'Sungenis inherits the term without attribution' (`legacy`). WebFetch on the archive.org scan of Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I returns only a partial read (it reported finding neither 'Airy's failure' nor 'van der Kamp' anywhere, which is inconsistent with our own ARG-A03 passage quoting the book's 'Airy's failure' sentence, so the fetch is not covering the text). Whether GWW credits van der Kamp in a footnote, acknowledgement or bibliography is unresolved.

UNCHECKED, not failed — 'He also passed over Michelson-Gale-Pearson (1925)'. Absent from De Labore Solis (1988) and from Biblical Astronomer no. 66 on targeted fetches; the 37 Bulletins of the Tychonian Society (1971-1984) are not available online for search, so this is an unsourced negative across a corpus we have not seen.

VERIFIED — dates 5 March 1913 - 26 January 1998 (obituary); Tychonian Society founded 1971 (geocentricity.com society history: 'The Tychonian Society was founded in Canada in 1971 by the late Dutch-Canadian educator, Walter van der Kamp'); Bulletin edited to March 1984, No. 37 his last (obituary); 'went nowhere fast' is van der Kamp's own words quoted by Bouw ('In Walter's own words, it "went nowhere fast"'); ~fifty people and institutions, four encouraging responses (obituary); thirty-two pages, January 1968 (van der Kamp, Whys and Wherefores of Geocentrism, part 1: 'in January 1968 I privately published a thirty-two page brochure, The heart of the Matter'); affirming the consequent, De Labore Solis p. 28 ('Logically considered, this conclusion uses that invalid theoretical syllogism, the modus ponendo ponens'); 24 items across six clusters (A01, A03, A04, A26, R01, R03) confirmed by running scripts/assign.py against scripts/clusters.py.

holes.quoted_phrase: and over stellar aberration, which exists at all only because the Earth moves
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `ignored`. This says van der Kamp passed over stellar aberration. He did the opposite: De Labore Solis: Airy's Failure Reconsidered (1988) — the sole entry in his works[] and the work whose title we put on his card — is a book-length treatment of stellar aberration. It walks through Bradley and Molyneux at the chimney stack (p. 27), builds the whole argument on the aberration angle ('If the angle in this manner obtained is larger than the one measured by Bradley, the Earth indeed orbits... If no different value is registered, then the starry sphere swings', p. 29), and endorses the Boscovich water-telescope test as the decisive way to settle it. He kept the phenomenon and relocated the motion. The field renders under the heading 'The data they had, and passed over — Available to them, and not engaged. This is the difference between being wrong and being unserious', i.e. we are calling him unserious about the one topic he wrote a book on. And render.py prints 'Arguments originating here' on the same card, which for this person includes ARG-A04 'Stellar aberration is optical/parallax, not Earth's motion'. A defender needs one click to show the card contradicting itself.
holes.recommendation: Replace the clause with: "He also passed over Michelson–Gale–Pearson (1925), a positive detection of the Earth's rotation published in the Astrophysical Journal — it appears neither in De Labore Solis nor in his later Biblical Astronomer restatement. Stellar aberration he did not pass over: De Labore Solis is a book about it. What he passed over is what aberration is evidence of. He kept Bradley's phenomenon and moved the motion — then the starry sphere swings — and never accounted for why the swing should imitate the Earth's orbit so exactly. His own successor declined to follow him there: Bouw rebuilt the model to keep aberration."
holes.short_summary: Says he ignored aberration; his only cited book is about it

holes.quoted_phrase: Bouw's obituary of him credits the coinage by name
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `legacy`. The obituary at https://www.geocentricity.com/ba1/no084/obits.pdf, which is the source we list for this, does not credit van der Kamp with coining anything. Its single Airy sentence is: 'Through Walter's pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure and the Michelson-Morley experiments, Walter may truly be called the father of modern geocentricity.' Bouw is using the phrase as settled vocabulary and crediting the work, not the word. This is our own severity-critical category — a claim about what a source says that the source does not say — and it is the sole support for the coinage claim that also occupies the always-visible role line. The same sentence also carries a universal negative ('exists nowhere in the physics literature') that our own works.py states more carefully as 'earliest DOCUMENTED use'.
holes.recommendation: Replace both sentences with: "“Airy's failure” is not a term of art in physics: no use of it as a name for the 1871 water-telescope experiment has been found outside this movement, and the earliest documented occurrence is van der Kamp's own 1988 subtitle. Bouw's obituary does not credit him with the coinage, but it uses the phrase as settled vocabulary, credits his “pioneering work in pointing out the geocentric nature of Airy's failure,” and calls him “the father of modern geocentricity.”"
holes.short_summary: Obituary cited for a coinage credit it does not contain

holes.quoted_phrase: Coined “Airy's failure”.
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `role`. render.py prints `role` as a bare paragraph directly under the name, outside every <details> toggle — it is the one line every reader of the People tab sees. It states the coinage flatly. Nothing we hold supports 'coined': the obituary does not say it, works.py itself records that the 1968/1970 precursor Airy Reconsidered is titled without the word and that 'whether the phrase appears inside it is unverified', and van der Kamp's own Biblical Astronomer no. 66 article uses the phrase as though it were an inherited designation. Reader impact is maximal and the correct wording already exists elsewhere in our codebase.
holes.recommendation: Replace `role` with: "Founder of modern geocentrism. Earliest documented user of the phrase “Airy's failure”."
holes.short_summary: Role line asserts a coinage no source supports

holes.quoted_phrase: That both nulls had been predicted in advance, by two different theories
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `ignored`, opening sentence. Nothing predicted the Michelson-Morley null in advance. Lorentz-FitzGerald contraction was constructed after the 1887 result to accommodate it, and special relativity postdates it by eighteen years. The sentence's own two supporting clauses — Fresnel's coefficient, and relativity's transformation of ray direction — are both about Airy's null, so the paragraph asserts 'both' and substantiates one. This is the first line of the accusation section and it hands a defender a free hit ('predicted in advance by whom?').
holes.recommendation: Replace the first two sentences with: "That Airy's null had been predicted in advance. Fresnel's dragging coefficient, published decades before Airy ran the experiment and already confirmed by Fizeau in 1851, predicts exactly the result Airy got; special relativity predicts it again from the transformation of ray direction between frames. The Michelson–Morley null is a different case, and he treats it as the same one: nothing predicted that result in advance, but relativity accounts for it without a stationary Earth, so it fails to discriminate rather than favouring him."
holes.short_summary: Michelson-Morley null was not predicted in advance

holes.quoted_phrase: both nulls were genuinely awkward for the aether physics of their own moment
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `had`. False for Airy, and it contradicts our own ARG-A03. Airy's 1871 null was the result the dominant aether theory of 1871 — Fresnel's partial drag, confirmed by Fizeau in 1851 — already predicted. It was awkward only for Klinkerfues's stationary-aether variant, which is the whole point of A03's kernel ('the null is the predicted result'). Conceding in the biography that Airy's null embarrassed the aether physics of its day gives away the central claim of the argument page, and a critic assembling 'this site contradicts itself' would start here.
holes.recommendation: Replace the sentence with: "He identified correctly that Michelson–Morley returned a null, that Airy's 1871 water-telescope experiment returned a null, and that the Michelson–Morley null was genuinely awkward for the aether physics of its own moment. He was also right that Airy's test was a real test of a real prediction — Klinkerfues's, from a stationary aether — and not a formality."
holes.short_summary: Airy's null was predicted by 1871 aether physics, not awkward for it

holes.quoted_phrase: he read Popper and Dingle to sharpen the point
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `formation`. Dingle is solid — De Labore Solis quotes him at length on the twin paradox, pp. 58-59. Popper is unsourced: not named in De Labore Solis on two targeted fetches, not in Biblical Astronomer no. 66, and not attested anywhere else we hold. It is a claim about what a real person read. The named thinkers he does use are Dingle, Polanyi, Russell, Mach, Eddington and Herman Dooyeweerd — and Dooyeweerd, the Reformed philosopher, independently corroborates the preceding sentence about coming to geocentrism through Reformed theology, so the sourced version is also the stronger one.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "and he read Dingle, Polanyi and the Reformed philosopher Herman Dooyeweerd to sharpen the point"
holes.short_summary: Popper unsourced; Dooyeweerd is attested and stronger

holes.quoted_phrase: 32 pages — to about fifty people in 1967
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `formation`. Two objects conflated. The obituary: 'In 1967 Walter privately published and circulated a rough draft of a booklet called The Heart of the Matter. Walter sent it to about fifty people and institutions, from whom he garnered four encouraging responses. The booklet was printed in January 1968.' Van der Kamp's own history: 'in January 1968 I privately published a thirty-two page brochure, The heart of the Matter.' So the thing that went to fifty people was a 1967 rough draft; the thirty-two-page brochure is January 1968, and Faulkner's account agrees. Our clusters.py meanwhile dates the same work to 1968 in three places (A01, R01, R03), so the site states 1967 and 1968 for one object. On a project whose standing warning is that edition dating is the trap that has caught us four times, this is the same class of error.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "and circulated a rough draft of his first brochure, The Heart of the Matter, to about fifty people and institutions in 1967, drawing four encouraging replies; the printed thirty-two-page version followed in January 1968"
holes.short_summary: 1967 draft and 32-page Jan 1968 brochure conflated

holes.quoted_phrase: conceded in print that the model is observationally equivalent to heliocentrism
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `kernel`. This is the load-bearing claim of the whole steelman — why_it_doesnt_save_claim is built entirely on it — and it is a claim about a named third party with no citation in this record's sources[]. It also recurs at the site level: scripts/works.py WRK-BOUW-1992 still carries url='https://creation.com/geocentric-gobbledegook' with the note 'Concedes the model is observationally equivalent to heliocentrism', which is precisely the citation review/corrections.json entry 1 (2026-08-02) retracted after finding the page is Faulkner reviewing Marshall Hall. The correction was applied to source-genealogy.md only; the retracted URL is still in the build.
holes.recommendation: Add to PER-VANDERKAMP sources[]: dict(label="Faulkner, 'Geocentrism and Creation', Journal of Creation 15(2), 2001 — states the essential difference is a coordinate change", url="https://creation.com/geocentrism-and-creation") and dict(label="Bowden, Journal of Creation 16(2), 2002, p. 80 — concedes the Michelson–Gale measurement", url="https://creation.com/images/pdfs/tj/j16_2/j16_2_79-81.pdf"), and separately replace the WRK-BOUW-1992 url in scripts/works.py, which still points at the citation corrections.json entry 1 withdrew.
holes.short_summary: Bouw concession uncited here; retracted URL still live in works.py

holes.quoted_phrase: Sungenis inherits the term without attribution
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `legacy`. Sungenis is living, and on a provenance site 'inherits the term without attribution' reads as an accusation about citation practice. It is an unverified universal negative: it requires that Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I credits van der Kamp nowhere — not in a footnote, not in the acknowledgements, not in the bibliography. WebFetch could not full-text search the archive.org scan (it reported finding neither 'Airy's failure' nor 'van der Kamp' at all, which contradicts our own ARG-A03 passage quoting the book's 'Airy's failure' sentence, so the fetch is not reading the text). The substantive point — the passive voice hiding the caller, and the false gloss about the experimenters' thoughts — survives without the negative and does not need it.
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "Sungenis and Bennett carry the term into Galileo Was Wrong Vol. I, writing that the experiment “was called” that — a passive that leaves the caller unnamed — and adding the gloss, false, that it reflects “the thoughts of the experimenters during this era.”"
holes.short_summary: Unverified 'without attribution' claim about a living author

holes.quoted_phrase: the early issues handwritten and photocopied
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `formation`. The obituary we cite says the Bulletin 'was mimeographed and the \'society\' consisted at that time of probably no more than a hundred people', and that 'In the summer of 1974, after an interval of two years, Bulletins No. 6 was typed and stenciled'. Mimeograph and stencil are not photocopying. The only 'longhand' in the obituary is about his personal letters, not the Bulletin. Small, but it is a detail contradicted by the single source on the card, and the sourced version carries a better fact (the hundred-person readership).
holes.recommendation: Replace with: "He founded the Tychonian Society in 1971 and edited its Bulletin through March 1984 — thirty-seven issues, mimeographed, for what Bouw put at “probably no more than a hundred people.”"
holes.short_summary: Bulletin was mimeographed and stencilled, not photocopied

holes.quoted_phrase: works=["WRK-VDK-1988"]
holes.description: scripts/people.py, PER-VANDERKAMP `works`. Three of his six clusters — A01, R01 and R03, together 19 of his 24 items — name 'The Heart of the Matter' as originator_work, and A04 names 'Bulletin of the Tychonian Society'. Named as originator_work for A01, R01 and R03.") and "WRK-VDK-BULLETIN": dict(author="PER-VANDERKAMP", year="1971–1984", pd=False, title="Bulletin of the Tychonian Society", imprint="Mimeographed, Pitt Meadows, B.C.
